#6772. Peptides Are About to Flood the Market. And Bro Science Is Coming for Us All

This past February, Health and Human Services secretary and MAHA Final Boss Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made it known during an interview with Joe Rogan that he intended to direct the FDA to lessen restrictions on a handful of peptides that had previously been banned under the Biden administration. The peptides in question, which included influencer favorites BPC-157 and TB-500 (collectively dubbed the “Wolverine stack” for their reported regenerative properties) had been placed on the FDA’s “do not compound” list, effectively barring pharmacies from providing them to patients, for reasons including serious safety concerns and a general lack of comprehensive human trials. No new research had emerged to prompt RFK Jr.’s announcement. Rather, the HHS head, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, believed the drugs should never have been banned in the first place—a decision that, in his view, was responsible for the subsequent explosion of a thriving black market for peptides online. So, for the past eight months, healthcare professionals have been waiting with baited breath for the other shoe to drop.

And then this past Wednesday hit with a thud.

In a seemingly unilateral decision—one that flies in the face of FDA scientists who warned earlier this year of the potential, largely unknown implications of effectively releasing scantily researched injectables into the wild—RFK announced that patients (or anyone with a prescription) would now have access to six of these previously outlawed peptides through a loophole-like policy called “enforcement discretion.”

Internet-famous peptides like BPC-157 and TB-500 might be the future, but right now they’re a shot in the dark.

To explain exactly what that means, I called up Edgar J. Asebey, a life sciences regulatory and transactional attorney at the law firm Frier Levitt. “I always tell people I speak three languages: English, Spanish, and FDA,” he says. “Enforcement discretion means that the FDA will not enforce a certain regulation. And in this case, it's the prohibition against compounding these six peptides. That's what it boils down to.”

Enforcement discretion is typically considered a break-in-case-of-emergency avenue for freeing up availability of certain drugs when warranted, Asebey says. “For example, when the GLP-1s were in shortage, pharmacies could lawfully compound exact copies of Ozempic and Wegovy.” In other words, the six peptides in question—BPC-157, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax, KPV, and Epitalon—are still categorically unapproved by the FDA for human use, but Kennedy is going to allow pharmacies to dispense them as if they were, until further notice.

While this may seem outrageous, not everybody is outraged. For one, obviously, peptides are big business. (Market research firm Grand View Research valued the global peptide industry at over 140 billion in 2025, with North America accounting for more than 60% of that revenue.) Aside from that, however, one of Kennedy’s stated motivations is to reduce people’s incentive to procure peptides from regulation-skirting med spas and the dark corners of the internet, where substances like BPC-157 can be ordered to your door with the same ease as buying paper towels on Amazon. Since July, the Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies (ASOP Global) has tracked nearly 21,000 peptide listings across more than 300 websites, including upwards of 8,800 listings for BPC-157 alone. As you might imagine, quality and safety present serious concerns to anyone choosing to go that route—that is, beyond the potential risks of using these peptides even in their purest forms—hence the burgeoning cottage industry of peptide purity trackers and testing services.

“My view is simple,” says Meena Verma, MD, MPH, a board-certified internist and nephrologist, and founder of Blue Coast Longevity in Newport Beach, CA. “People are already using these peptides, and there is an urgent need for harm reduction. Allowing licensed pharmacies to compound them under physician guidance means patients can now have an accountable channel with assurance of safety.”

But how this policy change plays out may not be quite that simple. Whereas purveyors of these six peptides—whether operating online or in person—were previously identifiable as unlawful simply by virtue of offering the unapproved drugs, Kennedy's mandate to usher these peptides into the broader health marketplace muddies the waters, making it harder for consumers to tell which providers are legit. "The online market is already flush with illegal actors who now can more easily hide amongst the masses with limited risk of getting caught,” reads a statement that ASOP Global released within hours of Kennedy’s announcement on Wednesday. “Without enhanced and consistent new enforcement of the market, today’s policy will allow criminals to hide amongst the newly compliant.”

Kennedy’s plan notes that compounding pharmacies will be subject to specific safety criteria, like requiring that the peptides are manufactured in an FDA-registered facility, but as The New York Times has pointed out, “the step basically only requires a manufacturer to notify the agency of its address.”

When you consider the scale of the peptide market alongside the reality of what the FDA is actually capable of policing with its post-DOGE workforce—following the laying off of 3,500 workers—it begs the question of whether the criteria laid out in Kennedy’s plan will even matter at all.

"For one, if you're going to have guardrails, you're going to need to enforce them,” says Leigh Verbois, PhD, ASOP's global board chair and the former director of the FDA’s Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response. “There needs to be resources to actually take action, full stop. And two, the organizations that are intended to utilize those guardrails may not even look at them. There are too many [compounding pharmacies] to be able to enforce against."

But I’d argue there’s something far more dangerous, and more consequential, than the possibility that this latest decision might inadvertently feed the back-alley peptide market rather than curtail it. After all, not everyone is out there looking for peptides. (I know I’m certainly not.) But we all need to go to the doctor at some point—something that could now conceivably land you on the receiving end of a prescription for a drug that has never even been researched in a human being.

“To classify this as safe would just be irresponsible,” says Motisola Lewis, MD, an Internal Medicine physician and the founder of Lewis Medical NY. “If you have a cancer patient—say, a woman who just had breast cancer—and she wants to fix her knee that just got injured, and she ends up getting an injection of BPC-157. This is known to promote tissue growth. This is known to promote vascularization. We don't know what effect it has on a patient who has had cancer. Does it promote cancer growth? We don't know.”

Peptides are blurring the line between supplements and prescription drugs.

The inescapable irony here is that not long ago it was the MAHA movement that was encouraging people to be skeptical of mainstream medical providers, to do your own research before just allowing your doctor to jab you with a COVID-19 vaccine. And now, by injecting these six potentially harmful peptides into mainstream medicine, where they will be readily available to physicians with varying degrees of familiarity with the substances themselves and the politics surrounding them, the administration has gone ahead and given the rest of us a very real reason to do our own research. Sure, this only applies to peptides at the moment, but a precedent has been set. And you can no longer afford not to pay attention. None of us can.

“When patients walk into their physician's office, or talk to a telehealth provider, they have an assumption that there will be a positive outcome—that the patient is seeking and that the physician is intending to meet,” says Dr. Verbois. “But without any of the quality, safety, or efficacy, it's completely the wild, wild west. If anyone in my family, in need of a drug for treatment, were to ask me if they should go down a path of utilizing a peptide of this sort, my response to them would be, ‘Never. Instead, seek out a treatment for that disease that's been shown to be safe and effective. These have not been, and you are putting yourself in harm's way.’”

“Some weeks will be better than others, and that’s okay. I’m only human,” she wrote, in part.

Maura Higgins is opening up after tackling her Disney Night choreography as Tinker Bell on Dancing With the Stars. The Love Island alum got candid in a lengthy statement she penned alongside a carousel of behind-the-scenes photos from Monday night’s episode after fans criticized her performance in Team Slaytopia’s group number.

“This week was definitely one of the toughest I’ve had so far. The Traitors star uplifted her pro partner and “biggest support throughout this journey,” Mark Ballas, before seemingly addressing harsh feedback from viewers who criticized her “low energy” performances in both of her numbers this week.

#6769. Brittany Howard and Anna-Maria Babcock’s Tennessee Wedding Was a Celebration of Their Mexican and Southern Roots

Given their day jobs, musician Brittany Howard and record executive and artist Anna-Maria Babcock’s meet-cute feels entirely appropriate: they first crossed paths at a concert. “We met at a friend’s album release show on October 10, 2023, at The Blue Room in Nashville,” Anna-Maria explains. Brittany, who is best known as the lead singer and guitarist of Alabama Shakes, was helping out at the merch table after the show. “I walked up to the table and a mutual friend introduced us by putting our hands in each other’s while asking, ‘Have y’all met yet?’ It was love at first sight for the both of us,” says Anna-Maria. A few days later, the two went on their first real date and fell in love over pizza rolls and mocktails at Brittany’s home. “The first date that never ended!” Anna-Maria jokes.

Just over a year later, Anna-Maria proposed on November 15, 2024, at Smith Lake in Alabama. After an extensive tour year, she encouraged Brittany to come with her on a fishing trip. “Little did I know, this was more than a fishing trip,” says Brittany. “On the first night of our stay, under the last full supermoon of the year, Anna-Maria got on one knee in a freshly made wood-fired hot tub. After the proposal, I said, ‘yes!’” Despite spending hours preparing the hot tub, the couple jumped out to share the news with their friends and family. “All those hours to prepare the hot tub, just to get out after five minutes! It’s okay though,” says Brittany. “We got all of our life together to make another fire.” Adds Anna-Maria, “Brittany followed up with a double proposal (the gay way) during our trip to Portugal for my birthday just a few months later! I also said yes to forever!”

Anna-Maria and Brittany spent the next two years planning their perfect wedding celebration. The big day arrived on October 24, 2026, at the Southall Farm & Inn in Franklin, Tennessee. The couple describes planning as both “so much fun” and “a lot of work.” “We had a hand in every single design aspect of the night; we wanted the space to feel like us,” says Anna-Maria. Alongside planner Carly Pickett, the brides lent their handwriting to save-the-dates, made an ofrenda to honor ancestors, and hand-selected planters from home to fill with florals. Says Anna-Maria, “We wanted our people to feel like they knew exactly whose wedding they were at—one that was very Black, very Mexican, and very queer!”

The couple also wanted to feel their cultures reflected through their fashion choices for the wedding weekend. “We wanted to feel gender affirmed, beautiful, sexy, and ourselves,” says Anna-Maria. “We were not interested in traditional wedding wear, so designing our own garments and sourcing from small women-owned, Black-owned, Indigenous-owned, and queer-owned brands was extremely important to us.” She adds that wearing family heirlooms was also an important part of their wardrobe curation. “We wanted our ancestors to be honored in this space,” says Anna-Maria.

For her wedding look, Brittany worked with stylist Courtney Mays to craft a custom gown with a detailed bodice and dramatic off-the-shoulder cape. Later in the evening, she changed into a bright red ensemble with diaphanous flowing fabric designed alongside Loulette Bride. Anna-Maria found a halter Danielle Frankel dress at Nashville bridal salon The Dress Theory. To walk down the aisle, she paired it with a veil from queer-owned brand Tanner Fletcher.

When Brittany changed into her red reception look, Anna-Maria changed into a textured, red dress of her own that was designed alongside Mays. The brides also created a mood board for their wedding party and even helped style some looks for them. “We wanted our wedding party to be more concerned with having fun, letting loose, and connecting with others—not with whether or not they liked the outfits we picked out for them that they will never wear again,” says Anna-Maria.

The weekend kicked off with an intimate sunset dinner overlooking the Tennessee hills. The rehearsal dinner was hosted by Anna-Maria’s parents, Sylvia and Randy Babcock. “We ate delicious Mexican food, danced to cumbia, and cried hysterically as our wedding party, parents, and grandmas expressed their love for us,” recalls Anna-Maria. “The feeling of watching your blood family and chosen family fall in love with each other was nothing short of magical and healing.”

The ceremony took place the next day in a meadow along a creek. Guests were surrounded by nature and gathered amongst florals that lined the aisle. “We walked to everyone’s smiling, expectant faces under a beautiful fall sunset while the mariachi band played a rendition of ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face,’” describes Brittany. The couple walked towards one another on the arms of their parents. “When we got to the altar, we then encouraged our two-year-old nephew, who was the ring bearer, to come meet us up there! Holding a wooden fish ring box—the one Anna-Maria gifted me when she proposed—in one hand and picking his nose with the other, he joyfully ran up to us while stopping to smell the flowers halfway down the aisle,” she recalls. “A perfect reminder of what’s important in life. Always stop to smell the flowers.”

Anna-Maria’s Tía Pinky read a poem written by the bride’s late grandfather, Roberto. “His words reminded us of why we are here and why it’s important to not waste time with the ones we love,” says Brittany. Remembers Anna-Maria, “I was so giddy and my cheeks hurt from smiling so much. I felt so excited and humbled watching our family grow right before my eyes. I felt proud of myself for never giving up on love. Little us would be so proud.” Brittany emphasizes that she felt “full of pride” throughout the ceremony and as if the moment was “magical and sacred.” This magic was made complete as a rainbow appeared in the sky once the brides kissed. “We think that was a little sign from the ancestors that we were all right where we were supposed to be,” says Anna-Maria.

The mariachi band led the way towards the reception, followed by the newlyweds and their community as “Isn’t She Lovely” played. “We danced and sang our way around the lake to cocktail hour where the sun finally went down over the hill in a blaze of pinks, reds, purples and oranges,” recalls Brittany. “The moon was so bright it would stop us in our tracks.” Cocktail hour followed with reunions, hugs, and tears of joy. “We drank and danced to cumbia before walking over to the ofrenda to pay our respects to our loved ones who couldn’t physically be there with us,” says Anna-Maria. “We could feel their spirit throughout the entire night.”

The reception moved indoors for a dinner full of Mexican and Southern cuisine, along with a night full of music. “Lloyd Buchanan, who plays with my touring bands, led an incredible band during reception where he played our first dance song, ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face’ by Roberta Flack in a hauntingly beautiful rendition,” says Brittany. “This song also happens to be Anna-Maria’s grandparents Maria and Roberto’s wedding song. Anna-Maria and I both took turns dancing to the end of the song with her 86-year-old grandmother.” She recalls, “There wasn’t a dry eye in the room.” The newlyweds then danced with their fathers and also did a special dance with their moms to “I Say A Little Prayer” by Aretha Franklin before welcoming all their guests onto the floor.

Special performances went on throughout the evening. “I come from a long line of family drummers, and my Uncle Scott and little brother Robert graced the stage, playing drums to Sinatra’s ‘Fly Me To The Moon’ and Bobby Caldwell’s ‘What You Won’t Do For Love’ respectively,” says Anna-Maria. “The very first time I saw live music, it was at an underground jazz club in DC where my uncle would play with his big band. When Uncle Scott was up there playing at the reception, I was instantly transported back to that club when I was a little girl.”

The after-party was held at Dottie’s, a speakeasy on the grounds of the property. The couple’s friend, DJ T1BG, spun until 2 a.m. “The room was vibrant with belly laughs, dirty dancing, wigs, bologna sandwiches, hot dogs, and deep conversations around the fire pit,” says Anna-Maria. “Our feet were aching—with Brittany nursing my blisters at 4 a.m.—but our hearts were exploding with love.” Adds Brittany, “We were so moved seeing our family and friends from thousands of miles away dancing together and making their own relationships. It’s the very thing we wanted our wedding to embody: communion.”

While the brides share they are truly excited to settle into their married lives with each other and enjoy the simplicity and joy of being newlyweds, they also emphasize how grateful they are to share their love today: “Getting married in the South as Black and brown lesbians feels extra heavy in today’s political climate. We live in a country where we have a Supreme Court justice who wants to ban interracial marriage. We live in a state where LGBTQIA+ rights are under attack, and the local government is working with ICE to tear families apart. We aren’t going anywhere. This is our home and we are here to stay. We are here to dig in deeper—into love and into our beautifully diverse and queer community. We believe love always wins, and it certainly felt like that at our wedding. While we were the first gay couple to get married at this venue in Franklin, Tennessee, we certainly won’t be the last!”

We started the most perfect weekend with our rehearsal dinner at golden hour overlooking the rolling hills of central Tennessee. Nothing beats Mexican food, our favorite people, cumbia music, and lots of happy tears. —Anna-Maria

We loved working with our wedding planner Carly Pickett on all paper goods! Carly also happens to be a close friend and an incredible visual artist, so working on these designs with her was so fun! We came up with our own custom gay quail lovers logo and custom icons to represent us as a couple. A lot of love went into these so that hopefully our guests could frame and display them in their homes to forever remember the special weekend we shared together. —Anna-Maria

My mom, dad, tías, and sister planned and decorated our beautiful rehearsal dinner. My mom has always been the party planner of the family—always making everyone feel so special and celebrated. The smells of the tortillas cooking, the floral arrangements made by my mom and sister Caroline, and the way the custom-made “Anna-Maria & Brittany” papel picado looked blowing in the breeze made us feel right at home. —Anna-Maria

Sure, decorating my house, lighting a fresh pine-scented candle, and listening to Christmas music all day, every day get me in the holiday spirit, but what really does it for me? A pair of matching holiday pajamas. As someone who wears a two-piece set to bed pretty much every single night, I love swapping in new prints and colors to fit the time of year. There’s just something about a festive set that really completes the cozy vibe!

That said, I’m not the type of person who’ll settle for a basic plaid set and call it a day. With brands dropping holiday PJs in everything from cool patterns to out-of-the-box color combos, you'll find plenty of unique options to choose from. Ahead, I rounded up five brands with seriously cute designs that'll give your nighttime wardrobe a seasonal refresh. They also make great gifts for loved ones or the perfect picks for your next matching-pajama party with friends and family!

For as long as I can remember, Old Navy has been one of the go-tos for holiday pajama sets. The brand always comes through with cute designs at affordable prices—something that feels increasingly rare in this economy! Its iconic flannel sets come in all kinds of styles, from classic plaid and gingerbread prints to lively options featuring elves, stripes, and mistletoe. Even better? Tons of this season’s styles are currently 60% off, so I’d run, not walk!

Known for its fun, quirky designs, Roller Rabbit has perfected the art of making PJs that feel anything but basic (the monkeys!) while still being incredibly cozy. Its holiday collection is no exception, with colorful prints, funky patterns, and plenty of personality. If you're a maximalist or you just love a bold pajama set, this is where to get them! I know they’re on the pricier side, but I promise they’re worth the splurge! (Ahem, these tend to sell out pretty quickly, so I’d add them to your cart ASAP if you have your eye on a pair!)

You know and love SKIMS for its buttery-soft loungewear and impressive shapewear, and I’m happy to report that its pajama selection is just as good. Right now, the holiday sets are especially gorgeous! I love how the brand sticks to the classics with familiar silhouettes, like cami sets, while giving them a festive update. Personally, I’ll be buying the bright pink plaid set!

From my teenage years to now, Victoria's Secret has always been at the top of my list for bras, underwear, loungewear, and, of course, incredibly cute pajama sets. I remember feeling so grown-up whenever I'd get a new pair from the brand, and honestly, that hasn't changed! Its 2026 holiday collection is just as good as ever, with on-trend designs that feel a little more dressed-up than your everyday PJs. Choose from cute short sets and long flannel styles for those who love something extra cozy, to silky satin sets and lightweight Henley styles for the girls who tend to run hot. There's something for every kind of sleeper!

When I think of the silkiest, most luxe pajamas I’ve ever worn, Eberjey instantly comes to mind. They’re exactly what you’d imagine sleeping in a five-star hotel would feel like: silky to the touch, featherlight, and soft as a cloud. And the holiday styles are just as dreamy! Available in the brand’s beloved TENCEL™ Modal and flannel sets, there’s a range of festive yet chic designs to choose from, including polka dots, bows, holly berries, and more.

#6766. Reckoning With Borat, 20 Years Later

Last month, I sat in a packed-to-the-gills movie theater to experience the latest release from a controversial comedian whose work regularly blurs the line between docu-reality and narrative fiction. I am, of course, referring to Ali G: Who Iz I?—the cinematic return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s once-and-still-somewhat-beloved durag-doffing titular character.

Before the film was unceremoniously dumped on Prime Video last week, I managed to snag a ticket to the only New York City screening that wasn’t totally sold-out, booking a seat—last row, tucked in an alcove of the theater—with the intention of isolated note-taking and (gasp!) the occasional phone-glance should the movie prove tedious. The recliners next to me were eventually claimed by a gentleman decked in a very Ali G-esque skull cap and wraparounds, who unleashed a deafening “BOOYAKASHA!” after Nicole Kidman’s AMC intro.

Cohen’s brand of confrontational cringe comedy continues to attract a level of interest, thanks in part to a certain mustached-and-mankini’d Kazakh journalist. The cultural explosion that was Borat! Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (has any movie title so padded the word count?) turns 20 years old this week, and it remains a curious artifact of the 2000s: impossibly dated and slightly better than you might remember, even as its creator’s talent has slowly and unmistakably eroded.

If you were just old enough to purchase a ticket to an R-rated movie in 2006, Borat felt like a truly out-of-nowhere phenomenon in terms of mass impact. But the character, armed with little more than a shabby suit and an aggressive cheer, emerged from Cohen’s cult favorite Da Ali G Show, which ran for one season on BBC’s Channel 4 in 2000 before making the leap to HBO in 2003. Alongside Ali G and the gay Austrian fashion correspondent Brüno, Borat Sagdiyev was just one of the many personalities Cohen regularly deployed in the thorny thickets of gotcha-mentary, trading in culturally oblivious and antisemitic observations supposedly inherited from his Kazakh homeland, often to the shock and dismay of his unsuspecting subjects.

These fool-me-once hijinks weren’t necessarily groundbreaking, even for HBO’s then-provocative late-night programming. Several years prior, The Chris Rock Show engaged in similar man-on-the-street shenanigans (once, he polled residents of NYC’s notoriously hate-crime-prone Howard Beach region about renaming a street after Tupac Shakur). But segments in which Ali G addressed Buzz Aldrin as Buzz Lightyear, or the one where Borat led a bar full of Arizonans in a rousing chorus of “Throw the Jew Down the Well,” were practically reverse-engineered for virality in the internet’s pre-social-media infancy, and the appeal of Cohen’s approach—how far will he go, and will ordinary folk follow him?—was easy to understand, regardless of the visceral discomfort it may have generated.

Straying from the sketch-based format of Da Ali G Show, Borat embraced a loose narrative structure, with its titular inquirer setting out for America to make a documentary on the country’s social peccadilloes with the intent of eventually romancing Pamela Anderson. If you want to get highfalutin about it, the plot itself situates Borat within the legacy of films about Europeans attempting to understand America—a small-but-fascinating subgenre that includes Paul Verhoeven’s fairytale-cum-nightmare Showgirls, the post-hippie pessimism of Michaelangelo Antonioni’s Zabriskie Point, and Kristoffer Borgli’s social-mores rom-dramedy The Drama.

Don’t get it twisted, though: Borat was and still is best enjoyed as a showcase of physical comedy and inflammatory non sequiturs. It’s no less funny in 2026 to watch a grown man wash his face in a toilet bowl, or gesture toward a tortoise while sincerely asking, “What type of dog is this?” The scene in which an etiquette coach attempts to guide Borat through the intricacies of comic timing is itself an excellent study in comic timing; the notorious full-frontal hotel chase sequence between Borat and his producer Azamat (portrayed by steadily-working character actor Ken Davitian) is a marvel for its sheer escalation alone. This stuff killed in a massive Northern New Jersey movie theater when I was 19, and it still kills from the confines of my couch 20 years on.

Unlike much of Cohen’s subsequent work, Borat is not an explicitly political film. Nonetheless, a good deal of its “GREAT SUCCESS!”—$262 million in box receipts off an $18 million budget, with a Best Actor Golden Globe for Cohen himself—is undoubtedly owed to a different sort of comic timing. The film came out in the throes of George W. Bush’s second presidential term, with the US mired in two wars abroad and a hell of its own making. Americans were thirsty for easy targets to shoulder the blame and, if possible, provide some cheap laughs in the process.

Their thirst was quenched in the form of Borat’s many unsuspecting subjects. Some of this was low-hanging fruit: Borat telling a group of feminists to smile more, or acting like a literal bull in a china shop amidst Confederate memorabilia. But the film’s more sensational material depicted rough corners of the American psyche long hidden in plain sight. Most memorably, Borat encounters a group of rowdy frat boys who huff about white pride and express dismay at the abolishment of slavery before engaging in a viewing of Anderson’s infamous leaked sex tape with ex-husband Tommy Lee.

Not everyone was displeased at their portrayal, though. Joe and Miriam Behar, the Jewish couple who offered Borat and Azamat room and board, were good-natured in a 2006 interview with the Boston Globe. For her part, Miriam shrugged off Borat’s naked antisemitism. “To me it's an anti-Muslim movie, not anti-Jewish, because Kazakhstan is mostly Muslim,” she offered.

Behar’s observation underlines the casual bigotry that otherwise stains Borat. The film’s portrayal of Kazakh culture is undoubtedly offensive, and provoked mixed reactions from the country’s government for years to come. For what it’s worth, Cohen pushes back—intentionally or not—on anti-Muslim sentiments during the film’s rodeo sequence, in which Borat tells a particularly racist attendee that he is indeed “not Muslim.”

But given the post-9/11 climate into which Borat was launched, the implications of a foreign correspondent from a majority-Muslim country espousing antisemitic and misogynistic viewpoints are crystal-clear, and Cohen himself seems too smart to sincerely profess a lack of awareness as to how this might be received. It doesn’t help that his subsequent projects resulted in exponential escalations of offense: 2012’s more narratively-focused The Dictator spared no quarter when it came to stereotypes of Arab culture, while the astoundingly homophobic Brüno, from 2009, was loaded with gags about anal sex and resulted in an out-of-court settlement with a Palestinian grocer who was falsely credited as a former terrorist in the film itself.

After 2016’s box-office bomb Grimsby, which is most notable for the allegations of on-set sexual harassment co-star Rebel Wilson later brought toward Cohen, his work went in a more explicitly political direction. There was his 2018 docu-satire series Who Is America?—two episodes of which featured writing and directing contributions from Nathan Fielder—and 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, a second-verse-same-as-the-first sequel which earned several Oscar nominations and brought a truly bizarre “October surprise” to that year’s presidential election involving actress Maria Bakalova, Rudy Giuliani, and the former New York City Mayor’s pants zipper.

Both of those films were more explicitly message-y than they were riotously funny. Cohen’s latest, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is neither, carrying the all-too-familiar stink of a comedian insisting that their capacity to offend amounts to protected speech. At 55, Cohen is clearly not as willing to submit himself to the ragdoll physics he once deployed; in its place is an often-sullen-looking Ali G, his dreads now gray, weighing the merits of cultural appropriation and sparring with a DEI coordinator about the origins of the durag. The entire affair is belabored and depressing.

It made me think of the Who Is America? character Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, a send-up of Rachel Dolezal-flavored liberals in the form of a Berkeley professor who dons dashikis and keffiyehs. Early in the film, he rages against Ali G’s culturally appropriative ways to a majority-Black community meeting in Oakland. “We don’t care!,” shouts one participant. In hindsight, it’s as much an expression of exhaustion with the dictates of capital-D discourse as it is a referendum on Cohen’s confrontational method, which now yields far less interesting insights about the national psyche than it did when Borat arrived on American soil in 2006.

The biggest and brightest names in American fashion all came together last night for the 45th annual CFDA Awards, which are often referred to as the Oscars of Fashion. Taking place at New York’s Natural History Museum, the night celebrates both the unique contributions of American designers throughout the previous year and honors those who have made an indelible mark on the industry throughout their illustrious careers.

“Continue to share important stories and do work that means so much to you,” said CFDA chairman Thom Browne at the ceremony. “Work that you couldn’t imagine doing anything else, because the true marker of success is being able to do something you love always at the highest level. And never sacrifice the true creativity and quality of what you do.”

Awards were presented to Ralph Lauren, Rachel Scott of Diotima, the jewelry designer Ana Khouri, and Colleen Allen. Fashion world luminaries were also honored, including Tory Burch, Linda Fargo, Peter Marino, Susan Cianciolo, and Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin.

The night welcomed a retinue of A-listers to help celebrate, proving that fashion now touches every part of culture, from entertainment to tech to sports. Bold-faced names included the night’s host, Keke Palmer; presenters Zoe Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, Rosé, Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, Naomi Osaka, Demi Moore, and Cole Escola; and celebrity attendees Gracie Abrams, Megan Thee Stallion, Travis Scott, PinkPantheress, and many more.

“Anthony is not only an extraordinary designer, but also an extraordinary human being,” said Zoe Kravitz while presenting Anthony Vaccarello with his honor for International Designer of the Year. “He has this rare ability to make you feel completely understood, and that is reflected in everything he creates.”

“Anthony doesn't just design clothes,” added Rosé. “He creates an attitude, a sense of freedom and confidence that is distinctly his own.”

Donatella Versace, who attended with Vaccarello, had this to say about the honor. “I love what Anthony has built at Saint Laurent over the last decade and cannot wait to see what he does next. New chapters are always inspiring.”

Last week, Calvin Klein dropped a hint of their next underwear campaign star via Instagram. The clip featured a guy gliding his fingers from his boxers up to his chest. Very suggestive. Very sexy. Instagram, obviously, went wild. A teaser of a teaser, you might say.

Shot by Oliver Hadlee Pearch on a hot Madrid day, the campaign features Bellingham posing against a clean white background—all the better to keep the focus squarely on the England international. Bellingham wears the rest of the Icon Cotton Stretch collection (and nothing else) throughout the campaign, which includes the new Stretch Shine Trunk with a shiny Infinity Bond logo waistband, the Boxer Brief, Low Rise Trunk and Hip Brief. In one shot, he’s pictured doing his goal celebration, which means the image may pop into your head the next time he scores on the pitch.

Maybe it’s obvious from the campaign, but the 23-year-old took to the role of model very naturally. He attributes his ease in front of the camera to the underwear.

“I really enjoyed working on this campaign,” Bellingham says via email. “I liked the idea of ‘the icon underneath’—that confidence starts with feeling comfortable in yourself. Calvin Klein is such an iconic brand, so it was great to bring that idea to life in my own way.”

Over the years, CK has linked up with its fair share of footballers. In 2023, the label shot Liverpool captain Virgil Van Dijk. #6757. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6754. Inside Sophie Bille Brahe’s Danish Seaside Home, Where Every Object Tells a Story

It’s almost dusk in Copenhagen when jewelry designer Sophie Bille Brahe tells me over the phone that she’s about to take a quick dip in the ocean before dinner. It’s a small ritual tied to the reason she chose her five-bedroom, three-bathroom seaside home, 20 minutes north of the city center, in the first place. Designed by Danish architect Ib Lunding in 1929, the house sits on one of three small streets of similar homes in what Danes call the “flower neighborhood,” each one a slight variation on the next. For Bille Brahe, it’s this setting—and the sensory elements that come with it—that were non-negotiable. “I open up my window and I can see trees. I can smell the sea,” she says. “For me, that’s very important to have in my life every day.”

The space is a respite for the designer, who views the home as a collection of memories and a backdrop for her bustling family life, kids, and border collie included. It’s also where her namesake fine jewelry line begins. In fact, Bille Brahe often develops her designs within the home’s walls before she ever takes them to the workshop. “I sometimes catch these sensations, these small ideas, and make them a little bit more stable by doing drawings of them here at home. And then, when I have an idea of what I want to do, I’m ready to go to the workshop and start,” she explains. In those beginning stages, she works alone. “I need to be able to make really ugly things or really great things,” she says. “I need a bubble around me.”

That bubble is her workspace, an all-white room anchored by an 1870s Swedish fireplace Bille Brahe had installed when she moved in. “It has gold detailing, and it’s so beautiful,” she says. “A fireplace has a way of gathering family and speaks to a house built with love.” Nearby sits her desk, which belonged to her father’s best friend. “It’s basically where everything I make starts,” she says. “I’d loved it since I was a kid.”

Pulled up to the desk is a chair that visitors to her New York showroom may recognize: a curved stainless-steel design by Mats Theselius reupholstered in Sahco zebra fabric. The same seating appears in the showroom, a throughline between her personal and professional worlds. Marc Chagall’s Soleil Couchant, a Le Klint lamp, a neon work by Gun Gordillo, and a collection of seashells share the desk with her sketches and notes. The room opens onto the dining room, centered on a Børge Mogensen Øresund table surrounded by Gio Ponti chairs and a bouquet of sunflowers resting on it.

Of course, Bille Brahe furnished her boutiques with intention. In Copenhagen, she sought out one-of-a-kind Danish furniture and even began making her own vases in Murano. In New York, she tracked down a rare Poul Kjærholm table, square with a gray leather top instead of the round marble version many Danes grew up eating breakfast at. At home, she followed a similar rule and took her time, layering pieces slowly and making sure each one felt collected and had a story connected. “It took me many years to find a sofa, because every time I bought one I’d almost have a panic attack about the idea of buying something new, something everybody could have,” she says. “Everything I have in my home I’ve inherited, borrowed, or a friend made for me. If something doesn’t have a story, it doesn’t belong.”

Her jewel-toned Svenskt Tenn sofa is piled with pillows, each one a gift from a Swedish friend who came to visit. Beside it sits a slim side table, part drink trolley, stacked with books, a seashell, and a lamp she inherited from her grandfather. Most of the lighting in the house is inherited, except the Noguchi lanterns, which she brings back one at a time from trips to Japan. Another Japan find, the Nextmaruni Armless Chair by the architect duo SANAA (known as the Rabbit Chair for its ear-like back), sits beneath a pink painting by Danish artist Tal R.

Above all, though, it is a family house at its core. “It never feels like it’s an empty house,” she says. “I absolutely love my life with kids.” That’s particularly evident in the kitchen, where the day begins with coffee, breakfast for the kids, and, when the weather allows, the garden door thrown open. “It’s not a big house, so the kitchen needs to be efficient,” she says. “I cook a lot, so it ends up being a kitchen that can manage a lot of food without a lot of space.” Despite its small footprint, the room is warm, with kids’ art hung above the seating, embroidered tablecloths dressing the table, and an airy pendant overhead.

The same energy carries into the hallway, with its rounded window (a signature of the neighborhood’s houses) and walls in a blush pink by Farrow & Ball, the same color as the hallway in her previous home. When she moved, she changed everything else but kept the pink. “I normally don’t like colors on walls,” she says. “But I felt this was bringing something I used to love into the new house.”

Outside on the terrace, that pull toward nature continues. Every plant on the deck is one she’s had for 15 years or more, from a pomegranate tree she’s carried from home to home to the pink nerines called the “autumn flower,” and she has a story for each of them. According to Bille Brahe, there’s no need for more than this. If the trees are close enough to smell and the sea near enough to hear, she’s set and then some. “I’m not a person who needs a lot. I just need something close and clear, and if I have that, I can do what I need to do.”

#6753. Why El Clasico Is the Best Grudge Match in All of Sports

Last Saturday, before the biggest grudge match in international soccer, Spanish police officers decked out in riot gear surrounded my Barcelona hotel. Blue lights bounced from the sun-stained stone of the alley as kids scrambled away in the distance. In the skirmish, one had lost a single ASICS sneaker that sat idly in the road until, sometime between night and the light of day, someone snatched it up for themselves. You often hear of the way heated football rivalries and cup finals bring out a kind of mob mentality among fans. The match, however, wasn’t set to kick off for another 24 hours.

Three days prior I’d landed in Barcelona to attend FC Barcelona versus Real Madrid, better known as El Clásico, for which Tyler the Creator’s GOLF brand had partnered with Spotify on Barcelona’s gameday kits. If you care about football in the slightest you know about El Clásico, though it’s worth knowing about even if you don’t.

Since 1902—the year of Real Madrid’s founding, and three years after that of FC Barcelona—the two biggest football clubs in Spain have clashed in a rivalry match dubbed El Clásico (the face-off now happens twice a season, plus various tournament play that varies in schedule year to year). Before last week’s installment, the match had been played 264 times over 122 years. In most high-stakes football rivalries, one club holds a historical edge: Arsenal has a handy 20 to 30 wins over Tottenham Hotspur in the North London Derby, depending on when you start keeping track, while Manchester United edges out Liverpool in total wins. But heading into the first El Clásico of the 2026-27 La Liga season, Barcelona and Real Madrid stood deadlocked with 106 wins each.

American sports rivalries are often the result of proximity, with most pitting divisional neighbors and crosstown rivals against one another, with the exception of teams that share a bitter history of championship bouts (like the Lakers and the Celtics). But if we’re being honest, not even Yankees-Red Sox holds a candle to El Clásico. Apart from both competing in the upper echelon of La Liga’s clubs, FC Barcelona and Real Madrid’s rivalry has stewed in over a century of political turmoil between the Catalan capital and the city that houses the Spanish throne. During the 20th century as Spain looked to enforce a uniform identity across the nation, Catalonia sought to maintain its independence from the crown and, crucially, its right to speak Catalan rather than Spanish. Francisco Franco’s dictatorship brought more enmity, as Madrid became the proxy club for a centralized Spain while Barcelona came to represent Catalonia’s Republican Left. During the Franco years, when both the language and the flag of Catalan were banned, Barcelona’s Camp Nou stadium became a safe haven for the free expression of Catalan identity. Meanwhile, Franco’s foreign minister Fernando Maria de Castiella declared Real Madrid “the best embassy we’ve ever had.” The wounds of that era have hardly subsided: while the war may be over, as recently as 2017 the Catalan people voted on whether or not they’d remain a part of Spain (the vote was declared illegal by the Spanish government, and there was police intervention at polling stations).

Today, the clubs are recognized as polar opposites in every sense, from politics to style of play: Real Madrid stands for conservatism and a unified Spain, while Barcelona remains the club of the rebellious Left. Madrid takes an Evil Empire approach to roster construction, buying up the most exciting free agents on the market for record-breaking fees. (This century alone they’ve rostered Cristiano Ronaldo, David Beckham, and Zinedine Zidane, and the club currently boasts a striker line that includes Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, and Vinicius Jr.) Barcelona, on the other hand, has the most acclaimed and successful youth academy in all of football. The school, La Masia, has promoted a singular theory of football for decades, prioritizing position play and a dominant possession game perfected by FC Barcelona veterans like Lionel Messi, Xavi, Pep Guardiola, and Andrés Iniesta. When Spain won the World Cup this summer, they did so with eight former students of La Masia on the pitch (one of whom, Marc Cucarella, currently plays for Real Madrid).

To this day, the rivalry is characterized by an unmistakable hostility. In my four days in Barcelona, I didn’t see one person wearing Real Madrid’s crest, though the souvenir shops lining La Rambla were well-stocked with the club’s bootleg gear. At one point, I walked past a wall scrawled with graffiti: “SPANISH GO HOME.” When we finally got to the match, most Madrid fans were sequestered to a supporter section in the upper deck surrounded by protective plexiglass.

“This is the biggest match in club football,” explained Joel Jaggar, a British transplant who’s lived in Barcelona for a decade. Jaggar runs Real Vintage Football, a rare jersey boutique in El Raval (just outside of the city’s Gothic Quarter) that was unsurprisingly overwhelmed with visitors all weekend. He’d stocked up on at least a hundred Messi jerseys, all of which were gone by the time they closed on Friday. “A lot of people come to Barcelona specifically for this game,” he shared. “Big fans, sure, but also people who want to experience the game for the sake of the experience.” Globally, he argued, the word “Barcelona” is as closely associated with the club as it is the city. “You can’t say the same for Madrid,” he quipped.

Jaggar and I met the morning after a swell of student-organized protests regarding the city’s cost-of-living crisis boiled over into vandalism and looting near the neighborhood that houses his store. There was even suspicion El Clásico would have to be postponed or cancelled altogether. Come morning though, those anxieties had faded–as is so often the case, football continued uninterrupted.

Even with capacity capped at around 62,000 during ongoing renovations, Camp Nou is something to behold. Ahead of kickoff, supporters lifted color-coordinated pieces of poster nestled into each seat,forming a massive, stadium-wide tifo in the colors of the club and, in our section, the Catalonian flag. Fireworks exploded, and El Clásico began.

But much of the match’s first half was mired in tension, as Barcelona dominated possession but failed to score. The crowd finally began to pop when Madrid nabbed their first goal, then properly exploded when Barca tied it up in the second half. When Mbappé scored his second goal of the evening at ‘87 minutes after a beautiful assist from Bellingham, he vaulted over to the gate of the Barcelona supporters’ section, taunting them as trash thrown from the crowd rained over him. Madrid held on, gaining the tiniest of advantages in the El Clásico win count: 107 to their rivals’ 106.

As we walked out of Camp Nou, which will hold a whopping 105,000 spectators when its renovation is complete, I thought about the sort of sporting events that tend to grace bucket lists: Super Bowls and World Cup Finals and World Series games. So often the point is the spectacle of a season or tournament ending—the big trophy, the championship ring, the confetti and fireworks. El Clásico is different. There’s no trophy at the end, no ultimate resolution. Like the ideological divide for which it’s become a proxy, El Clásico is in a constant state of ebb and flow. Each time Barcelona and Real Madrid take the pitch, there’s no decisive victory so much as another brick laid in the foundation of football’s greatest rivalry. These clubs have come to blows 265 times. But as long as there are football stadiums in Barcelona and Madrid, El Clásico will endure as a conduit for the enduring rancor between the country's two biggest cities.

#6752. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6747. The Best Exercises for Lymphatic Drainage, Courtesy of a Detox Expert

We are a world obsessed with the lymphatic system right now and the best exercise for lymphatic drainage. Google searches for lymphatic drainage have gone up by 60% across America year over year, while on TikTok there are more than 79 million views of the term and growing.

Lymphatic drainage massage (and other techniques like dry body brushing) can help reduce water retention, puffiness, and inflammation by flushing out toxins and excess liquids. Celebrities love it, but is it accessible to the rest of us?

The easy answer—happily!—is yes. And celebrity lymphatic specialist Rebecca Faria (known as @DetoxbyRebecca on Instagram) is leading the charge. Based in Beverly Hills, Faria specializes in Brazilian lymphatic drainage (a rhythmic massage that combines pressure and long strokes) and has a roster of A-list clients who swear by her techniques (including Jennifer Aniston, Hailey Bieber, Ariana Grande, and Anne Hathaway). While a treatment with one of Faria’s team starts at $350, she has shared some of her favorite (easy) exercises that are designed to stimulate your lymphatic system at home. And they’re free.

Done while either lying down, seated, or standing, knee hugs aren’t just good to get the lymphatic system going but help release back tension. Hug one knee into your chest and hold for 20 seconds, then do the other side.

Lie on your back and place the soles of your feet together, letting your knees fall out in a butterfly formation. This stretch is also a fantastic way to stretch your hips as well as release your pelvic floor.

While lying down, hold your legs straight up, then lift one as you lower the other. These are called flutter kicks–do 20 of them. (Incidentally, these are also great for your core, a muscle group that has long-term benefits to help with bloating.)

These aren’t just for your Pilates class. Remain lying down. With one leg on the floor, lift the other leg and move in a circular motion 20 times. Repeat on the other leg.

No bike needed. With your legs in a tabletop position, straighten one leg, then the other, 20 times.

Another Pilates movement to try out. Lying on your left-hand side and keeping the legs relatively straight, circle your right leg 20 times. Do the same on the other leg.

Stand with your feet flat on the floor, then raise up onto your toes, lifting your heels off the ground. Do this 20 times. This is also a favorite movement of Jesse Inchauspé (a.k.a. the Glucose Goddess) to help with balancing blood sugar.

These outfits prove white denim has no off-season

White jeans are now a year-round staple, no longer relegated to the summer months between Memorial Day and Labor Day. From work-ready looks anchored by tailored denim to relaxed ensembles made for weekend getaways, these white-denim outfits do it all. This fall, take inspiration from a few of our favorite street-style looks. The lineup includes everything from straight-leg and relaxed fits to low-rise baggy silhouettes, in a range of soft hues like off-white and ecru. When paired with capsule wardrobe classics, such as a white T-shirt, a brightly colored button-down shirt, or a barn jacket, the results are stylish and equally easy to pull off.

Below, discover ten white jeans outfits that prove how cool they can look throughout the fall/winter months.

There’s a reason winter whites are a perennial favorite. Matching white jeans with your outerwear creates a clean, fresh monochromatic look. For a subtle sliver of color, layer an icy blue cardigan underneath, then add classic black pumps, and finish with sculptural gold earrings.

A simple way to wear white jeans during the fall is pairing them with a ladylike jacket in brown check print. The cropped silhouette offers a flattering counterpoint to relaxed denim, while black accessories—a roomy shoulder bag and ballet flats—lend a refined touch. Consider this an easy fall workwear formula you can wear on repeat.

If you’re a minimalist, try playing with contrasting textures to make your white jeans feel even more seasonally appropriate. Style them with a roomy black suede funnel-neck jacket, pointed-toe boots, and an unexpected accessory, like this elegant tassel bag.

The best fall outfits start with great basics: White straight-leg jeans, a white T-shirt, and a lightweight trench, which are all part of a well-rounded capsule wardrobe. Give these classics a hint of surprise by tying a pop of red knit around your shoulders and slipping into mules for an unexpected detail. They’re ideal for peak fall days, when it’s not too hot or too cold, and you can get away with a little peep-toe.

A striped long-sleeve T-shirt lends a touch of nautical charm to white jeans. Go for an oversized option in red to play up the relaxed, off-duty vibe. Black shoes—whether boots, loafers, or sleek sneakers—anchor the look, while a leather bucket bag and aviator frames complete the outfit.

Barn jackets remain a major trend for fall 2026. Make a case for wearing pastels well into the cooler months with a pale pink version and white jeans, offset by a black sweater, loafers, and a brown suede bag. Whether for a casual day spent running errands in the city or a weekend away, this combination strikes the perfect balance.

White jeans don’t always have to be worn in casual settings only. Make yours feel more elegant with a tuxedo-style blazer, silk camisole, and smoking slippers. A structured top-handle bag adds a polished finishing touch, taking the look effortlessly from desk to dinner.

Dip your toes into the season’s brightest color trends by putting a bright button-down shirt with otherwise simple styling pieces, such as a white T-shirt and straight-leg jeans. A leather belt and high-vamp shoes provide pared-back elegance.

French girls know how to layer the je ne sais quoi way, and denim is often the base. White jeans get a Parisian twist when paired with not one but three fall jackets—after all, temperatures are always unpredictable. A chore coat, plaid blazer, and windbreaker jacket can all be part of your layering essentials.

Nothing is more classically cool than wearing black and white during fall/winter. Bring your baggy white jeans into the winter months with a black turtleneck cardigan and sleek textural accessories—an embossed belt, suede flats, and a rich leather bag. Use this look as a base, then add a leather jacket or a tailored wool coat for extra warmth when needed.

Over the years, we’ve seen plenty of stars pull off denim-on-denim fits, but never with something quite like this.

#6740. What Writing a Book About JFK Jr. Taught Me About Personal Style

John F. Kennedy Jr. wasn’t the first guy to ride a bike wearing a suit. Likewise, the presidential scion and People’s 1988 Sexiest Man Alive didn’t invent the backward Kangol cap, the pinstriped suit, or wearing a waistcoat with jeans—he just did it better than pretty much anybody else. That’s a big part of why he was one of the most photographed men on the planet in the 1990s, and why he remains a menswear moodboard staple today, nearly 30 years after his untimely death. Still, no matter how hard you try, and no matter how closely you hew to the source material, all attempts to replicate JFK Jr.’s style are destined to leave you looking like a runner-up in a Washington Square Park lookalike contest.

Ask anyone who encountered John-John in his prime—which, in my experience, is virtually everyone who lived in Manhattan in the 1990s—and the first thing they’ll mention is his magnetism, his charm, and the fact that, against all odds, he was actually better-looking in person. I know this because, having recently written a book about JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve spent a good part of the last year poring over photos, reading biographies, speaking to people who knew him, and otherwise immersing myself in his world. Among the conclusions I’ve come to is that you probably won’t look as cool as JFK Jr. did wearing rollerblades, but there are a few style moves you can borrow from his playbook without resorting to full Kennedy cosplay.

JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was built on four pillars: tailoring, preppy basics, workwear, and sportswear. But it was the idiosyncratic way he combined them (i.e., a backward baseball cap with a suit, a polo neck sweater under a tweed blazer, hiking boots with tailored trousers) that resulted in some of his most memorable looks. Surprisingly, while the combination of straight-leg jeans, a button-up dress shirt, and a blazer has become shorthand for JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve never seen any evidence of him wearing it. In fact, he seldom wore jeans at all (some speculate his mother thought they looked shabby, while others told me that jeans didn’t complement his active lifestyle). That said, plenty of other ’90s style icons, from Ralph Lauren to Jerry Seinfeld, rocked this particular look, and it’s a pretty easy one to pull off. As with everything about JFK Jr.’s style, it’s not about lifting these combinations wholesale, but understanding the precise balance of contrast that makes them work.

One of the most consistent elements of JFK Jr.’s style was his love of discordant accessories, from his collection of flat caps to his ever-present wallet chain to his Oakley Eye Jacket shades. Some of these were practical—he was so prone to misplacing his wallet and keys that he needed to chain them to his pants—but others reflected his love of color (funky knit caps), his enthusiasm for skiing (fleece headbands), and his passion for travel (various hats picked up on trips to India and Thailand). Some accessories will suit you better than others, but if you have a personal connection to it, all the better. And most importantly, limit yourself to one standout add-on per outfit.

Speaking of accessories: JFK Jr. was a dedicated scarf guy, and he’d pair one with everything from joggers and sneakers to his best navy blue suit. Rather than draping a scarf loosely around his neck, he tended to tie it in either a dressy overhand or classic Parisian knot, both of which lend a more formal look. He also loved wearing a thick scarf as outerwear, throwing it over a sweatshirt on a chilly day instead of a coat, often paired with a knit cap. For best results, don’t pick a scarf that matches the rest of your outfit too closely.

Among the most surprising things I discovered about JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was his watch collection. I wasn’t able to uncover any evidence of him wearing the long-lost Rolex Daytona given to him by Aristotle Onassis (a watch that, if ever found, would give Paul Newman a run for his money), but I did identify an unusually wide range of other pieces in his collection, from a Victorinox Swiss Army field watch to a Swatch chronograph to a vintage Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is of a piece with everything else we know about JFK Jr.: he wasn’t bound by any single style, brand, or price point, and got just as much enjoyment out of a cheap quartz watch as a luxury mechanical one.

As a rich kid raised on the Upper East Side, JFK Jr.’s closet included plenty of blazers, chinos, and polos. He was a gym rat who loved playing sports, so he also had a lot of sweats, tees, and sneakers. He was a downtown socialite, so he owned a lot of nice suits and tuxes, too. He also had an enviable collection of graphic tees from NYC institutions like the Russian & Turkish Baths in the East Village and the New York Athletic Club, as well as some commemorating events like the 1984 NYC Fresh Festival, a seminal moment in hip-hop history. What stands out to me—and what I believe makes his style so distinctive—is that JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was an authentic reflection of who he was, where he came from, and what he loved. This might be the most important style lesson any of us can learn from him: Great personal style is less about clothes than wearing them in a way that expresses your individuality.

American Style: The Look and Legacy of JFK Jr. is now available for pre-order.

#6737. 14 Best Work Jackets for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

For better or worse, the best work jackets for men are no longer associated with garages, factory floors, and loading docks. Instead, as the likes of Paul Mescal and Austin Butler (who told GQ he wore his for a year straight) continue to fly their flag, a great work jacket has become every guy's fastest route to semi-rugged heartthrob style.

Honestly, they make looking good almost too easy. First, they inject your fits with casual, weekend tough-guy energy. (This, to be clear, is a plus.) Second, they flatter you in all the right places, framing your shoulders and neatening up your waistline whether you’re pairing them with jeans or the kinds of wide, puddling trousers we've long been yapping about.

Better still, you don’t have to spend a fortune. The classics from Dickies and Carhartt are as dependable as ever, and even the independent designer options are within reach of your budget—this is a cotton-forward option, after all. Here are 14 of our favorites, all of which will only look better after a few years (and a few scuffs) of real wear.

The Carhartt Detroit work jacket is the classic for a reason. It’s been around for more than 70 years—not quite as old as blue jeans or cowboy boots, but easily in the upper echelon of American fashion’s great exports. So much so that today, luxury brands are riffing on it, even selling pre-distressed, washed-down versions at triple the price. (And yes, this is also the work jacket that Austin Butler told us he wears.)

Cut to the waist, and built from thick, stiff canvas with three perfectly placed front pockets, the Detroit is an Eisenhower-style silhouette (during WWII, the then-Army General overhauled U.S. military dress and introduced the cropped, boxy jacket to American forces). Its insulated blanket lining and corduroy collar also make it one of the few true year-round, toasty work jackets out there. Simply put, this is a real piece of clothing for real life. (Though if it's not fancy enough for you, there’s always the street-ready, slimmer, unlined Carhartt WIP version.)

Just like Dickies' iconic 874 work pants, the brand's insulated Eisenhower jacket (there he is again) is a hard-wearing, warm, wallet-friendly piece of gear that fits incredibly well. Nearly as old as the Detroit Jacket above, it doesn’t always get the same respect. But maybe that's just because it flies a little more under the radar, with its logo patch tucked discreetly near the hem. Decades in, it remains a low-key, low-cost icon—less shouty than its Carhartt cousin, but every bit as authentic.

Wallace & Barnes, J.Crew's workwear line, is back with tough fabrics, heritage details, and a big hit of #menswear-era nostalgia—and this wool-lined work jacket shows exactly why folks missed it so much. It has all of the heartthrob-coded details you probably had in mind when you decided to look for a jacket like this: Corduroy collar, zippered chest pocket, slightly cropped fit. But it isn't just good-looking. It also has a wool-blend blanket lining, for superior warmth to help you enjoy it even if the depths of winter. And that, if cost-per-wear logic still applies, makes it more than worth its slightly higher price point.

Welcome to the world of truly warm fabrics, and actually glove-friendly pockets. Filson’s been mastering cold-weather gear since your great-great-grandfather was in short pants, and this work jacket continues that legacy. Based on the brand’s original 1914 Cruiser, it’s cut from 24-ounce Mackinaw wool — a tightly woven twill that truly blocks wind, sheds rain, and stays warm even when wet. Without being mean, it’s built to outlast even you. Pricey? Sure. But it’s the kind of thing your kids will remember you by (and fight for) someday.

Buck Mason’s archive is full to bursting with vintage pieces from decades past, which explains why its collections are filled with absolute bangers these days. Here the brand has taken a mid-century work jacket and remade it, tweaking the fit to make it a touch more relaxed, and using a soft Italian doeskin cotton fabric that’s more plush than anything a worksite would have issued back in the day. There's even more to love in the details: Shoulder pleats for easy movement, real horn buttons on the chest pockets, and a dressy point collar.

For Lo-heads, Polo Ralph Lauren's hard-wearing zipper jackets are the stuff of legend. And while you might have grown up with an inherited cotton example from your dad, in the last decade of so, Polo has been pushing its ‘Bi-Swing’ polyester and/or nylon takes instead. That's fine, but some of us aren't so willing to trade in the soft, rugged comfort of a full-cotton jacket. That's where the rarer Bayport Poplin jacket comes in. A work jacket with no delusions, it’s not stealing the working man’s valor — it knows exactly what it is. It’s Ralph Lauren, and it knows you’re working hard at hardly working. But it's also strong enough to handle whatever activities you throw at it, leisure or otherwise.

Sure, Copenhagen's Mfpen has its silhouettes dialed, but don't overlook its fabrications. Here, it’s a dense wool-blend with a multi-tonal yarn construction. Textured, substantive, perfect.

While most waxed cotton jackets lean more country estate than work site, Tom Beckbe's high-quality range include a few closer, more modern fits. Perfect for those looking for a work jacket that's also waterproof.

A designer-adjacent example for the fashion crowd, this piece from South Korea's FrizmWORKS doesn't just look good, it feels good too, thanks to that soft leather collar that's just buttery once it's flipped up.

Stan Ray is part of what you might call the big three of American workwear, alongside Dickies and Carhartt). The Texas-born brand’s aptly named Roughneck Jacket delivers exactly what you’d expect. It’s tough, practical, and built for wear. Ribbed cuffs keep the cold out, while the washed-out hue delivers a perfectly broken-in look from day one.

This jacket from New York's Corridor—made from a hefty cotton-blend twill—is a more colorful take on the work jacket, and bound to give any fall fit a lift.

Just as the Polo jacket above is an RL icon, so is this faithfully-recreated nautical deck jacket from Ralph's RRL line. It's restocked every fall, it sells out every fall.

A key feature of all work jackets is their shorter length, but for those of us who want to make sure ours hits right at the belt, look no further than Abercrombie’s entry.

A leading Parisian purveyor of vintage garms, BRUT has recently moved into making its own stuff, all rooted in the archival vintage styles they obsess over. The results are, how you say, on point.

These days, work jackets seem to have an undeniable stranglehold on the imagination of guys who spend all day staring at their keyboards. (There’s a political element to this, of course. Whether or not you act in solidarity with your fellow laborers under capitalism, a work jacket allows you to look the part of the everyman.) But also, they’re just a great jacket for busy lives! There’s a generally accommodating cut that doesn’t restrict your movement, plenty of pockets, and hardy materials that can easily handle a snag, or sudden shower.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6735. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.
