#6725. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6721. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6719. Owen Wilson Breaks Down the World’s Best Golf Courses

The PGA Tour may be wrapping up in just a few short weeks, but this week marks the official beginning of Stick Season. No, not the Noah Kahan song, but Owen Wilson’s charming Apple TV+ comedy, whose second season premieres this Wednesday, November 4th. The show follows Wilson’s Pryce “Stick” Cahill, a former pro golfer who crashed out in a Kenny Powers-esque blaze of almost-glory a couple decades ago. Season one tracked his reentry into the game as the mentor of a talented but troubled young golfer played by Peter Dager. But in Season two, Stick has his eyes on a new prize: becoming the oldest player to ever win the U.S. Open.

Wilson himself might not be winning majors any time soon, but his experience filming the show has turned him into a real golf nut. He hadn’t played much beforehand, he told me, so the last couple of years have been a real crash course in one of the most difficult sports in the world. Still, it hasn’t taken much for him to compile a list of his favorite courses—and a bucket list of ones he’s dying to play a round or two on. Ahead of the show’s return, the 57-year-old actor hit the links with GQ.

“I have gotten an invite from a member to play, so I think that will happen at some point. What's always funny about that is that they close right after The Masters, so they're closed all summer. I’ve got to find a time that works for them where I could go play. That would be incredible.”

“My brother says St. Andrews and some of the other courses in Scotland are incredible. Out there the links style is pretty different from the courses in Dallas. And the people in Scotland, Luke says, are so knowledgeable about the game and friendly. I have not played link style and sometimes I wonder, Well, maybe my game would suit that because sometimes I'm not getting a lot of lift on the ball. And I am very comfortable with a putter. So yeah, maybe that's where I'll really prove that I'm good at the game.”

“Playing in Makena on Maui, that's a beautiful course that I love playing where you're getting to see the ocean and the beautiful Hawaiian features.”

“I played this one in Sydney that's kind of their [version of] Pebble Beach. It’s on the ocean, and there are some dramatic holes where you see waves breaking. I played lousy that day, but I'd like another crack at it.”

“I remember asking Collin Morikawa what his favorite course was and he said Riviera. Getting to play Riviera, I kind of feel like I've gotten to know more about the game. In the beginning, it was sort of lost on me—like getting a really good bottle of wine, and I couldn't really tell the difference. But now that I'm getting better, I can appreciate how incredible that course is. That first hole, where you're kind of teeing off from way up above. Just the other day, on number 10, I had a par four where I drove the green and just barely made it to the front of the green. But I was immediately on the phone calling to let my brothers and friends know that I had an eagle putt, which I missed. But that kind of kicked off a good little stretch where I birdied three out of four holes. That was a rare kind of day. More often, I'm kind of experiencing how challenging golf is.”

“I’ve stayed [at the Manor] and the course where they’re going to hold the Ryder Cup next year looked beautiful.”

“When I was training for the show, I learned how to play at Maui Country Club, a little nine-hole course kind of near where I am on the North Shore. [Maui] and Mākena, those were the two places that I really played a lot.”

“I played my best round at King Kamehameha with [former NBA coach] Don Nelson. I'd only been playing for a year-and-a-half where I was able to shoot in the low 80s, and everything just was very simple that day. Like, you hit your drive on the fairway, and then on the fairway you just hit it on the green, and then you two-putt and move on. I was with Nellie when he got his last hole in one. At that point I think he was maybe 83, and he was able to shoot his age and get a hole in one. I have not gotten a hole in one yet, but it's very exciting to witness one.”

#6718. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

Sofia Coppola, Julio Torres, and Marion Cotillard also attended the gala.

#6716. The 77 Best Red-Carpet Looks of All Time (and What You Can Learn From Them)

What does it mean to truly own the red carpet? It means showing out the way that stars have at the biggest events on the planet for generations now: In the swankiest, swerviest, most spotlight-stealing fashion possible.

Maybe that’s stunting in a disco-tinged jumpsuit like a ruffled John Malkovich at the 2026 Venice Film Festival, suiting up in sumptuous red velvet like Gwenyth Paltrow in 1999, keeping things simmeringly subtle like Frank Ocean’s Prada look at the 2019 Met Gala, or popping out the big lapels on a suede tux like Tom Holland at GQ’s Men of the Year 2021. Whatever your interpretation, the best red-carpet looks need to feel unexpected, look unforgettable, and radiate confidence.

To help jumpstart your own legendary party ensembles, here are 77 of the greatest red-carpet moments ever—and what you can learn from each.

Don’t be afraid to lean into your sex appeal.

As one wise Twitter user once put it, “Colman Domingo always dresses like he's stepped out of a GQ Mag shoot.”

This lush Gucci velvet suit became so instantly legendary that Gwenyth herself recreated the look more than 20 years later.

Frank caused some consternation (though not around these parts) when he showed up to 2019’s camp-themed Met Gala in an understated, decidedly un-camp look. Four years on, though, his outfit remains a great reminder that sticking to the classics—in this case, black-and-white Prada from head to toe—is never a poor choice.

Ruffles have ridges, and so does this suit.

Leaning retro can sometimes go awry on the red carpet, but Stanfield managed to pull the ‘70s look off with funky ease when he pulled this giant-collared, razor-sharp Saint Laurent jumpsuit out for the Oscars.

This outfit looks like it comes with its own walk-in music, and it’s loud.

The right to rock bare-chested suit isn’t something you demand—it’s something you earn.

Keanu is no stranger to high-low tailoring—he’s been known to rock work boots with sharp suits and graphic hoodies with sport coats. But he’s never pulled that trick off better than he did here in ‘93, layering a badass leather motorcycle vest under a roomy three-button number.

Julia Effin’ Roberts in a Big Effin’ Suit. That’s it. That’s the caption.

Wearing Prada, like Wright at the 2023 Golden Globes, is a surefire way to get a lot of compliments. The brand makes you look stylish and smart. Don’t you just want to ask Wright which local art gallery to visit?

Gerber’s disco-ball gown is stunning, but it’s Butler’s silky, sumptuous, pussy-bow blouse—designed by Saint Laurent, as was his exquisitely tailored tux—that utterly steals the show.

#6713. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6712. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6711. 16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6710. Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes Documentary, You Can See Everything: What We Know So Far

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Elizabeth Holmes’s story is getting told in a new project with Nathan Fielder at the helm. The comedian has released his new documentary titled You Can See Everything about Holmes, founder of the now-defunct biotech company Theranos, before she began serving her 11-year prison sentence for committing fraud.

Unlike a typical documentary, the film features Fielder chatting with Holmes in a Q&A format, while an unnamed A-list actress reenacts the events of the documentary in asides as Holmes. Here’s everything we know about You Can See Everything.

The official logline for the documentary reads: “34 days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. From boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim comes You Can See Everything.”

Audiences were buzzing at Telluride Film Festival, where the doc premiered with a surprise screening on September 6. Variety called the doc “a shameless, fascinating, reality-TV-eats-its-tail look at entitled duplicity” and said “the sensation of ‘WTF? I’ve got to watch this!’ did not subside as the movie went on. It only intensified.”

Deadline reported that “the nearly three-hour-long film drew continuous laughter, frequently triggered by hilarious reaction shots of Fielder...attempting to process what Holmes and Evans [Holmes’s partner] are pushing.” And the L.A. Times said the movie contains “mind-bending twists that meld reality and performance.”

The documentary is currently available to watch in theaters, but it will likely hit HBO Max when it comes to streaming. Warner Bros. Discovery owns HBO and HBO Max, and the company has an agreement that states A24 titles will automatically go to HBO Max as their first stop on streaming after the theatrical window and PVOD (Premium Video on Demand) release windows are over. You Can See Everything currently has no streaming release date.

In addition to Fielder and Holmes, The Hollywood Reporter confirmed that an unnamed “A-list actress” has a role in the making of the documentary. Her identity has not been revealed, as “the filmmakers and fest [Telluride Film Festival] requested that her identity be kept secret until more people have a chance to see the movie.”

As for what viewers can expect from the A-list actress, THR reports her cameo is “the craziest twist of a crazy film,” but her involvement is accidental. After agreeing to meet with Fielder, she finds herself wanting to be involved in the filming process and “winds up becoming a full-fledged collaborator in the film, appearing throughout the rest of it alternatingly as herself, giving commentary on the insanity of the situation, and then in reenactments—long Fielder’s go-to way of making sense of things—as Holmes.”

The first official trailer for the documentary arrived on September 8, featuring Fielder and Holmes having an unsettling conversation.

“I don’t have anything to deceive you on. Of course I’m not deceiving you. I’m engaging with you as a human being. Why would I deceive you? There’s no...there’s no reason for me to do that,” Holmes tells Fielder.

“You’re being real right now?” he asks her, to which Holmes replies, “I’m always being real.”

A first-look image was also released with the trailer, which shows Holmes preparing to give an item to a child, while Fielder looks at her from the background.

The first official trailer arrived on September 23 and provides a close look into some of the conversations that Fielder and Holmes had with each other throughout the film.

“You really feel you did nothing wrong?” Fielder asks her, to which Holmes replies, “I did not.”

He presses her and follows up the question with, “So where did things get lost? How are you where you are right now?”

Holmes finds herself at a loss: “I wish I knew. I don’t know. I don’t feel like I understand that,” she tells him.

At another point in the trailer, Fielder questions how Holmes could be so calm about his filming her every move. When he asks Holmes if she has any “worry” about him being at her home 24/7, she answers, “I don’t think so. I think this is the moment in time to capture this story before I’m gone.”

The comedian also manages to interview Holmes’s partner, William “Billy” Evans, who reveals he fell in love with her in their first conversation. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asks.

Evans coolly responds, “100 percent, but what does she has to gain from me?”

When Fielder reminds him that his family is wealthy—Evans is the heir to the Evans Hotel Group—he responds, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.”

Neither Holmes nor Evans have seen the doc, Oppenheim revealed during an October Q&A after the film’s Los Angeles screening. “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it,” the director said, with The Hollywood Reporter adding that Evans has “a strained relationship with the crew.”

Fielder added that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

On November 2, Evans revealed the “one misconception” about his relationship with Holmes following the release of the movie. “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious,” he responded to an X user.

Evans added, “She’s fiercely independent, strong willed, and my best friend. We are partners in every sense. We challenge each other, disagree, and face the world together. Her closest friends are also some of my closest friends. If I ever mistreated her, they’d have my head.”

Yes. In 2019, HBO released The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, which explored the rise and fall of Holmes and her multibillion-dollar company, Theranos.

In 2022, The Dropout—also about the rise and fall of Holmes and Theranos—premiered on Hulu. Amanda Seyfried starred as Holmes in the miniseries.

#6709. Chicken Pozole Verde

This chicken pozole verde recipe puts a whole bird to work, making a fragrant broth and plenty of tender shredded meat in one go. Roasted tomatillos and a mix of green chiles give the Mexican stew its tang and heat; a final swirl of cilantro purée adds fresh flavor and turns the whole pot brilliantly green.

The tomatillos and peppers roast while the chicken simmers. Toasting the canned hominy—a tip from Test Kitchen alum Rick Martinez—gives it a flavor “almost like a corn nut.” But if that’s one step too many, skip it—the stew will still be awesome.

Set out red onion, cilantro, dried oregano, and lime wedges, and let everyone load up their own bowl. Add avocado for creaminess, or shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, and crushed tortilla chips for crunch.

Canned white or golden hominy works here. These plump, chewy corn kernels give the stew its hearty texture. Dried hominy needs to be cooked separately before adding it to the pot.

Mexican oregano is a different herb from Mediterranean oregano, with floral, citrusy notes and a hint of anise. We prefer it in this pozole, but regular dried oregano works too.

No. The whole chicken simmers in water with onion, garlic, and spices to make the broth. Before adding the shredded chicken and cilantro purée, taste the broth and season with salt and pepper.

Can I make pozole verde ahead or freeze it?

Yes. Cook the chicken up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its broth, then finish the recipe when you’re ready to serve. You can also freeze the finished pozole. Take Rick’s advice and stash a quart for your next weeknight dinner emergency.

Heat ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Cook 1 large yellow onion, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, seasoning with kosher salt and stirring occasionally, until very tender, 12–15 minutes. Add 2 tsp. ground coriander, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ tsp. dried oregano, preferably Mexican, and cook, stirring constantly, until very fragrant, about 1 minute.

Place one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken in pot and pour in 12 cups water. Bring to a simmer and cook chicken, uncovered and reducing heat as needed to maintain a very gentle simmer (and turning once or twice if it isn’t completely submerged), until cooked through and legs wiggle easily in their joints, 40–50 minutes.

Meanwhile, preheat oven to 425°. Spread out 4 poblano chiles, 2 Cubanelle peppers or 2 more poblano chiles, 3 serrano chiles, and 1½ lb. tomatillos, husks removed, rinsed, on a large rimmed baking sheet. Roast, tossing once or twice, until chiles and peppers are browned and collapsing and tomatillos are tender, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Transfer chicken to a cutting board; set broth in pot aside. Let chicken sit until cool enough to handle. Pull meat from bones and shred into bite-size pieces; discard chicken skin and bones.

Split open chiles and peppers; remove stems and seeds and discard. Remove any skin that can be easily peeled off and discard. Transfer chiles and peppers to a blender and add tomatillos; reserve baking sheet. Blend until smooth. Stir chile purée into reserved broth and bring to a simmer. Reserve blender.

Spread out two 15-oz. cans golden or white hominy, rinsed, in an even layer on reserved baking sheet and roast, tossing halfway through, until very fragrant and hominy around edges of baking sheet are just beginning to brown, 12–18 minutes. Scrape into pot with broth.

Season broth with salt and freshly ground black pepper and simmer, uncovered, until flavors come together and broth is rich tasting, about 20 minutes. Ladle ½ cup broth into reserved blender. Add 2 cups cilantro leaves with tender stems and purée until smooth and very bright green, at least 1 minute. Add chicken to broth and cook until heated through, then stir in cilantro purée. Taste posole and season with more salt if needed.

Divide posole among bowls. Top with ½ small red onion, thinly sliced, and more cilantro leaves and dried oregano. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

Do Ahead: Chicken can be cooked 3 days ahead. Let cool in broth; cover and chill.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in 2017 as ‘Posole Verde With Chicken’; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more hearty soup recipes from Epicurious →

#6708. Mariah Carey Answers Vogue’s Holiday Questions

Now that Halloween has come and gone, we can officially put spooky season to rest—and the festive holiday season has come in to fill the void. And who better to ring in this cheery time of year than with Mariah Carey—the undisputed queen of Christmas? (Because, as she would say: “It’s tiiiime!”)

Consider her defrosted: This week, Carey was announced as the new star of Gucci’s 2026 holiday campaign, and last night the singer attended the Italian label’s private store event in New York City to kick off the festive party season.

In the new campaign video, Carey arrives at a holiday party decked out in full Demna-era Gucci—mix-and-mingling with guests, set to the tune of—what else?—her enduring hit “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” Last night, Carey kept the celebrations going by handing out (Gucci!) gifts to all of the party attendees. A full choir even sang renditions of some of her best Christmas hits.

Pre-soirée, however, Vogue couldn’t resist the chance to catch a private moment with Carey and ask her some of our burning questions. From her festive styling tips to her party hosting no-nos, read on for the superstar’s hottest holiday takes.

Mariah Carey: It was so fun shooting the campaign. I had a lot of favorite moments—mainly the one with the dog. Did you see the dog? So cute. That was festive.

I love everything about this time of year. It’s just … something that I can’t explain. I’ve been in love with Christmas my whole life, and now when we celebrate and we do all of the things, it opens up a whole other moment of festivity.

What are my traditions in the morning? I’m not a morning person, that’s the thing. I wait till mid-afternoon, and then we start with the opening of the gifts and all the things. It’s fun and festive.

I do—but they will take a long time to explain. We see Santa every year. We go on a sleigh ride together with him. We drink hot chocolate.

I do cook during the holidays. It’s one of my favorite things to do, and I don’t cook earlier in the year. I wait ’til Christmas Eve, or the day before Christmas Eve, and I make linguini with white clam sauce—the way my dad used to make it. Everybody has that. I also make a red sauce. It’s one of my favorite things. And then I’ll just eat that for the next few days.

Eggnog. Come on! You put whatever brown liquor you have, and then just throw it into the eggnog, and it’s eggnog.

I don’t usually have a holiday bash, because I’m just doing my own thing. Is that not good? I’m not big on hosting. I’d rather go to something [where] someone’s a really good hostess or host, and then I can just join in on the fun.

I’m going to have Marilyn Monroe. Tupac. And then I’m just going to set up a table for my dogs, and make them really happy. The dogs get a seat at the table. They have to be there.

I love the song today, yesterday—whenever. It’s just something that I wrote. I wasn’t trying to write the biggest holiday song [ever]. I was just there writing my little song that ended up lasting. So it’s been a great experience.

It’s too much work to go from Halloween straight into Christmas, and then think of a New Year's resolution. I don’t know. We’ll have to wait and see what else happens between now and New Year’s.

#6707. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6706. Simu Liu’s First Favorite Brand Was Abercrombie & Fitch

Simu Liu is no stranger to fashion’s biggest night, so, when I met him at his hotel in SoHo Monday night, he figured the Council of Fashion Designers of America Awards show should be a cinch. “I think everything’s a little bit more chill than the Met Gala,” Liu says. “So I’m looking forward to having a little bit of a more relaxed environment to talk to fashion houses and meet people from the different brands and also just to see friends.”

We speak just a few hours before the 37-year-old actor is about to make his first appearance at the Oscars of fashion and it’s hard to tell that he just hopped off a plane from Los Angeles this morning. The Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings actor has had a packed year, from making his Broadway debut in Oh, Mary! between February and April to getting married back in October. He’s preparing to start promotion for the highly anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he’s set to reprise his role as the superhero Shang-Chi. Marvel fans haven’t seen him on the screen since his record-breaking film debut in 2021. “It’s been a long, long time,” he jokes.

For now, he’s clad in a robe sitting barefoot on the sofa, swiping a metallic device across his unblemished, glowing face. “I think it’s like a gua sha, but it’s cold,” he speculates. (His makeup artist, Alex Keating, confirms that it’s Shark Beauty’s Depuffi, a hot-and-cold contrast therapy gua sha that basically “gives you a full facial.”) A room service trolley is sitting inches away from him, allowing him quick access to a plate of chicken tenders and fries. And a Diet Coke. Don’t forget the Diet Coke.

Keating makes good use of Liu’s wavy locks, hairspraying a Superman-like curl into permanent place on his forehead as he sips his fridge cigarette. The actor’s dad cut his hair until he was 18 and he says it took him a while to learn what worked for his own mane. He envied the typical stick-straight Asian hair others had, but through his work with groomers learned the power of salt sprays to lean into his hair’s natural texture. It admittedly took a while for Liu to develop his own fashion sense as an adult, too.

“When you grow up working class and you grow up with parents whose purchasing habits were just the furthest thing from luxurious, I think it just takes time for you to learn about fashion,” he says. “The first brand that I remember really caring about was Abercrombie & Fitch.”

Tonight, though, Liu has moved far beyond the mall. He’s attending the CFDA Awards on behalf of White Rabbit Trust, an organization that supports AAPI creatives and entrepreneurs. It's hosting the award’s Emerging Designers Table, which allows industry leaders—this year, Jason Wu—to mentor AAPI designers who create custom looks for the muse of their choosing. In Liu’s case, he’s been dressed by Asian-Canadian designer Haoran Li of the brand Private Policy.

The look for the evening was a matching set made from black silk jacquard woven with bamboo paired with a shiny new silver wedding ring and a Rolex Batman GMT-Master II. His cropped trucker-style jacket, accented by hand-knotted Chinese buttons, sat over a crisp frayed-hem white button-down with wide-legged pants that draped over low-profile black shoes. “In Chinese culture, bamboo is one of the Four Gentlemen, a symbol of integrity and resilience,” Li says. “It bends in the storm but never breaks. That felt like Simu, who has spent his career pushing through doors that weren’t built for us.”

I ask if he’s ever bothered by the responsibility of representing the Asian diaspora. “Right around the time Crazy Rich Asians came out, it was the first studio Asian movie in 25 years,” he recalls. “Then Shang-Chi was the first Asian Marvel superhero movie. For a while it was just like first this, first this, first this. So I felt like innately the stakes were high and I put pressure on myself. I don’t regret doing that. I just remember looking around and not really seeing anyone doing that. So I thought, well it might as well be me.”

To that point, this isn’t the first time Liu has used his name to promote an indie AAPI brand. At the the premiere of Shang-Chi in 2021, he spotlighted Singaporean-British designer Chelsea Scott-Blackhall’s label Dzojchen, wearing the brand’s silk kimono tuxedo.

Prominence in Hollywood has meant more to him than giving him the opportunity to wear really nice clothes. He’s decided to take more agency in his career, he says. Last year, he starred and executive produced the spy thriller series The Copenhagen Test, which despite favorable reviews was cancelled after one season. That hasn’t slowed his aspirations for new creative outlets: "I think actually right now I’m really excited by the idea of becoming a director."

But before we get to see “Directed by Simu Liu” on the big screen, the star has an awards show to attend—and a plate of tendies to devour. Just as quickly as he’s touched down here in New York, he’s off again to Hong Kong tomorrow.

#6705. Safe Word: The Best Jewelry Launches of November 2026

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry launches are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely new territory. First up, Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reimagines the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; and Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up.”

Elsewhere, Grace Winfrey looks to Italian good-luck charms for the colorful “Poppy Fortuna”; Robinson Pelham checks into “Suite 96” to celebrate 30 years of bold jewelry; Le Vian brings Georgian-era romance to Jared with a new collection of warm-toned diamonds; and Wempe puts traditional goldsmithing at the center of “au:thentic,” inspired by the humble jump ring. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back.

For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Reimagined for today in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a New York Holiday

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in New York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier’s ‘Trottola’ Takes on a New Form

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a new interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a new customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection launches with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Reimagines the Bow in Fine Jewelry

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a new fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s Latest Collection Is All About Good Fortune

Grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a new fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary

Robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign reimagines jewelry as the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the launches celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance

Le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its new exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection reimagines historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary update. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing

Wempe’s new gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

#6704. 23 Thanksgiving Bread Recipes: Rolls, Biscuits, and More

Pies get most of the Thanksgiving baking glory. But these Thanksgiving bread recipes make a strong case for saving some oven space for buttery dinner rolls, flaky biscuits, and midnight-sandwich-ready loaves. Think golden sweet potato buns soft enough to nap on, buttermilk cornbread to eat with butter or bake into dressing, and tender sweet loaves to nibble on Thanksgiving morning. Several recipes have make-ahead options too.

There’s no need to overhaul a classic. Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, these Parker House rolls have buttery folds, golden tops, and a finish of flaky salt. Pair them with our classic Thanksgiving menu.

These pillowy rolls get their warm color and gentle sweetness from mashed sweet potato. Bake and freeze them up to a month ahead, then reheat and brush with melted butter before serving.

Butter tucked inside each roll melts as it bakes, crisping the bottom. “If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer,” says Hana Asbrink.

Pillowy rolls swirled with sweet-salty pork floss, mayo, scallions, and furikake. Bake and freeze them up to three months ahead, then warm them through while everyone finds a seat.

A tangzhong—a cooked flour-and-milk paste—helps these sour cream and chive rolls stay exceptionally soft. Tear one off to mop up gravy, then save a few for tomorrow’s turkey sandwiches.

Garlic bread, meet buttery dinner roll. Fresh and dried dill work their way into these pillowy buns, which get a generous brushing of garlic butter after baking. Save one for a gravy swipe.

So many layers, you’ll feel like a geologist unearthing them. Claire Saffitz’s biscuits get their height from a cut-and-stack technique. Another reason to love them: You can freeze the unbaked biscuits up to a month ahead.

All the herby goodness of Thanksgiving stuffing, packed into a biscuit: sage, rosemary, fennel seed, and scallions. Save a few for breakfast the next morning, preferably under a generous ladle of leftover gravy.

No rolling pin, no biscuit cutter, no problem. Canned creamed corn keeps these drop biscuits tender, while Calabrian chile honey butter brings a little heat.

For the guest who always takes the biggest piece of garlic bread: flaky buttermilk biscuits loaded with Parmesan and parsley. Freeze them unbaked, then bake straight from frozen when the oven frees up.

Biscuits or cornbread? This cheesy mash-up means you don’t have to choose. Sharp cheddar and fresh sage work their way into flaky, buttery layers that feel right at home on the Thanksgiving table.

Looking to start a fight? Declare a cornbread recipe “best.” This version strikes a balance: a tender crumb, buttermilk tang, and a touch of sweetness. Eat it with butter—or turn it into cornbread dressing.

Cheddar, caramelized corn, and hot honey butter take this cornbread well beyond the usual. Nervous about the flip? “Don’t be afraid of flipping the bread—I promise you can do it,” says former BA food editor Rachel Gurjar.

Pumpkin purée gives this fall-ish rendition of our no-knead focaccia recipe its golden color and gentle sweetness. Finish with rosemary and flaky salt, then tear off a piece for dipping in olive oil. You can bake it a day ahead.

Leave the oven to the turkey. These flaky, skillet-cooked parathas have brown butter and sage tucked between their layers. Parcook them a day ahead, then fry until golden just before dinner.

A garlic knot with centerpiece ambitions. This braided loaf wraps buttery dough around garlic, Parmesan, and parsley, then gets another garlicky brush after baking. Start the dough a day ahead.

Leave the stand mixer where it is. This focaccia asks for a little patience, not much elbow grease, to produce its airy crumb and golden crust. An overnight rise gets you started; garlic butter finishes the job.

Focaccia’s leaf-shaped French cousin deserves a turn in the Thanksgiving bread basket. Green olives, rosemary, and lemon zest bring plenty of flavor. And yes, the dough comes together in one bowl.

In this crusty yeast bread recipe, apple juice replaces water. The apple flavor is subtle, but the appeal of a warm slice with butter is not.

Oats and chia seeds give this gluten-free loaf a dense, chewy crumb. No kneading, shaping, or scoring; just be sure to use the gluten-free oats and oat flour specified in the recipe.

Give Thanksgiving morning the sticky-bun treatment. This pull-apart bread packs tender apples between cinnamon-sugar-coated bites, with tangy cider caramel coating the whole thing. Put on a pot of coffee and let everyone help themselves.

Chocolate or vanilla? Rick Martinez’s conchas give you both, with a two-tone sugar topping over buttery Mexican sweet buns. Another reason to love them: You can bake them up to three days ahead.

Start the holiday with a thick slice of ginger-spiked pumpkin bread and a generous schmear of salted maple butter. You can bake the loaf up to four days ahead, leaving Thanksgiving morning for coffee and slicing—and, uh, all that other prep.

Maple-glazed turkey, garlicky mashed potatoes, pumpkin chiffon pie, and more recipes worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

From hot toddies to big-batch punch, these festive drinks will get you in the holiday spirit.

Like pumpkin flan de queso, rosemary-pear snacking cake, Amish pecan cream pie, and more.
