#6703. This Eccentric Village Pub Hotel on Loch Lomond Is Scotland’s Most Charming New Stay

Even if you have never set foot in Scotland, there is a good chance you already know the chorus to “The Bonnie Banks o’ Loch Lomond.” The wistful 18th-century folk ballad—all about taking the high road or the low road back to the country’s largest and arguably most romantic expanse of water—has cropped up everywhere from The Simpsons to, well, every Scottish wedding on earth.

But for the millions of travelers who actually make the pilgrimage up the A82 highway from Glasgow each year, the experience of those famous shores is often reduced to a fleeting blur of slate-blue water through a car window as they head deeper into the Highlands. Even for those who do pull over in Luss—an almost absurdly pretty conservation village of climbing rose-covered sandstone cottages and slate roofs on the loch’s western shore—it has historically been for a quick stroll down the pier (and maybe an ice cream) before getting right back on the road.

Yet when I arrived in Luss on a gloriously sunny weekend in late summer, the village was in peak form, filled with hikers in boots and day-trippers clutching coffees and ambling down the winding lanes toward the glittering water. And as I pulled up to the newly reopened Loch Lomond Arms, I spotted a steady stream of curious locals popping their heads through its antler-crowned yellow door. Set inside a 17th-century former coaching inn at the heart of this tiny community of just 120 residents, the property has long been a beloved local watering hole. And now, following a whirlwind six-month transformation, it’s been reborn as one of Scotland’s most characterful new stays.

The mastermind behind this reinvention is Patrick Colquhoun—son of the current chief of Clan Colquhoun (pronounced ka-hoon, for the uninitiated), the family that has held the surrounding 45,000-acre Luss Estate for more than 800 years—who enlisted the celebrated British interior designer Russell Sage to help breathe new life into the building. Sage is no stranger to high-end Scottish hospitality, having previously conjured the maximalist wonderland of The Fife Arms in Braemar, the whimsical, art-stuffed Victorian hotel backed by mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth.

Here, though, the brief was intentionally more modest. “I said right from the outset, it’s a coaching inn and it’s a pub—we’re not trying to be a five-star hotel,” Sage tells me. Colquhoun felt similarly, noting that while Scotland has seen plenty of big-budget luxury openings over the past decade, he wanted “an inn where the design, the food, and the welcome are taken as seriously as they would be in a grand hotel, but where you can still find yourself mixing with local residents.”

That sense of laid-back, unpretentious warmth was evident the moment I crossed the threshold. There is no formal reception desk; instead, I was greeted like an old pal by a member of the affable, mostly local team decked out in butterscotch yellow waistcoats, and ushered into the Map Room, a snug where pink velvet chairs and sturdy antique tables sit beneath a ceiling papered entirely in vintage hand-drawn charts inherited from Colquhoun’s grandfather. After a marathon journey involving three connecting flights to reach Glasgow—and coming off the back of a particularly hectic week that had left me feeling a little under the weather—the lack of fuss was firmly appreciated. Better still was what awaited upstairs when I was led to my bedroom: a golden dram of Scotch whisky and a plate of crumbly cheese straws laid out on a side table. I snacked on a straw and opened my window, plunking myself down onto the super-king four-poster bed to let the loch-side air work its magic. (By which I mean: I fell into a coma-like stupor.)

After rousing myself for a wander around, I discovered there are no room numbers at the Loch Lomond Arms. Instead, each of the 15 bedrooms (which start at a remarkably reasonable rate, given the pedigree) is named after an eccentric figure or episode from the Colquhoun family history, brought to life after Sage and his team were let loose on eight centuries of archives, attics, and outbuildings. “Fifteen rooms turns out to be about the right number,” Colquhoun jokes. “If we had 30 we might have run out of colorful relatives!”

I was ensconced in The Wallabies, an ocean-blue suite layered with tartan and curiosities that looks out over the rooftops of the village. Its name pays tribute to Patrick’s great-aunt, Fiona Colquhoun—later the Countess of Arran—who in the 1940s famously packed a mob of red-necked wallabies into the back of her E-Type Jaguar and released them onto the nearby island of Inchconnachan, where a wild colony still hops around to this day. (In a delightful touch, if I wanted my sheets changed, I simply had to leave the stuffed toy wallaby provided on the bed.)

On a subsequent tour of the property, every corner of the inn seemed to burst with history. Rather than purchasing new furniture, Sage’s team stripped, restored, and hand-painted heirloom pieces pulled straight from the family’s cupboards and drawers. “The idea of getting people engaged with a place through telling its stories is really important to me,” Sage explained. You can see it in the hallway’s stuffed lion, a nod to Patrick’s great-grandfather Sir Iain, who casually took a pet lion cub with him to the trenches during World War I (and was later court-martialed for keeping a written account of the 1914 Christmas truce). Or in Nova Scotia Love Potion, a russet-walled room tucked into the eaves with cabinetry hand-painted by artist Lizzie Bentley, dedicated to a 16th-century ancestor dubbed “the last witch in Scotland” after he concocted an illicit elixir to seduce his sister-in-law. Yes, really.

Most delightful of all, perhaps, is the room dedicated to the aforementioned Countess of Arran’s later years, when she walked a pet badger around Luss on a leash—and, at the age of 62, piloted a powerboat at 102 miles per hour to earn the moniker “the fastest granny on the water” in the British tabloids. “We had 800 years of history sitting in the family archives and a building in the village that seemed a perfect opportunity to bring the stories to life,” Patrick notes. There are QR codes subtly etched on panels on the doors that tell those stories, which could easily be the basis for a particularly unhinged Wes Anderson film—if he decided to make one set around a Scottish loch, that is. (Get writing, Wes.)

Those ancestral tales spill out of the bedrooms and into the surrounding landscape, with guest excursions designed around the very figures whose portraits line the walls. While my lingering travel fatigue meant I reluctantly had to skip a speedboat trip across the loch to Inchconnachan aboard the Beau Jangles—for this, you’ll channel the free-wheeling spirit of Lady Arran by roaring between the loch's wooded islands and dropping anchor for a glass of champagne—I did manage to head out on an exhilarating 4x4 safari into the dramatic hill ground rising behind the village. Bumping along rugged tracks, we passed through sweeping glens and areas of active peatland and native woodland restoration—part of a centuries-old commitment to conservation that makes the wild, cinematic beauty of the Highlands feel newly alive.

Honestly, though, if you need a proper recharge, there’s no shame in spending the bulk of your stay simply hunkered down inside the inn. (I say this partly to justify the fact that is what I mostly did.) What truly elevates the Loch Lomond Arms from a handsome design project into a soul-restoring getaway is its staff, most of whom hail from the local area. I spent a lovely afternoon being guided around the town by the church beadle John Taylor, whose genuinely fascinating insights into local history—I was particularly dazzled by a Viking gravestone dating back to the 11th century in the churchyard—proved that Luss has been drawing raucous overseas tourists for well over a millennium. (John even came decked out in a kilt and a sporran for our wander, an impressive display of local dedication given the afternoon heat.) And that local spirit was especially apparent on the food and beverage front, overseen by the endlessly knowledgeable Matt, who guided me through an early-evening tasting in the Map Room as a fire crackled in the hearth; I regularly spotted him throughout my stay whizzing around pouring rare Scottish malts, alongside small-batch spirits from the village’s own Luss Distillery, for other guests.

Then, there’s the food in the inn’s bustling pub and dining room, The Stag & Two Hounds, where the walls are wrapped in bespoke Trossachs-inspired wallpaper by Dundee artist Freya Cumming and the kitchen leans heavily on produce reared, caught, or foraged on the estate. My dinner began with crisp pork and apple croquettes—delivering all the hearty comfort of a Sunday roast in just a few sweet-and-savory bites—followed by silky slivers of Scottish salmon, cured in-house, of course. The real showstopper, however, was a killer steak and Lomond ale pie: tender estate beef slow-braised in dark and malty local beer beneath a lid of buttery pastry. (And for those planning a visit soon, there’s even more to look forward to on the culinary front: alongside the sun-dappled outdoor tables of The Gathering, the team is gearing up to unveil The Treasury, an intimate, candlelit fine-dining room hidden behind a curtain that will showcase the very best of the estate’s larder atop priceless family heirlooms.)

By the time I packed my bags to head back to Glasgow Airport—feeling entirely, miraculously restored after 48 hours of Highland hospitality—the Loch Lomond Arms had done exactly what it set out to do. And, it turns out, this is just the beginning of an ambitious new chapter for Luss Estates, which also offers a collection of charming historic cottages for rent around the village and has plans to bring the same design-led, high-craft ethos to future projects across the land. To paraphrase that famous old ballad: the banks of Loch Lomond just got a wee bit more bonnie.

#6702. Who Is Elizabeth Holmes’s Partner, Billy Evans?

This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.

When Nathan Fielder asked Elizabeth Holmes to document the days leading up to her serving her prison sentence for his new A24 documentary, You Can See Everything, the proposition meant that he would also be spending a large portion of the shoot with Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans.

The documentary spends time delving into Holmes’s public legal scandal with Theranos—the now-defunct biotech company that saw her committing investment fraud—but it also sheds light on Holmes and Evans’s relationship and how they have managed to thrive despite her sentencing.

As the documentary, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, progresses, Fielder’s focus shifts from Holmes to Evans. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asked him at one point, to which Evans responded, “100 percent, but what does she have to gain from me?” When presented with the knowledge of his family’s wealth, Evans defended Holmes and said, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.” Things only snowball from there.

Evans’s grandparents, William and Anne Evans, own the Evans Hotel Group. Founded in 1953, Evans Hotels consists of three luxury properties, which include The Lodge Terry Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel, and the Catamaran Resort Hotel and Spa. All three of the properties are located in California.

Evans’s LinkedIn profile revealed that he attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology between 2011 and 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree in economics.

Evans’s LinkedIn also revealed that he’s the CEO of Haemanthus, his self-founded AI-driven medical testing startup; he’s held the role since 2022. The company aims to achieve a mission similar to that of Holmes’s Theranos, which sought to provide blood diagnostics through one drop of blood with the Edison machine. Instead of using one drop of blood for diagnostics, Haemanthus is working to create a device that tests blood in addition to urine and saliva for the presence of diseases.

“This is not Theranos 2.0. Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests. Our approach is fundamentally different. We use light to read the complete molecular story in biological fluids, seeing patterns current tests can’t detect. Not an improvement. A different paradigm,” the company shared in a statement to Fortune in 2025, following reports of Holmes advising on the project. “Setting the record straight. Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement in Haemanthus. We’ve learned from her company’s mistakes, but she has no role, now or future.”

In a 2023 joint interview with The New York Times, Evans revealed that he and Holmes fell for each other fast. “To say we immediately fell in love isn’t an overstatement,” he said.

Holmes, however, noted that Evans had some reservations about entering a relationship with her. “It had been two years of all this stuff written about me, and I think you get to know someone in a totally different way when you walk in with that skepticism versus if you meet when everything is sunshine and roses,” she said. “That allowed us to get to know each other in a really deep way.” The couple got engaged in August 2018.

Holmes gave birth to their son, William Holmes Evans, in 2021. By 2023, a court document revealed that Holmes gave birth to her and Evans’s second child, a daughter named Invicta.

Evans attended several of Holmes’s court dates, appearing by her side on the way to and from her hearings. In January 2022, she was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. She’s currently serving her sentence—which was reduced to nine years from 11 years—at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas. She will be transferred to a halfway house in August 2027.

While Holmes was sentenced, Evans asked the court in November 2022 to shorten her sentence so she could enjoy more special moments with their son. “My heart is broken with the thought of spending any days away from Liz, for a future in which my son grows up with a relationship with his mother on the other side of glass armed by guards,” he said. Evans still visits Holmes regularly, with him telling People in February 2025 that it has been “hell and torture” at the prison facility. The tech CEO added that it “shatters” Holmes when she says goodbye to him and her family.

You Can See Everything makes some shocking revelations about Evans, like that he posts from Holmes’s X account while she’s in prison (for a while, it was without her knowledge), and that he arranged to be paid for his and Holmes’s appearance in the documentary, which he ultimately rescinded. (It’s unclear whether Holmes knew about the deal.)

During a screening of the film in L.A. this month, Fielder said of the couple, “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it.” He added, according to The Hollywood Reporter, that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

Evans confirmed that he hasn’t seen the film during an interview with the All In podcast, which was released on October 15. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said, per Variety. He has seen the trailer and said that Holmes “looks insane” in it. Evans added, “Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure. With this, there’s certainly concern, but it’s ultimately our decision.”

On November 3, Evans revealed the “one misconception” about his relationship with Holmes following the release of the movie: “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious,” he responded to an X user.

Evans added, “She’s fiercely independent, strong willed, and my best friend. We are partners in every sense. We challenge each other, disagree, and face the world together. Her closest friends are also some of my closest friends. If I ever mistreated her, they’d have my head.”

In a separate tweet, Evans revealed that he misses “everything about [Holmes].” He wrote, “I miss her presence. Her touch. The way she runs her fingers through my hair. Her patience. She makes me a better person. And without her, I feel an emptiness that’s hard to describe. People often say they need someone when what they really mean is that they want them. I’ve thought a lot about that distinction. I need Liz. She should qualify as a medically necessary prescription.”

On All In, Evans elaborated on why he wanted to make the film ahead of Holmes’s 11-year sentence. “She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape, or form, and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” he said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was: Here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”

He explained that his own loved ones have thought he was “crazy” for knowing—and now being in a relationship with—Holmes. “And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift,” Evans said. “That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”

#6701. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6700. 25 Great Gifts for New Dads, According to GQ

Becoming a dad changes a lot of things. Your sleep schedule, for one. Your relationship with a clean shirt, for another. But just because a guy has entered his daddy era doesn't mean he's stopped caring about the things he cared about before.

With that in mind, we've rounded up the best gifts for new dads, with a little something for him and the little one. Some are practical things that'll make those early days of fatherhood a little easier. Others are simply things that'll make him feel good, look good, and a little more like himself.

Nothing doing? Check out the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

At some point, he'll emerge back into the world, and there's nothing like a great shirt to ease the reentry. This swaggy checked shirt from Beams has all the layering built right in, so he can look like he hasn't missed a step.

There's a lot to be said for clothes that don't require much thought, especially when you've got a new bundle. Take this double-faced merino wool bomber from Quince: warm, unfussy, and easy to throw on with just about anything.

Some brands really are thinking of the children. Everybody.World makes its Trash Zip Hoodie from 100% recycled cotton waste, giving discarded material a second life as a very good sweatshirt.

A good pair of sweatpants is nonnegotiable. From the true masters of the category, these midweight terry sweatpants from Reigning Champ come with a relaxed silhouette, an open hem, and a nicely lived-in patina.

The undisputed king of dad shoes has entered its seventh generation, with its first major redesign since 2022 bringing a sleeker suede-and-mesh upper, softer cushioning, and all the Made in USA pedigree you'd expect. For a guy who's just become a dad, the timing couldn't be better.

He's a dad now. A man of refinement, responsibility, and a pressing need for a do-it-all boot. Enter Blundstone's new Heritage boot, a top-shelf take on its legendary shit-stomper, upgraded with premium leather and Goodyear-welted construction.

The baby's developing a sense of sight, and there's no reason for dad to sacrifice his. Lalo's Play Gym II is a far better-looking alternative to what's out there, with plenty to keep little hands and eyes occupied, including sensory toys, teethers, and a bell. The brand's set of high-contrast art cards wouldn't hurt, either.

If they've already got a Tripp Trapp, this one's a no-brainer. The iconic high chair is part of MoMA's permanent collection, and now the museum's Design Store has a set of colorful cushions to go with it.

One thing new parents can never have enough of is a good place to put the baby down. Part quilt, part playmat, these organic cotton numbers from House of Noa are among the most handsome we've seen, with an heirloom quality that makes 'em worth holding on to long after the baby has outgrown tummy time.

The problem with BabyBjörn? Too many good things to choose from. But for new parents, the gift of a few hands-free minutes is hard to beat. The new Bouncer Begin is designed specifically for newborns, with a shallower seat than the brand's wildly popular Bouncer Bliss.

Bottle-washing is a dad duty. We don't make the rules. Baby Brezza's Bottle Washer Pro 360 makes the job considerably less miserable, washing, sterilizing, and drying bottles in one go.

Two things you can never have enough of with a newborn: muslin and blankets. Coyuchi's wonderfully soft muslin quilt takes care of both.

New dads live by the clock. Three hours between feeds, 20 minutes until the next nap, two minutes to themselves, if they're lucky. Braun's Time Teacher, with its clean, easy-to-read dial, colorful hands, and markings for phrases like "quarter past" and "half past," makes keeping track a little easier. And when the little one is old enough to tell time, it'll come in handy all over again.

Apple's finally getting into the smart display game. The new HomeView is the company's first dedicated smart home hub, bringing home controls, FaceTime, and the usual Apple ecosystem conveniences to one ittle screen. Its 12-megapixel camera should come in especially handy for keeping the grandparents supplied with baby sightings.

A sleeping baby is a beautiful thing. Hatch's portable Go sound machine is a little godsend, with soothing sounds, a rechargeable battery, and a handy clip for attaching it to the stroller or car seat.

Bose's new sport-minded open earbuds let him enjoy his music or a podcast without tuning out what's happening around him—like, say, an actual human baby. And on the rare occasion he gets out for a run, they'll be just as useful for logging a few miles.

For the dad with his hands full (read: all dads), Ray-Ban's Meta Zena glasses pair a snazzy cat-eye silhouette with the ability to capture first steps, film stroller outings, or video-call the grandparents, all without reaching for his phone.

Tiny Vinyl's miniature record player and four-inch records are pure novelty, but there's something rather charming about a tiny turntable for a tiny human. Start building the little one's record collection now, and they'll have something to grow into.

Fujifilm's new Instax Pal 2 gives dad another way to document his little one, packing a digital camera into an adorable, palm-sized package. He can send shots straight to his phone, or pair it with an Instax printer for a few keepsakes the grandparents can stick on the fridge.

there's something to be said for having a few memories you can actually hold in your hands. This new 35mm point-and-shoot from Kodak lets him capture the little one on film, with actual prints to show for it.

Coterie diapers really do live up to the hype. And the brand's skincare lineup is pretty terrific, too. This set brings together full-size bottles of its hair and body wash, all-over moisturizer, and diaper and dry skin balm.

Dad's going to need all the help he can get in the sleep department. No surprise there. What might surprise him is how much magnesium can help, from supporting normal muscle and nerve function to regulating the body's stress response and potentially improving sleep quality.

The Fitbit Air might be the sleekest screen-free fitness tracker around, and at a price that makes it an easy sell. For the new dad who just wants to keep tabs on his sleep and daily steps without getting too deep into the fitness-data weeds, it's a straightforward proposition.

A little time for some om-ing is a fine idea for any new dad. Walden's meditation set gives him a dedicated place to find his center, and the accompanying mat doubles as a nice spot for the little one to stretch out.

#6699. The Cheesecake Factory Drama, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered Italy’s looming food shortage.

Well, it’s over. Last Ditch, the bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that became the center of a tornado of scrutiny, ridicule, discourse, and, er, media coverage a few weeks ago is now closed as it searches for new co-owners, or to sell the bar to new owners. If your memory needs a refresh, the TL;DR is that the bar relaxed its COVID-conscious mask restrictions, and it tore the local community apart.

The Boston Globe covered the drama, and the story quickly went viral. But despite—or perhaps because of—its newfound infamy, the bar couldn’t attract enough clientele to stay open. Could new owners resurrect the beleaguered business?

Also in the discourse this week: Washington, DC residents will be voting on a foie gras ban which has prominent chefs coming out as firmly pro-foie, despite public backlash. José Andrés argues that the American food system also mistreats many other animals—and that we have bigger issues, like child hunger, to address.

Also in today’s Open Tab: why The Cheesecake Factory has made headlines this week, how salmon could decide Alaska’s midterm elections, a delivery platform acquisition for the ages, and a look inside LA’s buzzy Skywalker Grill.

This week the Cheesecake Factory’s name was splashed across headlines in a handful of national magazines and newspapers—a feat that hasn’t happened since…ever? It’s hard to say.

This story starts last weekend, when former president Barack Obama made a joke at a campaign rally in Ohio. “[President Trump’s] got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere,” he said.

Trump himself responded on Monday. “For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” he told reporters. The White House X account followed up with some AI-generated trolling.

Rick McCormack, the chain’s former vice president of design, also weighed in. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that sound bite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” he said.

Is the Cheesecake Factory designed to look like it was done by an Egypt-obsessed kid with an unrestricted budget and a lot of ambition? Yes. But that’s part of its charm. You need a maximalist setting to match a maximalist menu, a maximalist experience. As I see it, The Cheesecake Factory is designed as it is so that ordering an “all day morning cocktail” (?), or a slice of “Brownie Crunch Choc-o-Lot Cheesecake” suddenly doesn’t seem so crazy. The Cheesecake Factory, as we were reminded again and again this week, is an American institution. So, unfortunately, is a quips-based, sound-byte-heavy political system.

And don’t feel too bad about the beleaguered corporate chain, which operates 200-plus locations. The C-suite is laughing their way to the bank: Stock analysts were quick to point out it is among the highest performing stocks on the market.

A few weeks ago a friend who grew up in Alaska told me nonchalantly that the state’s upcoming primary would be decided by salmon. “It’s the only thing that matters,” he said.. According to a recent feature in the New Yorker, it looks like he was right.

For many Alaskans fishing is both a job and a way to nourish their family. The democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, even settled on the slogan ““Fish, Family, Freedom.” But in recent years, runs of king salmon and chum salmon have collapsed, and don’t seem to be recovering. Experts point to climate change, but activists point to the practice of trawling—a method of fishing that includes pulling an enormous net behind the boat— for pollack which also catches millions of salmon which get killed and discarded by fishermen.

“This is an ecological crisis, a cultural trauma, an economic emergency and a public-health disaster,” reads one op-ed in an Alaskan paper.

Today in sentences that a Victorian tween wouldn’t understand a single word of: Delivery platform DoorDash, most recently in the news for its new fleet of drones, will buy Instacart for $17 billion.

It’s hard to overstate just how enormous this deal will be. Instacart is among America’s dominant platforms for grocery delivery, and DoorDash corners the market on the country's restaurant delivery apparatus.

The size of the acquisition would, under most administrations, attract FTC scrutiny. This is a pretty big consolidation in the field, after all. But the Trump administration has been particularly permissive of giant companies coming together to maximize their joint slay. In this case “joint slay” means market share and monopoly.

Museums must have a buzzy restaurant attached these days, and Los Angeles’s Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is no different. That’s where you’ll find Skywalker Grill, which, despite its monied environs, features a menu that’s surprisingly approachable. As Bon Appétit contributor Khushbu Shah tells us, it’s quickly become one of the city’s hottest tables. She takes us inside the restaurant to break down its surprisingly accessible menu.

#6698. The Beast in Me Season 2: Everything We Know So Far

Netflix’s The Beast in Me brought Claire Danes back to TV and reunited her with creator Howard Gordon, with whom she spent eight seasons working on Homeland. That combination was already exciting enough, but the cast also included Matthew Rhys and Brittany Snow, and Conan O’Brien and Jodie Foster were among the producers.

Danes stars as Aggie, a successful author grappling with the grief of losing her son. Her fragile sense of stability is shaken when Nile (Rhys), a wealthy real estate figure once accused of murdering his wife, moves in next door. With just eight episodes, the series left viewers wondering whether Aggie’s story could continue beyond its initial run. Here’s what we know so far.

Yes. In September 2026, Variety confirmed that The Beast in Me would return for a second season on Netflix.

“We always told ourselves we’d only do a second season of The Beast in Me if we found a story that was worthy of the first—and I’m thrilled to say we found it,” Gordon said in a statement. “We loved making this show and our audience seemed to love watching it, so we’re enormously grateful to Jinny Howe and Netflix, and to Karey Burke and 20th Television for giving us the chance to get the band back together and do it again.”

Variety’s report confirmed that Danes would return to her role for The Beast in Me season 2. In October 2026, Deadline reported that John Goodman (Righteous Gemstones, Digger) would star as “Aggie’s dad, believed to be a long-time con artist.”

In November 2026, Deadline revealed that Lili Taylor (Outer Range, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping) joined the cast in a series regular role as Fiona, Aggie’s stepmother.

Gordon discussed the ending of season 1 with The Wrap and what it made him consider for season 2.

“I think that to the extent that Aggie is a writer who has been delivered to this next stage of her life, whatever that stage is,” he shared at the time. “If there is a story, there might be more. I am tempted by the character of her grifter father in some way. We’ll see how the show does and if an idea comes. But I think they’d be open to more.”

#6697. Emma Chamberlain Shares Her “Objects of Affection”

We’ve all seen just how glorious Emma Chamberlain’s L.A. home is—but have you ever wondered what the star’s most prized possessions are inside? If you have, we’ve got answers. In a new Vogue video, we dropped in on Chamberlain at home to explore what her personal “objects of affection” are. The short answer? One-of-a-kind items she simply cannot live without—from art to fashion and more.

Chamberlain began her house tour with a few of her fashion must-haves. She can’t imagine a day, for one, without using her everyday bags—including a Prada black shoulder schlepper or a green Comme des Garçons style. “I’m emotionally attached to these two bags—they’ve been everywhere with me,” she says. Then it was onto her most-worn shoes, including a white pair of the polarizing and fabulous footwear style, Margiela Tabis.

Next, the star took us to her gallery wall to share a few of her favorite art pieces, including a self-portrait. “I absolutely hate it, but I do like the eyes,” she says. There was also the abstract wooden sculpture-slash-painting of … a butt. “I got it at an antique store,” says Chamberlain. “It balances humor and aesthetic.” Also included in the mix were family heirlooms, like paintings passed down to her from her grandmother, or works made by her father. “There’s probably 20,” she says of her dad’s creations. “For the most part, he does a lot of landscapes.”

As for some of the more unexpected objects you can find in Chamberlain’s cabinet of curiosities? A big movie poster of Napoleon Dynamite (her favorite film), a drum kit—”I’ve been practicing and making some. . . improvements,” she says—and a wigged mannequin that she calls her body double. “I purchased her as a prop for my podcast set,” says Chamberlain. “She told me she wants to be called Emma.” There are two Emmas in the Chamberlain household.

#6696. Ralph Lauren’s 17 Best Outfits of All Time

On Monday night, the Council of Fashion Designers of America crowned Ralph Lauren as its menswear designer of the year—his 12th win since the show’s inaugural ceremony in 1981, minting him as the most decorated designer in CFDA history. The council even has a tradition of creating awards in Lauren’s honor, as they did with the Fashion Legend Award in 2007 and the CFDA Members Salute in 2018.

At age 87, Lauren is the consummate businessman of American fashion, and he’s still producing masterclass-caliber collections that build upon his label’s established codes. In addition to his business savvy and keen eye for tailoring, the designer remains as relevant as ever in 2026 because of something far more ineffable: a deep-rooted sense of personal style. For Lauren, clothes aren’t just a wardrobe; they are identity. His own relationship with getting dressed, from his deep and abiding love of Westernwear to his knack for blending Waspy blazers with rugged workwear and military pieces, has always been at the core of everything he does. Here are some of his best looks from the last 50 years.

Technical hiking gear was a relatively late addition to the RL oeuvre, but the man was wearing hikers in the city long before hipsters discovered Salomons.

Like a skilled party DJ, Ralph Lauren has an uncanny knack for combining unlikely elements—like a yachtsman’s sweater and a pair of worn-in blue jeans—with complete ease.

There’s black-tie, and then there’s RL black-tie. There’s no doubt that Lauren can wear a pair of tuxedo pants and patent leather shoes as well as anyone, but he is much more himself in jeans and cowboy boots.

A two-year stint at Baruch College in Manhattan was the closest Lauren came to the Ivy League, but that didn’t stop him from adopting repp ties, Oxford collar shirts, and other hallmarks of the East Coast elite. The juxtaposition of oversized aviator shades with this solidly trad look is quintessential Ralph.

Think a funky belt can’t be the defining element of an otherwise understated fit? Lauren would respectfully disagree.

Few people will ever look as good in a biker jacket as Ralph Lauren did at age 70. The difference is in the details—the flannel shirt unbuttoned and tucked, the crisp white henley—and the confidence.

Lauren is a master editor, but the magic of his greatest looks is in details like a vest tucked into trousers, a knotted belt, and a pair of precisely rolled sleeves.

Yacht club up top, honkey tonk downstairs. Another Lauren signature.

Ralph Lauren never learned how to sew, but he has an instinctive understanding of tailoring. By blending the stiff silhouettes of Savile Row with the breezy swagger of American ivy style, he created a look that was all his own.

Style is all about understanding the rules before you can break them. Lauren certainly does, and that’s why this ensemble—from the wide-spread collar and slim tie combination to the double-down on stripes—works as well as it does.

There’s perhaps no more challenging look to pull off than “office cowboy,” but Ralph Lauren makes it look easy.

Leather pants and a denim shirt under a tweed jacket is another decidedly advanced maneuver, but (if executed correctly) a potentially powerful one.

In recent decades, Lauren has increasingly swapped his signature cowboy boots for La Sportiva hikers, anointing gorpcore in the process.

Lauren has always revered the look of traditional British tailoring, from safari suits to Savile Row, but he’s just as likely to pair his flannel suits with cashmere turtlenecks and cowboy boots as neckties and Oxfords.

#6695. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6693. Colin Jost Takes Gift-Giving Seriously

The Weekend Update co-host and Kay campaign star shares his approach to holiday shopping.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Finding the perfect holiday gift isn’t easy. Between the pressure to get it right, the endless wish lists, and the people who insist they don’t want anything, shopping for loved ones can feel like an impossible mission. Even Colin Jost, who has spent years navigating the pressures of live television, admits that the process is incredibly stressful.

This festive season, the Weekend Update co-host is putting his comedic talents to work with Kay by starring in the jeweler’s latest holiday campaign, “Love All In.” The cheeky ad follows Jost on an increasingly ridiculous quest to find the perfect present, poking fun at the lengths we’ll go to for the people closest to us. It’s a fitting partnership for someone who knows a thing or two about making people laugh but also takes gifting pretty seriously.

“I think I’m a good gift giver,” Jost tells ELLE. “Giving gifts is stressful because I do want it to be a meaningful gift. I hate the idea of just buying something because you have to give someone something.”

For Jost, the secret to getting it right has less to do with how much you spend and more to do with how much thought goes into it. “At every kind of price point for any gift, there [are] thoughtful and unthoughtful versions,” he says. “Something can be really expensive but not thoughtful.”

It’s a sentiment that aligns with Kay’s latest campaign, which encourages shoppers to go “all in” when expressing their love. And while Jost might not be the first person you’d think to turn to for jewelry advice, he’s developed an appreciation for it over the years, thanks to his very chic wife, Scarlett Johansson.

“Until five years ago, I didn’t own a watch,” he admits. That changed when the actress gifted him his first one, introducing him to an entirely new world of accessories. As for whether she’s influenced his personal style? “In that it’s exclusively managed by her, yes, I would say she’s influenced it.”

Despite his Staten Island roots, Jost’s jewelry preferences are surprisingly understated. “I don’t really wear a ton of jewelry, but I also am from Staten Island, so I do have to have certain pieces, or else they won’t let me back over the Verrazano Bridge,” he jokes.

While browsing Kay’s assortment, he found himself drawn to simple gold pieces, including a ring, bracelet, and necklace. “They were really nice, but also they weren’t gaudy or anything,” he says. His preference for gold also comes with some rather unconventional reasoning: “If we get into a post-apocalyptic situation, it feels like it’s better to melt down for trading.”

When it comes to shopping for the people closest to him, Jost admits that both Johansson and his Weekend Update collaborator Michael Che are difficult to buy things for, though he found a creative solution for the latter. “I got Che a really large and heavy, realistic statue of a velociraptor,” he recalls. “It was so heavy that he literally can’t get rid of it.” The real expense wasn’t the dinosaur itself. “The main cost was shipping,” he says. “It was a huge eyesore, and it’s prohibitively expensive for him to have removed from his property.”

The hardest person to gift on Jost’s list? His father, who insists he doesn’t need anything. “I think he actually means it, but it’s so unhelpful,” Jost says. After years of nostalgic gifts inspired by his dad’s past, he’s running out of ideas. “I’ve got to figure out something that breaks through his defenses.”

In terms of gifting etiquette, Jost has a few rules of his own. For starters, he’s big on surprises. While he understands the appeal of a wish list for children, he thinks adults should leave a little room for the unexpected. “For adults, it’s got to be ‘surprise me,’” he says. “The surprise is half the fun, three-quarters of the fun.” Regifting, on the other hand, comes with a few conditions. He’s open to the idea, but only if the gift is a perfect fit for someone and there’s full disclosure.

But perhaps the most surprising revelation comes when I ask what’s on his own holiday wish list. After spending much of our conversation discussing what to buy everyone else, Jost seems relieved to finally be on the receiving end. “Oh, thank you! Finally, someone asked me. What do I want?”

His answer? Nothing material. “At this point in life, I mostly want experiences,” he says. Whether it’s a trip or simply someone taking the initiative to organize an outing, he’s more interested in making memories than collecting more things. “Even if it’s just the plan of, ‘Let’s go do this at this time,’ I think that’s a great gift.” Or, when in doubt, a velociraptor.

#6692. Everything We Know About The Batman: Part II Thanks to… Heidi Klum?

If you’d told me even a month ago we’d get significant spoilers for The Batman: Part II, the next Robert Pattinson-led Batman movie, in a photo Heidi Klum posted for her annual Halloween costume, I would find that both weirdly specific and entirely unbelievable.

And yet, that looks to be exactly what happened this past weekend when prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted BTS photos of the work prosthetics expert Mike Marino (who also worked to transform Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the first film and subsequent HBO Max series) was doing for Klum. If you’ve somehow been off-grid for the last few years, you may have missed that the famed supermodel takes Halloween incredibly seriously, frequently donning costumes with extensive makeup and designs that make her unrecognizable. This year was no exception, but it might have gone largely unnoticed had that photo not accidentally revealed clues about the upcoming superhero sequel, which is currently in production with an expected release date of February 18th, 2028.

In the photo, Marino, who provided a helping, ahem, hand in Klum’s costume together for the year, had a number of molds lingering in the background, which have seemingly confirmed that Brian Tyree Henry will play Two-Face, Sebastian Stan will play Victor Zsasz, and that Part II will feature the famed Court of Owls.

Henry’s mold appears to show the Atlanta actor with a disfigured face that mimics the iconic villain. Some, including me, in this very outlet, have, speculated that he might be playing either Dent or Detective Harvey Bullock, a hardened Gotham City cop who frequently works alongside Jim Gordon. But this seems to confirm it. Considering writer-director Matt Reeves has cited Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale’s The Long Halloween as an influence on his version of the Caped Crusader, it’s not ultimately a huge surprise, but perhaps a slight disappointment considering Reeves had stated his intention to move the sequel into uncharted territory by featuring a villain that had “never really been done in a film before.”

Which brings us to Victor Zsasz, who Stan seems to be playing. There was some speculation when he shaved his head upon joining the production he might be playing the character, but the cast looks to confirm the speculation. While the serial killer—who carves tally marks into his body for every person he’s killed—shows up in Batman Begins as a minor enforcer in Carmine Falcone’s crew, he’s got a much larger role in the comic books themselves. In Long Halloween, Zsasz is hired by Falcone to assassinate Dent before he's intercepted by Batman. Might Reeves look to flip the script here and disfigure Henry’s Dent in the process? This interpretation of Zsasz would certainly fit the extremely grounded approach Reeves took in the first installment. But there’s also some confusion here, as Stan was rumored to be playing Harvey when casting first broke and even went so far as to say he’d be playing the role in an interview over the summer. The French publication Le Journal du Dimanche did, however, later retract his statement.

The last accidental spoiler is a big scoop for comic book fans. Simply labeled “Owl 3,” this likely confirms that the Court of Owls will finally make their silver-screen debut. Created in 2012 by writer Scott Snyder and artist Greg Capullo, the Owls are one of the biggest new additions to the Batman canon in recent memory. The Court is a clandestine criminal society made up of Gotham’s wealthiest and most influential citizens, whose power and influence stretch back to the city’s earliest days. They have immeasurable resources and frequently deploy assassins, known as Talons, to do their bidding. This tracks with the story Reeves told in The Batman of a Gotham beset by a history of corruption. Owls are also bats' natural predators; so that, too, is bad news for Battinson.

While this potential leak is exciting and unexpected, it also raises doubts about the identity of Scarlett Johansson’s character, as she was rumored to be playing Harvey’s wife, Gilda Dent. Either way, never in a million lifetimes could we have guessed that Heidi Klum would be the one to spill the beans about one of the most anticipated comic book movies of the next few years.

#6690. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6689. 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November

As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

The good news? You don’t need to spend your whole Sunday cooking to make dinner feel special, so you’ll have plenty of time for that When Harry Met Sally rewatch. These 21 easy weeknight dinners deliver all the comfort without the commitment. There’s a three-ingredient pumpkin soup, gochujang chicken that gets a quick blast under the broiler, and a smoky one-pan pasta made with pantry staples. Plus a few Thanksgiving-adjacent flavors—sage, stuffing, squash—because the holiday is right around the corner.

Greek yogurt tenderizes the chicken quickly, but the real weeknight win is the broiler: just 15 minutes under high heat, and you’ve got dinner.

Juicy chicken meatballs and crisp-tender sesame green beans roast on opposite sides of the same sheet pan, streamlining both dinner prep and cleanup.

This speedy stir-fry recipe brings together thin strips of boneless pork shoulder and crisp-tender bok choy for a satisfying, weeknight-ready dinner.

Savory ground beef, fluffy scrambled eggs, and crisp vegetables turn a bowl of steamed rice into a satisfying Japanese dinner that’s ready in 35 minutes.

Give boxed stuffing mix a new lease on life with this clever, holiday-inspired crust. Mixed with Parmesan, lemon zest, parsley, and butter, it gives tender fish a golden, crispy topping. Genius.

Brushed with a sticky, sweet teriyaki sauce, then hurled under the broiler, this salmon develops a glossy, caramelized finish in a matter of minutes.

This easy sheet-pan dinner pairs tender cod with a savory chorizo topping. Big flavor, minimal effort, and only one pan to wash.

Canned chickpeas and frozen spinach make this richly spiced saag quick to prepare—and any leftovers taste even better the next day.

Inspired by satay, this saucy, lip-smacking tofu dish comes together in 30 minutes in just one skillet—so cleanup is a breeze.

Cheesy, creamy, and deeply comforting, these fondue-inspired beans bring a little alpine indulgence to an ordinary Tuesday. Serving them over crusty bread is a must.

Nutty brown butter, crunchy pecans, and hot Italian sausage make this an easy dinner bursting with fall flavors. One reader reports, “Made me feel like a 5-star chef.”

Buttery, garlicky shrimp scampi meets pasta in this weeknight-friendly dinner. A splash of white wine and a pinch of red pepper flakes make the sauce sing.

Canned butternut squash purée (find it by the canned pumpkin!) makes this cozy, cold-weather recipe come together in a snap. Vegetable broth and certified vegetarian parm keep it meat-free, but chicken broth works if that’s what you’ve got.

Four ingredients are all you need for these grown-up buttered noodles. Toasted almonds and parsley are totally optional, but add welcome texture and zing.

Pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and a gentle orange hue to this speedy ground beef chili, letting the flavors of the spices and aromatics shine.

Roasted squash, crispy bacon, and crunchy walnuts turn chopped salad into a proper fall dinner. Use pre-cut butternut squash to streamline prep.

This comforting chicken noodle soup is ideal for chilly evenings or sick days. Chicken breast, kabocha squash, and tiny ditalini cook right in the broth.

A vegetarian spin on the classic Reuben swaps in hearty kale for the meat but keeps the melty cheese and tangy sauerkraut. One reader reports, “I didn’t miss the pastrami one bit.”

Made almost entirely from pantry ingredients—S&B curry powder, red lentils, crushed tomatoes, and coconut milk—this cozy soup is, as one reviewer puts it, “way more delicious than it should be.”

When dinner needs to get on the table pronto, a tuna melt is hard to beat: pantry-friendly, cheesy, and comforting.

This fiery soup has a shockingly trim ingredient list: curry paste (we like Maesri), a can of pumpkin purée, and coconut milk. Perfect for busy November weeknights.

#6688. The Clarks Wallabee Goes Gorpcore

Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.

The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.

#6687. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6686. A Diwali Menu That’s Full of Joy (and Sticky Chicken Wings)

Growing up, I remember a steady stream of guests coming in and out of our home in the weeks leading up to Diwali. The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga. Our celebrations were led by women, my grandmother, mother, and aunts, who would meticulously clean the house and spend weeks preparing snacks and sweets. They taught me the art of hosting and how to share the joy of food with our community.

I came to associate Diwali with that sense of abundance, care, and graciousness. There was always more food than we needed, and always room for more people. When I moved to New York, I started to miss that deeply, so I began a tradition to share Diwali with my chosen family here, many of whom were experiencing the holiday through food for the first time.

I’m the kind of host who likes to enjoy her own party, which means being strategic about the menu. I lean on dishes like my homestyle chicken kari, which can be made ahead and tastes even better the next day. And then there are dishes that bring a little theater to the table, like the creamy rice pudding which gets torched before serving. I want food that feeds a crowd, feels special, and lets me spend less time in the kitchen and more time with the people I love.

Guests always ask me for this crowd-pleasing app. Japanese sweet potatoes have a creamy texture that pairs beautifully with the spicy, crunchy elements of chaat. Best of all, the spuds can be cooked ahead, with the toppings added just before serving. One less thing for you to do on the big day.

Wings reign supreme when it comes to a party appetizer, and these tamarind-glazed ones deliver tangy punch in every bite. The marinade combines tamarind purée, fish sauce, brown sugar, red pepper flakes, and cumin, with extra glaze brushed on for maximum flavor and char. Be sure to finish with fried onions for bonus crunch.

This tastes like you spent hours cooking, but actually it comes together in less than an hour. The best part? It’s even better the next day, making it ideal for hosting. Gently reheat the kari before guests arrive, letting the warm, heady spices fill your home before everyone gathers around the table.

Mushrooms are an underrated ingredient in Indian cooking, and this creamy masala puts the earthy veg front and center. Sautéing them in batches gives the shrooms beautifully caramelized edges, while deglazing the pot captures all those flavorful browned bits. Serve the masala with rice or warm flatbread to sop up all the savory sauce.

No Diwali celebration is complete without something sweet, but dessert doesn’t have to be elaborate to feel special. This recipe transforms a handful of pantry staples into a rich, creamy rice pudding. For a playful twist, finish it with a crackly brûléed sugar crust and serve with a scoop of mango sorbet.

#6685. 3 Key Takeaways From Lagos Fashion Week

Africa’s biggest and buzziest fashion week drew to a close on Sunday night with an intimate dinner held by Nigerian heavyweight designer Lisa Folawiyo, who returned to the official Lagos Fashion Week schedule after a seven-year break. The five-day event saw approximately 16,000 people in attendance, up from 15,000 last season. Some 65 designers flocked to the Nigerian metropolis to showcase their collections to an audience of press, influencers, and other industry figures.

This season, it was local talent who dominated the week, with several Nigerian designers showcasing their collections on and off-schedule. As with all Lagos Fashion Week events, shows happen on-site at the Federal Palace Hotel, while off-site shows take place around the city. Mainstay designers like Emmy Kasbit, Ugo Monye, and Sisano showcased their collections through a mix of presentations and runway shows. Other buzzy designers such as Hertunba welcomed guests to their new stores (in addition to their runway shows), while LFJ held her Spring/Summer 2027 runway at her concept store Akoko.

Even those who now show up at fashion week internationally like Iamisigo, who showcased her collection in Copenhagen, and Orange Culture and Fruché, who both presented their collections in Berlin, are committed to returning and being a part of the Lagos Fashion Week calendar, too.

Now in its 16th edition, the platform is gaining more international attention than ever before. International buyers and media were in town from the Middle East as well as neighboring African countries including Senegal and Ghana, while buzzy US influencers and models Eni Popoola and Alton Mason also flew in for the shows.

(Left) Jermaine Bleu, and Boyedoe (right).

During the week, guests gathered at the US General Consulate to witness Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week, receive an Excellence in Commercial and Creative Leadership Award from Consul General Brandon Hudspeth. Guests included Chioma Ude, founder of Africa International Film Festival, influencers Popoola and Akin Faminu, as well as designers like Ejiro Amos Tafiri. The award signifies Lagos Fashion Week’s ability to help springboard talent into the international market, particularly in the US.

“[Akerele] has built a platform that brings Nigerian fashion to the world,” said Consul General Hudspeth during Friday’s event. “American talent has found a home right here in Lagos. Last year, singer Ciara was right here making headlines on the Lagos runway during fashion week.” He also points to brands like US’s Tia Adeola and Studio 189, a label co-founded by actress Rosario Dawson, which have shown on the Lagos schedule.

Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week receiving an award from Brandon Hudspeth, the Consul General.

Beyond the runway, Nigerian designers are going global, Hudspeth acknowledged. “Nigerian designers are reaching American customers, and that creates business for Americans and Nigerians,” he added, pointing to New York-based e-commerce platform Moda Operandi, which holds digital trunk shows for Lagos Fashion Week designers, and trade shows like Coterie, which has featured local talent. “This, of course, is cultural diplomacy, but it is also commercial diplomacy, and the consulate is working to build these relations and connections.”

African designers who have spent more than two decades in the industry returned to the schedule, including Christie Brown and Lisa Folawiyo, as well as Bridget Awosika from Nigeria. “I feel it’s important that we were within the official calendar. It makes sense,” said Folawiyo. “It’s something I really thought about and I felt this is the right time.” The brand, which turned 21 years old this year, brought Lagos Fashion Week to a close with a candle lit five-course meal, surrounded by an intimate crowd of celebrities, influencers, friends and industry leaders.

For Ghana’s Christie Brown, returning to Lagos Fashion Week after an eight-year hiatus was part of a larger expansion strategy as the brand builds its presence across the continent. “As much as we’re building a global brand, we also do believe that there are certain key markets on the continent that we absolutely need to have a presence in,” said founder and creative director Aisha Ayensu. Those hotspots include Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa. “This is a re-entry into the market. We don’t want to come in guns blazing. We want to enter cautiously.” The brand now has a six-month residency at luxury retailer Temple Muse, giving local consumers an opportunity to shop Christie Brown pieces in Lagos.

Ugo Monye, the founder of his eponymous label, returned after a year-long break. The popular Nigerian designer explained that there’s an overwhelming pressure to create and prioritize design. Many simply enjoy the design process and do not pay attention to whether the backend business operations are in order. Unlike in the West, where designers are creating collections for four or more seasons, Monye and several African designers prefer to do one collection a year. He said his collections from two seasons ago are still in demand.

“Because I was having some backend issues, the workload was a lot and then to add fashion week on top of it, I just said, ‘You know what? Let me just take a break and catch my breath, then come back,’” he said, adding that he is the only person on his team overseeing the business. “Our industry is not fully structured yet, so you have to be a part of everything, even when you hire people.”

Despite the break, Monye is committed to showcasing in Lagos. “I’m not going anywhere. I’m here for a long time,” he said. “The brand [leaving] the fashion week calendar is out of the question.”

Showing during Lagos Fashion Week is increasingly important because of the rising media attention, said Abelia Anaba Franklyn, founder of couture house Weiz Dhurm Franklyn. “[Designers] want more coverage. It’s such an important moment in fashion, African fashion and Nigerian fashion,” she said. “Nigerians have the spending power. Once you have a distinct point of view that is not a regurgitation of another brand, people will acclimate toward you.” Now, the couturier is branching further into ready-to-wear where her pieces start from $600.

Elsewhere, others used fashion week as an opportunity to announce major business news. On Saturday, Post-Imperial shared that it was shutting down after 10 years. “I’ve said everything I needed to say with Post-Imperial,” said founder Niyi Okuboyejo backstage at his final show, which was a collaboration with Nigerian sustainable fashion brand This Is Us. Over the past decade, the brand built a strong wholesale model and was in over 200 retail stores, from Bergdorf Goodman in the US to Alára in Nigeria.

“Today’s a great day for me,” he added. “I also tried to expand the idea of what fashion is, and fashion shows aren’t necessarily just runway.” With this final collection, held in the courtyard, Okuboyejo gathered friends of the brands to walk the makeshift runway, including stylist Ugo Mozie, industrial designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello, and Dada Gallery’s Oyinkan Dada.

There’s often a misconception that Lagos Fashion Week is just for Nigerian designers. While they make up the majority, there are a handful of designers from across the continent who traveled to cash in on the buzz. This season saw some new and old international designers join the schedule, including Ghana’s Christie Brown and IGC Fashion from Uganda.

Unable to secure sponsorships in time, IGC Fashion self-funded its trip to Lagos Fashion Week, hoping to connect with media, a new audience and a larger fashion market. “We’re lacking media and big investors in the country. It’s a big opportunity for designers in Uganda to be at a stage like Lagos Fashion Week,” said brand founder Katende Godfrey.

Over in North Africa, Moroccan designer Scheherazade Essrhir shares a similar sentiment. After participating in Lagos Fashion Week’s Green Access, an incubator for young designers, Essrhir took some time away to perfect her craft. “Through Green Access, I learnt that being a designer is more than creating and designing. It’s a lot of work,” she said. “[At Lagos Fashion Week], they support us even when the show is over.” In Lagos, Essrhir feels she has support and community as the fashion week team schedules regular check-in calls and feedback.

From a business lens, South African designer Mzukisi Mbane, founder of Imprint ZA, believes Lagos is the place to be. “In South Africa, we have fashion shows. We have the glitz and the glamour. But for me, the bottom line is always important,” he said. “I want to be visible to people that can help the brand grow and be seen… even if [buyers] are not purchasing pieces, I’m still on their radar.” Mbane was named a recipient of this year’s Africa Fashion Up Award, an initiative dedicated to nurturing emerging regional designers, and will see him receive mentorship from Balenciaga, since the Kering-owned brand has on-going partnership with the platform.

British Nigerian designer Reni Abina chose to bring her collection to Lagos again this season. “As we expand internationally, it’s important to me that we remain connected to the city and the community that first embraced us,” Abina said. “We’ve always wanted to build a truly global fashion brand, but I don’t believe that global recognition should come at the expense of our roots.”

There were a handful of buyers in attendance this season, many of whom noticed a shift in the overall collections on display. “I’ve been coming [to Lagos Fashion Week] for a few years, and this is probably the most cohesive year that I’ve ever experienced,” says Arinola Fagbemi, a buyer at Lagos-based concept store Alara, adding that they are now building collections around who their client is and what they might want to buy from them.

Wearability is a key concern. This season, Alara partnered up with Lagos Fashion Week to host a showroom for designers after their runway shows. It’s a move that’s really helped buyers, including the Alara team, see the clothes in-person and gauge things like finishing, texture, and weight. Standout shows for her include Orange Culture, Dukun, and Orire. “We’re looking for the finishing. Clients are very discerning, especially the Alara client. They want things that are well made. They don’t care that it’s from Nigeria or from Africa. They expect the same level of detail,” she says.

African retailers are setting aside a separate budget for Lagos. “We’ve understood now that it works differently,” says Fagbemi, adding they do not follow the international buying calendar and place orders for every season. “The fortunate thing is that the turnaround time for a lot of African brands is very quick. So what we’re seeing on the runway now, many of them will have it ready for the holidays, because of Detty December [a festive period full of parties and live music events] and that peak period.” Alara buyers also attend Milan, London and Paris fashion weeks.

Viva Accra operates on a different model. “We have an allocation for African designers within our overall buying budget, rather than a completely separate budget for Lagos. It’s about finding the right brands and making considered buying decisions,” says Sacha Okoh, creative director and buyer at Viva Accra, a concept store in Ghana.

Lagos Fashion Week is an important discovery platform. “We have a genuine interest in growing our African designer offering,” continues Okoh, noting that the store currently carries a number of Nigerian and Ghanaian brands, but she is “always looking for designers whose work I feel can sit comfortably alongside our international labels.”

She adds: “A collection can be beautiful on the runway, but for me, it’s also about how those pieces translate into real wardrobes. I look for that balance between creativity, quality, wearability and commercial appeal.” Standout collections include Christie Brown, Jermaine Bleu and Boyedoe. Okoh regularly attends fashion weeks and trade shows in Milan, Paris, and London.

As Sunny Dolat, a researcher, consultant and Lagos Fashion Week SS27’s creative director, observes: “This year, the platform attracted an even larger international audience than last, with many visitors traveling to Nigeria specifically for fashion week,” he says. “This strongly indicates a platform that is not only well regarded and respected, but has firmly established itself as an important destination for discovering some of the most compelling design talent from across the African continent.”
