#6655. Carrie Coon Believes in the Future of American Fashion at the 2026 CFDA Awards

Much like her character Bertha Russell in HBO’s The Gilded Age, Carrie Coon is a strong, dynamic patron of the arts, with a burgeoning interest in fashion. That latter part of which her to the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards with American designer and CFDA member Nellie Partow yesterday evening.

“My relationship to fashion is nascent and so I am engaged in a process of education, but also discovery,” Coon told Vogue ahead of the big night. “I have had the pleasure of wearing established designers, but also many young, rising innovators, including independent female designers like Nellie Partow, who seeks out and champions strong, singular women.” Likewise, Partow shared her own adoration for the actress: “I’ve always admired women who are tenacious, grounded in who they are, and unapologetically themselves. Carrie embodies all of these qualities, which makes collaborating with her all the more meaningful,” she said.

Hair by Jimmy Paul & Make Up by Rebecca Restrepo.

Though Coon protests that she’s new to fashion, her CFDA Award gave off the energy of a well-seasoned attendee. It helps that this isn’t the first time that she’s donned a Partow creation. The two first connected through Coon’s stylist Alicia Lombardini while doing press alongside Elizabeth Olsen and Natasha Lyonne for the independent film, His Three Daughters. The form-fitting suit was an instant hit.

Final looks with creative director and founder Nellie Partow.

Dress is a 100% Silk Organza with ripstop Weave from a French mill founded in Lyon in the 1920s.

For yesterday evening, the dress’s inspiration was more of a feeling than a specific reference. On Coon’s end, she wanted to channel “a strong sense of self,” through the look’s vibrant fabric. “At 45, I have never felt more cohesive, and that integration is a solid foundation for taking risks,” she said. For Partow, the cerulean silk organza look was inspired by “a sense of levity and air.” (Like many things that exude ease, the dress still took over 100 hours to make.)

Nearly 100 hours of hand craftsmanship went into creating this custom Partow dress.

Great fashion often speaks to larger context than just the act of wearing clothes, and this storytelling is exactly what draws Coon to the industry. “Honestly, my occupations—actress and mother—always call me back to the present, and I am most focused on how we manifest a future that resists the story of the inevitability of a techno-fascist takeover,” she said. “Personal expression through fashion is a powerful avenue for asserting both our individuality and the creative potency of the human collective.”

Stepping onto the carpet at the 2026 CFDA.

Arriving at the Natural History Museum before walking the carpet.

#6654. The Best Teriyaki in Seattle

Who serves the best gorditas in Mexico City? Or Baltimore's can't-miss crab cakes? Welcome to Taste of the Town, where we call on a local expert to share the best versions of one of their city’s most iconic foods. Here, we explore Seattle’s take on teriyaki.

Seattle’s entire teriyaki universe exists because of one man, a pioneer of chargrilled chicken thighs. In 1976, Toshi Kasahara opened a restaurant serving lightly marinated and grilled chicken, glazed in a blend of soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sugar. This wasn’t any teriyaki you’d find in Japan, but a cheap, filling, flavor-packed translation aimed at a working-class city still unaware of the tech boom on the horizon.

Kasahara established and sold about 30 shops over the years, and copycats began copycatting. Teriyaki became ubiquitous, the Japanese name concealing its hometown heritage. Some locals don’t even realize teriyaki joints are a Seattle thing—that is, until they move elsewhere and try to find one.

Kitchens with Vietnamese roots began dishing up teriyaki alongside steaming bowlfuls of pho. Many spots still specialize in a classic interpretation, typically served with scoops of rice, some fried gyoza, and iceberg lettuce bathed in a thin mayo dressing. Enterprising Korean immigrants embraced teriyaki and opened their own outfits, adding bulgogi to the menu and gochujang to the chicken’s marinade.

The forward march of time, trends, and real estate prices means there’s sadly no longer a teriyaki business every few blocks. Those that remain include a few clunkers: Many have succumbed to shortcuts, serving sad chicken in gloopy, way-too-sweet gravy, which obscure the dish’s appeal to outsiders. But find a place still making its own sauce and blasting thighs on high heat, delivering bits of caramelized char that balance its teriyaki sweetness. Then you’ll understand.

Local wisdom dictates the best shop is the one closest to you, but here are eight greats, new and old.

Toshi Kasahara’s original restaurant, now long shuttered, was the archetype of a Seattle-style teriyaki spot—a spare cafeteria-like space with a streamlined menu built around Kasahara’s iconic chicken. Just a sprinkling of these shops still exist, but today only one is the real deal: a take-out operation deep in a Mill Creek strip mall. It’s open just a few hours in the evenings, with the 77-year-old Kasahara at the grill. He’s tweaked his methods slightly over the years, but his chicken is just as juicy and smoky as ever. No one in Seattle does it exactly like Toshi, but his sons do farther afield. One runs a Toshi’s food truck in San Francisco; the other is opening a Toshi’s outpost this winter in his father’s hometown of Ashikaga, Japan.

Hawaii has its own relationship to teriyaki. When restaurateur Matthew Parker opened his ode to the teriyaki counters that fueled his first 20 years in Seattle, he looked to his family’s roots in Oahu—specifically to huli huli chicken. That dish inspires Grillbird’s glossy house sauce, sweetened just enough with pineapple juice and ketchup. There’s no iceberg salad here; sides include mac salad and marinated cucumbers, dishes standard to plate lunch, Hawaii’s answer to the meat-and-three. Purists can grouse about how teriyaki shops should be old-school in every sense, but I welcome Grillbird’s modern touches, like online ordering and a mostly gluten-free menu. Grillbird’s original West Seattle outfit occupies a former Pizza Hut, which feels just right for this utilitarian dish. A second location in Phinney Ridge operates alongside sister concept Salad Party, for those looking to get their greens in.

When the Lee family lost the lease on their longtime teriyaki restaurant, the new location they’d scouted came with a catch: The strip mall that housed it already had a teriyaki shop. So matriarch Yoo-Mi Lee camouflaged her teriyaki menu with dishes from her Korean heritage and influences from the years the family lived in Brazil. Be thankful for that other teriyaki business, because Tá Jóia’s highly specific Brazilian-Korean-teriyaki remix is so vibrant and delicious, it could (should!) be a national fast-casual restaurant chain. Feijoada, a hearty slow-cooked black bean stew made with pork, bacon, and sausage, fits right in next to bulgogi, while the kitchen’s spectacular teriyaki hides in plain sight under the moniker “spicy chicken bowl.” It’s the chicken teriyaki of your hottest, most chili-spiked dreams, brightened with a scoop of pico and a drizzle of creamy house cilantro sauce.

No matter which member of the Kim family is behind the counter here, chances are they will offer you tea while you wait for your order. If the hospitality is great, the food is even better. Chicken teriyaki looks like it came off a photo shoot, deeply juicy with properly charred edges. It’s chicken that needs no supporting cast, but with so many combos on the menu, it’s fun to compare how the gingery sauce hits different proteins including beef, pork, prawn, or tofu. (If you’re exceedingly hungry, go for the formidable triple combo, which delivers chicken and beef teriyaki, golden-fried gyoza with a flaky, blistered exterior, and fragrant mounds of fried rice.) Teriyaki lovers are especially protective of Rainier Teriyaki since its late owner, Hansoo Kim, was tragically killed during a 2023 attempted armed robbery; the family banded together and reopened the restaurant in his honor.

Most people show up at Fremont’s busy donburi shop craving its chirashi bowl, but the chicken teriyaki imagines what Seattle’s signature dish might have looked like if it actually hailed from Japan. Butterflied thighs with the lightest of marinades come straight off the grill to be dressed with a sauce that’s thin by Seattle standards, but nonetheless lands a careful balance of savory and sweet. I appreciate this subtler rendition of chicken teriyaki, which complements an otherwise traditionally Japanese menu of rice bowls. Granted, people don’t usually crave Seattle teriyaki for its subtlety; add a dose of the house chili oil for texture and kick. Fremont Bowl is a kiosk-driven take-out machine, but the dine-in vibes are friendly, provided you can find a free table.

Ask a local about their favorite teriyaki shop, and chances are high it’s this been-there-forever counter next to a laundromat not far from Lake Union’s north end—not to be confused with other very similarly named Seattle teriyaki practitioners, including one on this list. A high ratio of dark soy makes for a standout sauce, while the thin mayo-based salad dressing plays well against the crispness of the fresh iceberg lettuce. The kitchen even uses an old-school mold to press rice into a pleasing half-football shape. Many teriyaki shops also have chicken katsu and egg rolls on the menu, but the versions here are standouts for their nongreasy crispy exteriors. The tables are mostly waiting zones for people ordering takeout, destined for a lunch in Gas Works Park, the nearby brewery taprooms, or just back to the surrounding tech offices. Come hungry: Portions are huge, even by generous teriyaki shop standards.

Nikko is busy most of the day, feeding a bustling lunch rush, teenagers after school, and evening take-out crowds. That turnover means teriyaki that’s always fresh, swiped with sauce that’s more soy than sugar and thick without verging on gummy. Jong Kwon and his family have run this West Seattle staple with warmth for more than two decades. Step inside the narrow shop and you’re transported back to Seattle’s era of peak teriyaki, a simpler time when one ordered off pictures on the wall rather than QR codes and the cashier remembered your name.

Clamshell take-out containers are so inherent to the teriyaki experience that nobody asks if you want your food to go, they generally just assume you do. But visit this Georgetown favorite (no relation to I Love Teriyaki) and you’ll witness a rare sight: Diners eating off actual plates. After a three-year closure following a fire, owners Don and Eva Lo rebuilt the original building (once a KFC) into a shiny new space. Aromas of grilled meat hit you from the parking lot, and the cheerful dining room is usually full. Skip the newish teriyaki burritos, and run, don’t walk, to the short ribs teriyaki, so smoky and tender that you might almost be tempted to bypass the chicken altogether. Almost.

#6653. ‘The Gilded Age’ Is Back! Here’s What to Eat While You Watch the Show

The good china is coming out, but the sweatpants are staying on. The Gilded Age season four is back on Nov. 1, and this is everything I'm eating for the series return.

I can be persuaded to watch almost anything that promises extravagant set designs and beautiful costumes. If there’s history and a little mischievous social maneuvering involved, even better. My coworkers recently recommended The Gilded Age, and within two weeks, I’d watched all three seasons just in time for season four to drop.

There’s plenty to admire: Bertha Russell’s determination, Peggy Scott’s writing career and rooms furnished with a reassuring disregard for minimalism. I love the history, too, from the railroad fortunes and New York bankers to Lewis Latimer’s work in electric lighting and the woman who helped bring the Brooklyn Bridge to completion. Every episode gave me another reason to keep watching.

My husband is often still at the restaurant in the evenings, so once the kids are asleep, I have a few hours to settle in with a show. While I watched The Gilded Age, I usually poured a glass of wine (some of my favorites are under $25 at Walmart) and enjoyed the fire as Christine Baranski made an art of Agnes’s disapproval. But with the new season arriving on Nov. 1, I’m borrowing a few ideas from the show to make a watch party spread.

I have a decidedly romantic streak when it comes to my surroundings, so the show’s interiors have my full attention. I’m particularly taken with the glassware and china that can make even a small supper feel indulgent. With a few soft lamps and the fire going, I’m looking forward to borrowing a little of that grandeur for my own evening.

Dan Roberts for Taste of Home, Courtesy Barbra Nitke/ Courtesy Hbo

I’m more than happy to borrow the show’s habit of pouring wine into crystal glasses. Mine usually contains Champagne, but Ada’s season-three temperance campaign gives us a reason to put some thought into an alcohol-free option too.

Agnes’s feelings about wine appear to be settled, but there’s room for both sisters.

Jonathan Melendez for taste of Home, Courtesy Barbra Nitke/ Courtesy Hbo

The Russells may require a meticulously planned succession of courses, but I’d be content with a small selection of savory bites. Oysters, warm crab dip or little sandwiches would make a perfectly elegant dinner by the fire.

Mark Derse for Taste of Home, Courtesy Alison Cohen Rosa/ Courtesy Hbo

For something more substantial, you can look to the show’s luncheons as much as its elaborate dinner parties. A bowl of soup or a sandwich can feel quite grand when the ingredients are good and someone else is responsible for the evening’s drama.

Dan Roberts for taste of Home, Courtesy Karolina Wojtasik/ Courtesy Hbo

A pot of tea and something sweet would be enough for me on an evening when dinner is already behind us. I like having dessert ready before I sit down, whether that means a trifle waiting in the fridge or a few pastries brought home in a paper bag.

#6652. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

A hypothetical particle could have briefly held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which could help explain how matter won out over antimatter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang ‪—‬ changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all.

The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. Yet the Standard Model of particle physics predicts they should be massless.

One popular fix involves "right-handed" neutrinos. Particles spin a bit like tiny tops, and physicists call them left- or right-handed depending on how they spin relative to their direction of travel. A right-handed particle rotates like an ordinary screw being driven in, turning clockwise as it moves away from you. Every neutrino detected so far is left-handed and turns counterclockwise as it flies away, like a screw with a reverse thread.

"Right-handed neutrinos are hypothetical particles that do not feel the weak nuclear force, "unlike their left-handed counterparts, which are part of the Standard Model," study co-author Rishav Roshan, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southampton in the U.K., told Live Science via email. "They are characterized by having no electric charge and being much heavier."

"Right-handed neutrinos may mix with left-handed neutrinos, helping to explain the mass of the latter" and why they switch flavors, Roshan said.

The IceCube facility, photographed here beneath the Southern Lights, is Earth's premier neutrino detection facility. The proposed 'right-handed' neutrino has not yet been detected.

In quantum physics, particles that mix can exist as a blend of two identities at once. In a theoretical framework called the seesaw mechanism, each ordinary neutrino carries a faint trace of a heavy right-handed partner, and that trace gives it a tiny mass. The heavier the partner, the fainter the trace and the lighter the ordinary neutrino — hence the name, after the playground ride whose ends move in opposite directions.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The particles could solve other puzzles, too. They "aim to address several issues, including the origin of neutrino masses, the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe, and the nature of dark matter," Roshan said.

The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other, forbidding the universe as we know it from ever taking shape. Right-handed neutrinos play a crucial role in models' proposals that the "observed matter-antimatter imbalance arose from processes involving these neutrinos in the early universe," Roshan said.

In this picture, decaying heavy neutrinos left behind a slight excess of leptons — the particle family that includes electrons — that later became today's surplus of matter, he explained.

The seesaw framework usually includes three right-handed neutrinos, but because two are enough to explain the data, physicists often ignore the third, assuming it is too heavy or interacts too feebly with matter.

In the new study, Roshan and Sudipta Show, a physicist at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, examined what this neglected particle — which, in the team's main example, was about 100 trillion times as heavy as a proton — would have done after the Big Bang.

At first, the particle would have zipped around at nearly light speed, so its energy would have faded like that of light, which would have both spread out and stretched to weaker wavelengths as space expanded. But as the cosmos cooled, the particle would have slowed down and most of its energy would have become locked in its mass, which would have been only spread out. Its share of the cosmic energy therefore would have grown until it dominated, and the long-lived particle would have stayed in charge until it decayed into other particles, according to the team's computations.

The study reveals that the neglected right-handed neutrino "significantly impacts the early universe's expansion dynamics, driving a period of early matter domination," Roshan said. This change "affects various Standard Model interactions"‬ that could help to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry, Roshan added.

Each interaction would have switched on only once it outpaced the expansion of space. Because a universe dominated by the heavy neutrino would have expanded faster, the interactions would have had to wait until it cooled further.

These interactions would have let the early universe distinguish lepton flavors, which would have affected how the matter surplus formed. Thanks to the delay, the team found, a lighter right-handed neutrino about 100 billion times as heavy as a proton could have produced the observed amount of matter before the flavors could be told apart — even after the heavy neutrino's decay diluted part of it.

The heavy neutrino is far too massive to create in any particle accelerator, so tests must be indirect.

Gravitational waves — ripples in space-time — offer one such route. An era dominated by the heavy neutrino would have left a telltale kink in the background of early-universe gravitational waves, such as those from "cosmic strings" ‪—‬ hypothetical thread-like defects in space. The results can be tested through forthcoming facilities such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO), Roshan noted.

LISA, a space-based European Space Agency mission, is scheduled to launch around 2035, while SKAO, a giant radio telescope project being built in Australia and South Africa, could catch such waves by timing distant pulsars. Tests could come "as these facilities come online and begin data collection," Roshan said. A faint hum from the hot primordial plasma would carry the era's imprint too, but at frequencies beyond what existing detectors could pick up.

Roshan, R., & Show, S. (2026). Delayed charged Lepton Yukawa equilibration in minimal seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 137(11), 111802. https://doi.org/10.1103/nfkx-q6z7

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

#6650. French Onion Stuffing

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

This recipe for French onion stuffing takes caramelized onions, beef broth and Gruyere, and transforms them into a holiday-ready side dish.

Every year at Thanksgiving, I consider filling my plate with all the sides and foregoing the turkey altogether. (That’s what I did during my decade as a vegetarian—and I did not miss the meat.) Give me all the cranberry sauce, green bean casserole and mashed potatoes. But my absolute favorite Thanksgiving side dish is the stuffing. Since my vegetarian days, I’ve preferred the stuffing cooked outside the bird. Not only does this prevent common food-safety issues, it also ensures the stuffing cooks evenly and crisps up on top. Although I’m partial to my mom’s (a classic stuffing with celery, onions and day-old bread), I also like to experiment with new recipes and flavor combinations.

This recipe for French onion stuffing is a real crowd-pleaser. It takes the ingredients of classic French onion soup—caramelized onions, beef broth and Gruyere cheese—and transforms them into a savory stuffing recipe. The most important ingredient you need for this recipe is patience. Caramelization is a process that cannot be rushed, but the results are oh-so worth it. The sweet-savory onions truly take this stuffing recipe to the next level. Just like in a bowl of French onion soup, a generous amount of grated Gruyere cheese melted over top ensures each bite is mix of sweet and savory flavors.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Spread the bread cubes in an even layer on two baking sheets. Bake them for 10 minutes, then flip the cubes and rotate the baking sheets. Bake them until they’re very dry and golden brown, about five to eight minutes. Remove from the oven and set aside to cool.

Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven, heat the butter and olive oil over medium heat. Add the onions, and cook them until they’re softened, 10 to 15 minutes, stirring frequently. Stir in the salt and pepper. Reduce the heat to medium-low, and cook the onions until they’re deep golden brown, 40 to 50 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the garlic, and cook until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Add the dry sherry, and use a wooden spoon to scrape up any browned bits. Stir in the thyme. Remove the pan from the heat.

In a large bowl, whisk the eggs until they’re smooth. Stir in the cooked onions and bread cubes. Stir in the beef broth until the bread is evenly moistened.

Editor’s Tip: The stuffing should be moist but not soggy. If the mixture seems too dry, add more broth in 1/4-cup increments until evenly moistened.

Spoon the stuffing into a greased 13×9-inch or 3-quart baking dish. Cover it with foil, and bake the stuffing for 30 minutes. Uncover the dish, and bake the stuffing until it’s crispy and browned, 15 to 20 minutes.

Remove the stuffing from the oven, and increase the oven temperature to 425°. Sprinkle the cheese on top. Bake the stuffing until the cheese is melted and bubbly, three to five minutes. Garnish the stuffing with thyme before serving it.

After allowing the French onion stuffing to cool completely, store any leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days.

Absolutely! Caramelizing the onions requires low and slow cooking, and the process can’t be rushed. If you don’t have the time or the space to dedicate to making this dish all at once, you can make the caramelized onions up to four days in advance.

After caramelizing the onions, allow them to come to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container the fridge until you’re ready to use them. You can also prep the entire stuffing in advance up to a day in advance. Follow the recipe until it’s ready to bake, then cover and refrigerate it. Allow it to sit at room temperature for about 30 minutes, then bake it as directed, adding an extra 5 to 10 minutes to the baking time.

Or, you could try something new and use the microwave to caramelize onions. Yes, we tested it and it works!

Stuffing actually freezes really well. Cut the stuffing into large squares and wrap in a layer of storage wrap followed by a layer of foil. Freeze the stuffing squares for up to one month.

While there is a way to safely bake stuffing inside a turkey, this stuffing recipe is not an ideal candidate. By cooking it in the bird, it won’t be able to crisp up like it does when cooked it separately in a casserole dish.

You can start out with fresh bread for this recipe, but you will need to dry out the bread cubes in the oven before using them. Doing so helps to ensure the bread will soak up all the flavors of the stuffing without getting too soggy.

This stuffing recipe is baked both covered and uncovered. Covering the dish tightly with foil traps in steam, locking in moisture and allowing the stuffing to cook through without over-crisping the top. Cooking it uncovered allows the top to crisp up to golden brown.

#6649. Daniel Roseberry’s Victorious Fashion Journey Was Spotlighted at the Hirshhorn Gala

On Monday evening, the crowd at the annual Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden New York gala would have looked right at home at a Schiaparelli runway show. At every turn, guests inside Lincoln Center’s packed David Geffen Hall seemed to be outfitted in pieces crafted by creative director—and the evening’s honorees—Daniel Roseberry, from surrealist gowns and chain-accented dresses to handbags, pumps, and gold jewelry adorned with the keyholes and facial features he has made signatures at the French house.

Even if they weren’t in Schiaparelli looks, many attendees wore gilded accessories in honor of the designer, who received the Hirshhorn’s Leader in the Arts Award. “People ask, ‘Is fashion art?’ and ‘Are fashion designers artists?’ What is that boundary, what is that line,” Roseberry told Vogue. “It’s something I’ve always tried to cross a little bit, and to blur. Tonight feels like a very unexpected recognition of that.”

Roseberry had plenty of other artists on his mind, too. The occasion prompted the designer to muse on the “whole family” of creatives that have shaped his point of view, including his grandmother, mother, uncles, and sister Liz Fox Roseberry—whose social media videos ahead of her brother’s shows have also proven popular with the fashion crowd. Roseberry also reflected on artists who he has admired over the years, including Jeff Koons, whom he met for the first time recently. “When you’re meeting a bold-faced name that you’ve admired for so long, someone who has crossed so many boundaries, it’s always amazing to have a name become human, in a way,” Roseberry said of meeting the artist. “Jeff was so generous and gracious.”

Both of those adjectives are similar to how the night’s guests described Roseberry himself. “Daniel designed this for me for the Time100 Gala, but I wanted to wear it again,” said art collector and philanthropist Komal Shah of her attire for the gala. “It’s 3,000 paintbrushes and it represents all the artists who have gathered here. I think Daniel is one of the finest artists imaginable.”

When the bell rang to enter the mezzanine for dinner, everyone was greeted by rows of deep green tables blooming with purple calla lilies. Golden napkin rings set with metal sun rays, spikes, and stones brought a Schiaparelli-like flair to the space—and were quickly slipped into many evening bags as keepsakes.

After courses of mushroom carpaccio and Hudson Valley chicken, actress Emily Blunt took the stage to introduce Roseberry, deeming him a “tornado of talent” and commending his warmth and work ethic. “Daniel is someone who creates such an impact, one that is so lasting, and so resonant, not only amongst those who know, but even someone as fleece-wearing as my father, who still talks about that Oscars dress I wore with the levitating shoulders,” she said. “He was like, ‘It’s so avant-garde!’ I’d never heard him say those words in my life, and he also adored the extraordinary couture that Daniel let me snatch off the runway to wear to The Devil Wears Prada 2 premiere.”

Roseberry’s own heartfelt acceptance speech reflected on his trajectory, from Texas to the couture ateliers of Paris. “I’ve realized that my dreams were never the thing that was actually expensive,” Roseberry said. “What was expensive was living out other people’s dreams, muting my true self to conform to what others expected, and monitoring myself along the way. We get so occupied with this idea that we’re being watched that we stop seeing ourselves for who we really are.”

The Washington, D.C. museum’s outgoing director Melissa Chiu was honored for her leadership and risk-taking at the institution over the last 12 years—including completion of its newly renovated Sculpture Garden by Hiroshi Sugimoto. Chiu spoke of the Hirshhorn’s dedication to inspiring its 35 million annual guests, particularly the young children, with a wide-ranging variety of exhibits. Her departure coincides with the launch of the Melissa Chiu Museum Fund, which will support the museum’s educational projects, community engagement, and its new Hirshhorn Art School. (Chiu will soon take up her post as the new director of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.)

After the excitement and enthusiasm of the speeches, the evening concluded with a performance by Latin pop band Santos Bravos. Members Kauê Penna, Drew Venegas, Gabi Bermúdez, Alejandro Aramburú, and Kenneth Lavíll performed a lively medley of U.S.A. for Africa’s “We Are the World” and Whitney Houston’s “I Wanna Dance With Somebody” before closing out the festivities with their own song “MHM.”

As for Roseberry, he’s keeping his eyes on the prize this fall—including the completion of his first New York City Marathon on Sunday. After enjoying his first glass of Champagne since the summertime, he’s ready to celebrate the two back-to-back milestone achievements by momentarily going off grid. “I’m going to go to Connecticut this weekend and catch the very end of the leaves changing, and just unplug a little bit,” he said with a smile.

#6648. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years, as it approaches a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A pioneering NASA space telescope is no more. In sad news for Swifties everywhere, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years of tracking the most powerful explosions in the universe since the Big Bang.

According to a NASA announcement, the Swift team shut down the telescope's science operations Tuesday (Oct. 20) after the observatory fell too low in its orbit to continue taking reliable measurements of the cosmos. In the coming weeks, Swift will drop even further, eventually passing a point of no return and taking a fiery plunge through Earth's atmosphere.

The observatory is the latest victim of intense solar activity, which increases the drag on satellites in Earth orbit and makes it harder for spacecraft to stay aloft. Swift has been losing altitude for a while, but the final straw came in August, when a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed, ending with the would-be rescue craft burning up in the atmosphere after a series of hardware malfunctions.

Swift is now beyond saving and, orbiting at just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth, can no longer take reliable observations of space. NASA expects the spacecraft to break up upon reentry "in the next few weeks."

NASA knew Swift was in trouble when it went in; soon, it'll be lying on the cold hard ground. However, the Swift mission surpassed its goals by decades. According to NASA, the satellite launched in November 2004 on a primary mission intended to last just two years. In the end, Swift survived for 22 years, surpassing its intended lifespan by more than 10 times.

In that time, Swift made thousands of observations of exploding supernovas, intense gamma-ray bursts, and black-hole-related episodes of stellar destruction, contributing data to about 7,000 scientific papers, according to NASA.

An illustration of a stellar 'mega-flare' detected by Swift. The observatory excelled at catching powerful, fast-acting cosmic events.

Designed as a multiwavelength observatory, Swift watched the sky in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light that made it well suited to track the aftermath of powerful energy bursts. Its greatest asset, perhaps, was its rapid response time; if an explosion flashed somewhere in the sky, engineers could swivel Swift to study it within minutes, NASA said.

"Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more," S. Bradley Cenko, the mission's principal investigator at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said in the statement.

Swift's fast-acting observations "played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics," added Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters.

#6644. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6643. Can Botox Stop Working?

Botox loyalists claim something is amiss with their favorite injectable. The neurotoxin, which has been the go-to treatment to reduce the appearance of fine lines, is supposed to last three to four months. But some allege online that their Botox isn’t working as well—at least as well as it used to work.

From accusing providers of diluting solutions to get you to spend more on treatments to people believing they are now immune to Botox altogether, the theories are conspiracy-level complicated. But before anyone freaks out and cancels their next appointment, read what the experts have to say on what’s really going on with Botox.

The good news is that Botox itself hasn’t suddenly stopped working. As New York–based board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD, explains, because Botox arrives at a practice as a freeze-dried powder and is turned into a liquid with sterile saline before injection, there isn’t one universal correct way to dilute it. Different injectors use different dilution volumes based on their technique and treatment goals.

King says it’s more important to pay attention to the amount of units you’re receiving and not the concentration of the saline; the units you’re receiving determine how long it will last. “Twenty units is still 20 units whether it’s delivered in a smaller or larger volume,” she says.

In reality, there are many reasons why your Botox isn’t lasting as long as you’d like it to. Some common ones include:

King says that under-dosing is simply the biggest reason. “Many people are requesting a softer, more natural look (sometimes called baby Botox), which intentionally uses fewer units, [and] less product generally means a shorter duration of effect,” she explains.

Brian J. Abittan, MD, director of skin and hair rejuvenation and hair transplantation at the Kimberly and Eric J. Waldman Department of Dermatology at Mount Sinai, adds that patients want more movement in their faces and less of a “frozen” look, which can sometimes result in lighter doses that wear off faster.

King explains that people with very strong facial muscles (men, athletes, those who have very expressive faces, etc.) often metabolize Botox sooner because their muscles are more powerful.

How someone is going to respond to Botox varies from person to person. King says some patients may experience their Botox lasting three to four months, while others may only get to two to three months despite getting the same dose and treatment. It really just depends.

“Precise placement matters,” says King. “Even with the correct dose, injections that don’t optimally target the muscle can reduce the duration of effect.”

The type of practice where you get your Botox done also matters. If you’re going to a licensed professional, such as a board-certified dermatologist or plastic surgeon’s office, the risk of getting counterfeit Botox or improper injection techniques are slim to none. “Those situations are uncommon in reputable medical practices,” she says. “But [they] highlight why it’s important to seek treatment from qualified providers.”

King lists frequent intense exercise, high muscle activity, and a rapid metabolism as things that may make it seem like your Botox isn’t lasting as long as it used to. But she says evidence is mixed and these effects are generally modest.

For most patients, King says they don’t become tolerant to Botox. In fact, she says many long-term patients may find that they can sometimes maintain results with similar (or even go with slightly fewer) units because repeatedly relaxing the muscle may reduce its strength over time. She also points out that first-time patients might notice movement returning earlier than patients who have been getting treatment consistently over time.

There is a small subset of patients who do develop these neutralizing antibodies against Botox, she says, which will make treatments less effective. But these are usually seen in those who receive high doses for neurologic conditions, get frequent touchups, and get injections at intervals shorter than 12 weeks. Though possible, true resistance from Botox is uncommon. “An experienced injector will first rule out these more common explanations,” she says.

Many have already been feeling the Botox and filler fatigue and are looking to other procedures (XERF, facelifts, etc.) to fill other antiaging needs. Abittan says it’s important to pay attention to what each treatment actually does, as they each address different issues. Lasers, for example, can help with skin tightening, improve pigmentation or texture, and address wrinkles or lines at rest. Whereas neuromodulators like Botox work on movement-related wrinkles, he says.

“These treatments are complementary rather than competitive,” adds King. “The modern approach to facial rejuvenation is increasingly individualized and multimodal. Rather than replacing Botox, newer technologies give physicians more tools to address the specific cause of each patient’s aging concerns.”

And if you’re still unhappy with how long your Botox is lasting, consider a different product. She lists Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify, and Letybo as some options that are known to offer similar but longer-lasting results. Just be sure to go to a licensed professional before injecting anything new into your face.

#6641. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

Live Science spoke with comparative psychologist Christian Frings to discuss a new theory for why orcas are attacking yachts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Over the past six years, orcas have made headlines for a unique behavior: Some individuals have repeatedly damaged or destroyed rudders on boats. The behavior has prompted a wide range of explanations, including that it's playful, a form of revenge, a warning against getting too close to the pod, or even a type of cultural transmission, in which one orca observes another interacting with a boat and then imitates it.

But Christian Frings, a cognitive psychologist who studies how humans control their actions, thinks it could be deliberate.

While Frings, who is also chair of general psychology and methodology at Trier University in Germany, does not study orcas directly, he believes that theories developed to explain human behavior could provide insight into this orca behavior. Orcas (Orcinus orca), he said, may be a "test case" for whether a wide variety of species can anticipate how their actions will change the environment and then take those actions deliberately, with the goal of making those changes.

He published his theory as a commentary Sept. 8 in the journal Animal Cognition.

This doesn't necessarily mean orcas have wicked motives or are ramming boats with the goal of sinking them and scaring or harming people. It may be that orcas just like the sensation of smashing into a rudder or being in the water with a wonky, disabled boat. Once they learn this, they anticipate the effect — for example, how a boat moves or feels when the rudder is damaged — and then carry out the learned action sequence that creates that effect.

Frings' theory doesn't attempt to explain why orcas (also called killer whales) would seek to damage a boat or rudder. "Why they want this effect is a secondary question and while of course interesting it touches a quite different topic," Frings told Live Science via email.

Christian Frings is a cognitive psychology professor at the University of Trier in Germany and the director of the Institute for Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. His research explores how the human mind turns perception into action and why our recent experiences can shape what we do next, often without us noticing.

Live Science spoke with Frings about his hypothesis and why theories that describe how humans execute a series of motor behaviors — called action control frameworks — might help us understand how other complex animals behave in the wild.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: Why is it important to study orca behavior, and what can studying orcas tell us about animal cognition?

Christian Frings: In truth, I'm the wrong person to get that question because I should mention right from the start that I'm a cognitive psychologist. So usually, I'm studying human behavior. So, it's not really that I'm interested in orcas, per se, more in the question of what is actually comparable between human action control, human cognition and animal cognition.

KHC: Can you explain the action-control framework for our readers?

CF: It's a group of theories. The most important point is that agents — humans and maybe orcas — control their actions by actually anticipating the behavioral and the sensory consequences of their actions.

So let's take the example of turning the light on. The action starts with anticipating how it will look when the light is turned on. It does not start with pressing the light switch. It starts with the visual effect you're going to produce. This visual effect then actually retrieves from memory a motor program, and this motor program actually produces the anticipated effect. So it's all about anticipating action effects.

In the human action-control literature, that is the most dominant view from different theories of how humans actually control their behavior: by anticipating the effects they're going to produce.

KHC: How does that apply to the orca behavior?

CF: The typical explanation for [the boat-attacking behavior] is more stimulus response or cultural transmission. Stimulus response would mean, in this case, the rudder elicits an approach or attack behavior. So any rudder should just elicit this behavior. [Editor's note: Stimulus-response theory is a psychological concept in which a stimulus triggers a particular response from an individual. Examples include a cat being sprayed with water when on the couch and jumping off the couch in response, or a dog salivating when it smells food.]

Cultural transmission would actually be observational learning. That means one orca sees how another orca is attacking a rudder and then just imitates the behavior.

I'm not saying that these explanations [stimulus response or cultural transmission] are wrong, by the way. I just want to add an additional layer of explanation.

I suggest that they actually anticipate the sensory consequences of their action. So maybe they anticipate how it would look and how it would feel if they destroy the rudder. I would not call it [their behavior] play, but maybe they're just testing or probing what kind of effect they're going to produce.

It's a little bit like human babies, when they start to move — or move their arms or move their legs — they're also typically trying to produce effects, right? It's also when they develop language, this kind of babbling, right? That is a kind of testing or probing action effects.

Maybe this is something the orcas also do. I don't know. But at least it's [another theory].

Whale-watching tours help the public see orca behavior from a close-but-safe distance.

KHC: So would the orca be anticipating something like the boat becoming impossible to steer?

CF: Actually, no. Let's assume for a moment it [that a broken rudder is] what they want to produce — because they somehow anticipate how it would look and how it would feel if this yacht cannot be steered anymore.

If they can anticipate, then this anticipation of this effect will retrieve from their memory what they have to do to actually produce this effect. And it's not about [higher-order] thinking. That is a very important thing.

So we do not need human-like intentions to impose that on the orcas. I'm not saying that, because I really think it's, in a way, comparable with turning a light on. When you turn your light on, you also do not have big thoughts about that. You just want to turn your light on. So you want to produce an effect, and you do not think about all the different, quite complex muscle movements you have to do if you actually press the light switch.

I would say, again, it does not really need higher-order cognition or something like that. We do not have to impose motives or complex thoughts on the orcas for that.

My point is just to look at this behavior from this somewhat different angle, adding this layer about action effects.

KHC: What are the bigger implications if your theory is correct?

CF: My point is just to look at this behavior from this somewhat different angle, adding this layer about action effects. Because if you, for a moment, take my ideas for granted and say, "OK, maybe he has a point," then this opens up the possibility to manipulate the orca behavior.

Because if the orcas anticipate effects and this action effect produces a certain behavior, if you change the effect — let's say the rudder [material] or the shell of the boat so that the orca thinks he's producing a certain action effect — then he shows his behavior, but this behavior does not produce the action effect anymore. So the orca will probably change the behavior. It might be dangerous because it might elicit somewhat different — maybe even more dangerous — behavior of the orcas, but it might also stop it.

But it gives you a natural angle to manipulate the orca behavior. [Editor's note: In a follow-up email, Frings noted that this could involve testing a different version of the boat rudder. If the original rudder, when damaged, leaves the boat floating in a "helpless" way, a second one could be tested that allows the boat to be maneuverable even when attacked. If Frings' hypothesis is right, then by breaking the link between the orcas' planned actions (ramming the boat) and the outcome they want (helpless boat), you could change the orcas' behavior.]

But again, if you try to change it this way, it might be a little bit dangerous. So I would not suggest doing that with a boat with real people on it, because if you change the environmental consequences, they [the orcas] might actually go a little bit crazy. Maybe they might try to produce this effect with a different kind of behavior, and that could be even more aggressive. But I don't know. I can't predict that.

KHC: So the orcas are a case study to test this framework, right?

CF: Exactly. And for the general approach, it's important to try to find action frameworks that can travel across species that are not specific for one particular species. Because at the moment, we might have action-control models for humans or action-control models for the great apes.

But maybe we can just have a family of action-control frameworks, because maybe orcas and humans, and at least the great apes, control their behavior concerning action effects in quite the same way, to be honest.

Another important point here that makes it, for me personally, very interesting: This is behavior in the wild. So a lot of the research on action control is typically in the lab under very controlled conditions, so in a way, this is moving from humans to orcas but also from lab into wild behavior.

I think one misconception is actually that the models from the lab are not applicable to behavior in the wild. That's not only true for orcas; it's also true for humans. And I don't like that.

And again, this paper is a nice showcase that lab models can actually be used to explain behavior in the real world.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6639. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6637. Keke Palmer Wore Rare Bob Mackie—and Other Vintage Gems—at the 2026 CFDA Awards

As the host of last night’s 2026 CFDA Awards in New York City, all eyes were on Keke Palmer to deliver us a major fashion moment. The annual awards ceremony, after all, is all about celebrating American style and design. “Fashion is such a big part of how I tell stories, so getting to celebrate the people behind it was exciting,” Palmer tells Vogue today, post-CFDAs. “I love how a look can connect different eras, and bring a memory or a feeling into the present. To be in a room celebrating that creativity, while bringing my own personality and humor to the evening, felt like a beautiful fit.”

Of course, Palmer did not disappoint on that front. The star went archival for the night—as she is wont to do—bringing four vintage gems to the red carpet. “I wanted my looks to be unique, and celebrate some incredible talent from the past,” says Palmer of her fashion direction. “Everything with me is somehow a throwback or referential. That’s part of the kind of artist I am: Fashion becomes another way to tell that pop culture story.”

Working with stylist Molly Dickson, the duo wanted each of the four looks to have its own moment throughout the night. Palmer first hit the red carpet in a one-of-a-kind (and incredibly rare) Bob Mackie piece from the 1970s. The dress has a particularly noteworthy history: The strappy, shimmery-gold gown was originally custom-made for actor and singer Raquel Welch, which she wore to perform “I’m a Woman” alongside Cher on The Cher Show back in 1975. (You’ve all seen the clip.) “Wearing Bob Mackie was one of the first ideas I mentioned to Molly,” says Palmer. “His work holds so much entertainment history, and I loved being able to bring my own energy to a piece with that story. It’s classic, and it felt like the right way to step into the night.”

Turns out, the iconic piece of pop culture was sourced from the professional vintage dealer Timeless Vixen—a celebrity favorite that Sabrina Carpenter and Kylie Jenner also use for their extremely rare red carpet pulls. “When Keke’s styling team reached out looking for something special by Bob Mackie, this piece immediately came to mind,” says owner Lauren Lepire. “I’ve always adored his work, and with his recent passing, it’s especially meaningful to see Keke bring such an iconic design back into the spotlight.”

From there, Palmer then changed into her three other vintage frocks of the night. There was the black skin-revealing Marc Bouwer dress once worn by Toni Braxton; a striped, one-shouldered 1980s Halston number; And a slinky black 1970s Stephen Burrows to end with a bang. “For me, it was a story through the ages, celebrating these designers and the women who brought their clothes to life,” says Palmer. “We also told a black and gold color story, ending with a look that brought the two together. That sense of integration feels very connected to where I am artistically—bringing different references and parts of myself into one expression.”

While playing dress up was undoubtedly a highlight of the night for Palmer, her favorite moments included some unexpected run-ins with fellow stars. “You’re doing a show, but you also get to connect with people whose work you admire and enjoy being in the room together,” says Palmer. “I loved seeing Demi Moore backstage in between moments, seeing Law Roach, and catching up with Prabal Gurung. Those little moments in between everything are some of my favorites. Saw my girl Brandy, too!”

After delivering her statement fashions at the CFDAs, Palmer says she ended the night with one thing: “Bed! I’m a homebody.” Up next? She will be filming season two of The ’Burbs, and working on new music, too. (She just released her last video, “Keke Frankenstein,” this Halloween weekend.) “I’m building the world around my album, and having so much fun with ‘Keke Frankenstein,’” says Palmer. “I love when the music, visuals, fashion, and characters can all speak to one another.”

In other words: Palmer stays booked and busy. “Between motherhood, music, acting, and building Practice by Palmer, there’s always something happening,” says Palmer. “This fall, I’ve been making room for experiences that feed me as a person. The ‘play’ in me still has a way of becoming productive. #Virgo!”

Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

#6634. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii's Big Island. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photo? Hurricane Madeline (left) and Hurricane Lester (right)

Which satellite took the photo? Suomi NPP

This eye-catching satellite snap from a decade ago shows a pair of hurricanes barreling toward Hawaii. The clouds swirling around the twin cyclones make them look eerily like the eyes of a pale face smiling up at space. The sight appears even spookier when viewed on a weather map (see below).

The surprisingly symmetrical storms — Hurricane Madeline (left) and Hurricane Lester (right) — were the 14th and 13th named storms, respectively, during 2016's Pacific hurricane season, which is tied for the sixth-most-active year on record, with 22 total named storms.

Madeline peaked as a Category 4 storm on Aug. 30, reaching maximum wind speeds of around 130 mph (210 km/h). Lester also briefly became a Category 4 storm on Sept. 1, reaching a maximum speed just below Madeline's, but it quickly weakened to Category 3.

On Aug. 30, the day after the image was taken, Madeline was just under 400 miles (650 kilometers) from Hawaii's Big Island, while Lester was around 900 miles (1,450 km) behind on the same trajectory, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. At the time, meteorologists were uncertain whether the pair would hit the island.

The Central Pacific Hurricane Center later issued a hurricane warning for the state of Hawaii, saying that Madeline, in particular, would pass "dangerously close to the Big Island," according to the Earth Observatory. However, neither storm ended up making landfall. (In the photo, the Big Island is obscured by reflected sunlight, known as a sunglint, on the left side of the image.)

When viewed on a radar-based weather map, the hurricanes look like they are staring up into space even more.

Madeline eventually passed south of Hawaii on Aug. 31. However, by then, it had been downgraded to Category 1. Lester passed north of the Big Island on Sept. 2 and came within around 130 miles (210 km) of Honolulu, before sharply turning northward, where it petered out.

Although neither hurricane made landfall — meaning the eye of the storm did not pass over a landmass — they still caused high winds, heavy rainfall and strong surf across the state.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Despite being in the middle of the corridor where most Pacific hurricanes form, Hawaii's islands have surprising good luck in avoiding the supercharged storms.

For example, in 2025, Hurricane Kiko was similarly spotted from space bearing down on the island state. But like Madeline and Lester, it suddenly changed course and weakened at the last minute.

Hawaii usually manages to dodge the worst effects of hurricanes for two reasons. First, the islands are surrounded by a near-constant area of high pressure on their eastern side, where most hurricanes come from. Second, strong winds often blow eastward across the islands, according to FOX Weather. These factors create a sort of invisible shield around the islands, causing storms to skirt around them.

While hurricanes almost never make landfall in Hawaii, they often come close enough to trigger strong gusts of wind on the islands.

However, given the recent rise in extreme weather events across the globe — caused by human-caused climate change — as well as changes to regional weather patterns, the islands may not stay so lucky forever.

For example, in August and September, two hurricanes — Lowell and Lala — skimmed unusually closely past the island of Kauai, causing a significant amount of damage to power lines, boats and other coastal infrastructure. Researchers think the ongoing "super" El Niño, which officially began in May and has already caused record-breaking sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, may be partially to blame for these storms, according to The Guardian.

A 2016 satellite photo shows nearly a dozen, surprisingly pronounced dark spots swirling in the clouds over Heard Island in the Indian Ocean.

A 2021 satellite photo shows an unusual series of concentric cloud rings that appeared directly above an erupting volcano on La Palma in Spain's Canary Islands.

A 2015 satellite photo captured a series of stunning "von Kármán vortices" swirling off islands in the Atlantic. It is one of the best examples of this meteorological phenomenon ever seen.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.
