#6614. A Chef’s Guide to the Best Restaurants in Asheville, North Carolina

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

Part of what gives me so much joy about eating in Asheville is recognizing that we’re all part of a very integrated ecosystem. It feels like every restaurant I love is either run by an alum of one of the places I’ve been involved in, or by people that I’ve worked side by side with at hurricane-relief events, or by someone I know I’m going to see at the farmers market.

That’s what makes Asheville special. The folks that come in from out of town are lucky that there’s a virtuous cycle of talent here to keep the pipeline full. It’s so cool to see the evolution of this place, even if we locals don’t always realize how good we have it.It’s almost funny how not a big deal eating out here is. It’s so laid-back. We take it for granted that it’s going to be a great restaurant—of course it is! Having said that, the sheer range of restaurants is incredible. Given how small our town actually is, I sometimes find myself thinking, How lucky are we?

A hallmark of most of the restaurants I love is their connection to nearby farms. At my last count, there were more than a dozen farmers markets happening in Asheville, and there are probably more than twice as many local farms within an hour of here. Most people know the farmers by name, and nobody is precious about it. So when you go to a restaurant, they’ll just say, “It’s Evan’s greens tonight,” and everybody knows who Evan is.

The last thing is that whether it’s an Indian restaurant or a Filipino restaurant or Italian or Spanish, I love the Southern throughline in all of the dishes and hospitality here. That doesn’t mean there’s cornbread or okra in every dish; it’s honoring the fact that we all chose to open Indian or Italian restaurants here in Appalachia, so let’s not divorce the two from each other.

Let’s find a way to make it feel holistic. We do that really well. I was worried after the pandemic and Hurricane Helene that Asheville might not bounce back, but we have. I know that this place is going to continue to trailblaze for years to come.

20 Battery Park Avenue, Floor 1(828) 271-9808

Luminosa is hands down my wife, Molly, and my favorite date- night restaurant. It checks every box so beautifully. It’s intimate, but also a showstopper. It’s visually exciting to be in there, and yet [the design] doesn’t detract from the food, which they describe as “hyper-local Italian.” In the two years that they’ve been open, they’ve picked up a Michelin Green Star and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and they deserve it. Everything about it just feels very intentional. The food is brilliantly delicious and the menu changes a lot—which sometimes drives me crazy, but it works here, because I know there’s going to be something fun and new every time I go. Their style of service and hospitality is so old-fashioned it almost borders on being antiquated, but I love it. It’s a small town at the end of the day, and everybody touches your table.

One word: respect. Katie Button and her crew have been at the top of their game for so long, you almost forget that continuing to win the championship is really hard to do. But they execute at the exact same incredibly high level as they did the first time I walked in years ago. I go there because what they do is incredible, and it’s always good to be reminded of how well they represent the tapas side of Spanish cuisine. It’s also a really exciting restaurant to be in—there’s an energy and a vibe because of the open kitchen, and it feels so intimate and fun. It’s always packed—they’re a victim of their own success—but even if I’m just going in for a glass of sherry and a plate of jamón ibérico, it’s worth pulling whatever favors I must to get in.

701 Haywood Road, Suite 102(828) 552-3880

This is a true only-in-Asheville pick, a chest-swelling-with-pride kind of choice. The chef, Silver Iocovozzi, worked with me at [two of Irani’s erstwhile restaurants] MG Road and Buxton Hall, and now they get to showcase their own cuisine, Filipino. Neng Jr.’s feels like the kind of restaurant that this city is built for. It’s so tiny and so intimate, with maybe 12 seats, so you’re packed in and you really feel like you’re eating dinner at Silver’s house. The food feels so personal—it’s brilliant and fun and totally them, with flavor profiles that remind me of Indian street food in some ways, full of fermentation and funk.

First of all, this space was converted into a restaurant without doing much to disguise the fact that it used to be a house. You’re dining on the front porch or in the side yard or in the living room, but somehow it manages to make you feel like you’re in a small village in Provence. The food has a French focus, as well as an Americana element. They win all kinds of awards for their wine program, deservedly so. Leo’s is hard to describe. It feels like this rustic little bistro where you might order something as simple as a grilled cheese sandwich and tomato soup, but when it shows up, you realize this could actually be the best grilled cheese and tomato soup you’ve ever had in your life. It’s totally unique and transportive, and it’s become my go-to spontaneous dinner recommendation for friends visiting from out of town.

I’m going to throw it back a little to one of the first places that really popped in West Asheville. Ten or 15 years ago, The Admiral was essentially a dive bar in a cinder-block building next to a gas station where probably 80 percent of Asheville’s pot deals went down. There, a young chef named Elliot Moss [ed note: later Irani’s partner at Buxton Hall] was putting out gastropub food that was blowing people’s minds. After service, they’d push all the tables to the side to clear room for these legendary dance parties. Now the neighborhood isn’t as sketchy, Elliot is long gone, and they no longer push the tables aside, but the food has not lost an inch. When you’re eating, you can just feel that it’s world-class cuisine, and reservations are hard to get, so it still feels special to get to go to The Admiral.

The best way I can describe chef Matt Dawes’s food, or at least my experience of it, is that it’s elevated British pub cuisine with a French influence and a Southern twist. The menu swings from steak frites au poivre to the best shepherd’s pie you’ve ever had to a pitch-perfect Welsh rarebit (it’s also the first place I had Welsh rabbit). The restaurant is located maybe 30 feet from the railroad tracks, next to a dirt field and one of the noisiest outdoor breweries in Asheville, but don’t let that deter you. It’s one of the most reliable and satisfying restaurants in the city.

This is a newcomer to the scene. Chef Ashleigh Shanti Santi, a James Beard Award–winner and prominent Top Chef contestant, has been a passionate advocate for Black Southern foodways. Good Hot Fish is exactly what it sounds like: a fish counter with amazing hot fish sandwiches and seafood, plus the perfect sides. All of the fish she serves comes from local waterways. There’s fried catfish and Gulf shrimp burgers and fish dip with fried saltines. It’s literally just a counter with a few stools against the wall, but the technique is immaculate. The sandwiches are served on squishy white bread with buttermilk tartare sauce, and it delivers on its promise of being the best damn hot fish sandwich you’ve ever had.

I have to give a shout-out here to one of the OGs. To call All Souls just great pizza does it a disservice; you need to understand the backstory. David Bauer, was one of the first bread gurus/savants of Asheville. Farm and Sparrow, his bakery, helped usher in the modern renaissance of heirloom grains and bread that you now see everywhere. He grew his own grain, milled his own flour, and made these amazing breads. Then he helped open All Souls, which makes pizza using stone-ground heirloom grains, in a style I can only describe as Carolina pizza. It’s our own thing, with our own grains, cooked in a wood-fired oven with toppings that come from within 50 miles or so. It’s in a building that was a diner for decades in West Asheville, next to a big old field where you can spread out a picnic blanket if the restaurant is full. All Souls is a classic example of doing one thing, doing it well, and not being too uptight about it, which is everything I love about Asheville.

244 Short Coxe Avenue, #110(828) 505-1003

I have to include two bakeries here. Mother serves a full lunch and dinner menu, so it’s a little more on the restaurant side of things. It’s again in a weird part of Asheville, sandwiched between a sauna and a tire shop, with garage doors that open to a front patio that looks like a loading ramp for trucks. And yet, like so many places here, it’s totally transportive. You feel like you’re eating in Europe somehow. Their jambon-beurre sandwich is the closest I’ve had to Fauchon’s in Paris, and their pumpernickel bread is divine. It feels like a restaurant run by a group of passionate friends that care deeply about food and hospitality, who all got together to open a little place as a gift to the community, because that’s exactly what it is.

I would describe Owl as a bakery with Southern sensibilities and French technique. I’d put the lamination on their croissants up against anything in Stockholm. They’re known for their almond rose croissants, cardamom buns, and squirrel bread [a seed-and-nut loaf], and if you don’t get there right at 8 a.m. they’re going to be sold out. Sometimes I look at the people lining up, and I want to shake each and every one of them and yell, “Do you have any idea how good you have it right now?!” I actually have to resist doing that as I see them gabbing away over their morning pastries and lattes without a care in the world, not recognizing that the rest of us have to schlep around the world God knows how many times to find anything even close to this good in terms of quality and execution. And that’s just life in Asheville.

It’s an honorable mention, because I haven’t stepped foot in the restaurant for 17 years, but I get takeout from Rocky’s almost every Sunday, when I host a men’s group at my house where we discuss things like “How do you actually define electro music?” and play Crocodile, a weird Canadian board game. In the very crowded field of hot fried chicken, Rocky’s stands at the top, because their chicken is actually melt-your-face hot, not “oh-look-how-cute” Nashville hot. Beginners should get the medium. The hot is for veterans, and the extra hot is something the CIA should use to extract information. The crust is thin and it has the perfect amount of crunch, and the seasoning goes all the way through. But most importantly, every week we get the same order, and never once in 17 years have they messed up that order. I feel like a highly underrated aspect of a great restaurant is doing exactly the same thing 52 weeks out of the year, and I have mad respect for Rocky’s.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

Meherwan Irani, of Chai Pani and Spicewalla, shares his go-to places to eat and drink in his adopted hometown.

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

Part of what gives me so much joy about eating in Asheville is recognizing that we’re all part of a very integrated ecosystem. It feels like every restaurant I love is either run by an alum of one of the places I’ve been involved in, or by people that I’ve worked side by side with at hurricane-relief events, or by someone I know I’m going to see at the farmers market.

That’s what makes Asheville special. The folks that come in from out of town are lucky that there’s a virtuous cycle of talent here to keep the pipeline full. It’s so cool to see the evolution of this place, even if we locals don’t always realize how good we have it.It’s almost funny how not a big deal eating out here is. It’s so laid-back. We take it for granted that it’s going to be a great restaurant—of course it is! Having said that, the sheer range of restaurants is incredible. Given how small our town actually is, I sometimes find myself thinking, How lucky are we?

A hallmark of most of the restaurants I love is their connection to nearby farms. At my last count, there were more than a dozen farmers markets happening in Asheville, and there are probably more than twice as many local farms within an hour of here. Most people know the farmers by name, and nobody is precious about it. So when you go to a restaurant, they’ll just say, “It’s Evan’s greens tonight,” and everybody knows who Evan is.

The last thing is that whether it’s an Indian restaurant or a Filipino restaurant or Italian or Spanish, I love the Southern throughline in all of the dishes and hospitality here. That doesn’t mean there’s cornbread or okra in every dish; it’s honoring the fact that we all chose to open Indian or Italian restaurants here in Appalachia, so let’s not divorce the two from each other.

Let’s find a way to make it feel holistic. We do that really well. I was worried after the pandemic and Hurricane Helene that Asheville might not bounce back, but we have. I know that this place is going to continue to trailblaze for years to come.

20 Battery Park Avenue, Floor 1(828) 271-9808

Luminosa is hands down my wife, Molly, and my favorite date- night restaurant. It checks every box so beautifully. It’s intimate, but also a showstopper. It’s visually exciting to be in there, and yet [the design] doesn’t detract from the food, which they describe as “hyper-local Italian.” In the two years that they’ve been open, they’ve picked up a Michelin Green Star and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and they deserve it. Everything about it just feels very intentional. The food is brilliantly delicious and the menu changes a lot—which sometimes drives me crazy, but it works here, because I know there’s going to be something fun and new every time I go. Their style of service and hospitality is so old-fashioned it almost borders on being antiquated, but I love it. It’s a small town at the end of the day, and everybody touches your table.

One word: respect. Katie Button and her crew have been at the top of their game for so long, you almost forget that continuing to win the championship is really hard to do. But they execute at the exact same incredibly high level as they did the first time I walked in years ago. I go there because what they do is incredible, and it’s always good to be reminded of how well they represent the tapas side of Spanish cuisine. It’s also a really exciting restaurant to be in—there’s an energy and a vibe because of the open kitchen, and it feels so intimate and fun. It’s always packed—they’re a victim of their own success—but even if I’m just going in for a glass of sherry and a plate of jamón ibérico, it’s worth pulling whatever favors I must to get in.

701 Haywood Road, Suite 102(828) 552-3880

This is a true only-in-Asheville pick, a chest-swelling-with-pride kind of choice. The chef, Silver Iocovozzi, worked with me at [two of Irani’s erstwhile restaurants] MG Road and Buxton Hall, and now they get to showcase their own cuisine, Filipino. Neng Jr.’s feels like the kind of restaurant that this city is built for. It’s so tiny and so intimate, with maybe 12 seats, so you’re packed in and you really feel like you’re eating dinner at Silver’s house. The food feels so personal—it’s brilliant and fun and totally them, with flavor profiles that remind me of Indian street food in some ways, full of fermentation and funk.

First of all, this space was converted into a restaurant without doing much to disguise the fact that it used to be a house. You’re dining on the front porch or in the side yard or in the living room, but somehow it manages to make you feel like you’re in a small village in Provence. The food has a French focus, as well as an Americana element. They win all kinds of awards for their wine program, deservedly so. Leo’s is hard to describe. It feels like this rustic little bistro where you might order something as simple as a grilled cheese sandwich and tomato soup, but when it shows up, you realize this could actually be the best grilled cheese and tomato soup you’ve ever had in your life. It’s totally unique and transportive, and it’s become my go-to spontaneous dinner recommendation for friends visiting from out of town.

I’m going to throw it back a little to one of the first places that really popped in West Asheville. Ten or 15 years ago, The Admiral was essentially a dive bar in a cinder-block building next to a gas station where probably 80 percent of Asheville’s pot deals went down. There, a young chef named Elliot Moss [ed note: later Irani’s partner at Buxton Hall] was putting out gastropub food that was blowing people’s minds. After service, they’d push all the tables to the side to clear room for these legendary dance parties. Now the neighborhood isn’t as sketchy, Elliot is long gone, and they no longer push the tables aside, but the food has not lost an inch. When you’re eating, you can just feel that it’s world-class cuisine, and reservations are hard to get, so it still feels special to get to go to The Admiral.

The best way I can describe chef Matt Dawes’s food, or at least my experience of it, is that it’s elevated British pub cuisine with a French influence and a Southern twist. The menu swings from steak frites au poivre to the best shepherd’s pie you’ve ever had to a pitch-perfect Welsh rarebit (it’s also the first place I had Welsh rabbit). The restaurant is located maybe 30 feet from the railroad tracks, next to a dirt field and one of the noisiest outdoor breweries in Asheville, but don’t let that deter you. It’s one of the most reliable and satisfying restaurants in the city.

This is a newcomer to the scene. Chef Ashleigh Shanti Santi, a James Beard Award–winner and prominent Top Chef contestant, has been a passionate advocate for Black Southern foodways. Good Hot Fish is exactly what it sounds like: a fish counter with amazing hot fish sandwiches and seafood, plus the perfect sides. All of the fish she serves comes from local waterways. There’s fried catfish and Gulf shrimp burgers and fish dip with fried saltines. It’s literally just a counter with a few stools against the wall, but the technique is immaculate. The sandwiches are served on squishy white bread with buttermilk tartare sauce, and it delivers on its promise of being the best damn hot fish sandwich you’ve ever had.

I have to give a shout-out here to one of the OGs. To call All Souls just great pizza does it a disservice; you need to understand the backstory. David Bauer, was one of the first bread gurus/savants of Asheville. Farm and Sparrow, his bakery, helped usher in the modern renaissance of heirloom grains and bread that you now see everywhere. He grew his own grain, milled his own flour, and made these amazing breads. Then he helped open All Souls, which makes pizza using stone-ground heirloom grains, in a style I can only describe as Carolina pizza. It’s our own thing, with our own grains, cooked in a wood-fired oven with toppings that come from within 50 miles or so. It’s in a building that was a diner for decades in West Asheville, next to a big old field where you can spread out a picnic blanket if the restaurant is full. All Souls is a classic example of doing one thing, doing it well, and not being too uptight about it, which is everything I love about Asheville.

244 Short Coxe Avenue, #110(828) 505-1003

I have to include two bakeries here. Mother serves a full lunch and dinner menu, so it’s a little more on the restaurant side of things. It’s again in a weird part of Asheville, sandwiched between a sauna and a tire shop, with garage doors that open to a front patio that looks like a loading ramp for trucks. And yet, like so many places here, it’s totally transportive. You feel like you’re eating in Europe somehow. Their jambon-beurre sandwich is the closest I’ve had to Fauchon’s in Paris, and their pumpernickel bread is divine. It feels like a restaurant run by a group of passionate friends that care deeply about food and hospitality, who all got together to open a little place as a gift to the community, because that’s exactly what it is.

I would describe Owl as a bakery with Southern sensibilities and French technique. I’d put the lamination on their croissants up against anything in Stockholm. They’re known for their almond rose croissants, cardamom buns, and squirrel bread [a seed-and-nut loaf], and if you don’t get there right at 8 a.m. they’re going to be sold out. Sometimes I look at the people lining up, and I want to shake each and every one of them and yell, “Do you have any idea how good you have it right now?!” I actually have to resist doing that as I see them gabbing away over their morning pastries and lattes without a care in the world, not recognizing that the rest of us have to schlep around the world God knows how many times to find anything even close to this good in terms of quality and execution. And that’s just life in Asheville.

It’s an honorable mention, because I haven’t stepped foot in the restaurant for 17 years, but I get takeout from Rocky’s almost every Sunday, when I host a men’s group at my house where we discuss things like “How do you actually define electro music?” and play Crocodile, a weird Canadian board game. In the very crowded field of hot fried chicken, Rocky’s stands at the top, because their chicken is actually melt-your-face hot, not “oh-look-how-cute” Nashville hot. Beginners should get the medium. The hot is for veterans, and the extra hot is something the CIA should use to extract information. The crust is thin and it has the perfect amount of crunch, and the seasoning goes all the way through. But most importantly, every week we get the same order, and never once in 17 years have they messed up that order. I feel like a highly underrated aspect of a great restaurant is doing exactly the same thing 52 weeks out of the year, and I have mad respect for Rocky’s.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

#6613. Nostalgia Alert! 10 Decor Pieces That Bring Back the Magic of a ’90s Christmas

The '90s are back! From kitschy collectibles to vintage-style Christmas trees, we found the best decor pieces to help you relive this beloved era.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

As a child of the ’90s and lover of all things Christmas, I never really warmed to the minimalist, beige Christmas aesthetic. My childhood was filled with bright colors, big jolly Santas and plenty of tinsel. Now, that’s not to say modern decor isn’t lovely. The latest My Christmas House collection, for instance, is swoon-worthy. But my heart belongs to the colorful, often mismatched decor of Christmases past.

Much to my delight, the ’90s are coming back in all of their hokey glory. And now, it is my absolute pleasure to present you with 10 decor pieces that will transform your home into a ’90s Christmas wonderland.

The ’90s were a time of bold colors and patterns, big lights and collectibles galore. Burgundy, hunter green and gold were the colors of choice, and pops of sparkly silver tinsel adorned many a Christmas tree. Christmas villages sat nestled in fake snow atop mantles or credenzas while animated Santas stood in windows waving their candles. Blow molds adorned porches and homeowners scoured local stores in hopes of snagging a set of popular icicle lights.

Today’s 90s-inspired Christmas decor includes all of the above.  The items on our list are colorful, cheerful and bound to get you in the Christmas spirit.

This Vintage Pine Prelit Christmas tree screams ’90s. When she first saw this tree, tester Nancy Snyder was reminded of her own childhood decor. “Part of what makes the holidays so special is revisiting the traditions we loved as kids,” she writes in her full review. “If you’ve been looking for a tree that brings back the magic of childhood holidays, this one is worth a look.”

A holiday porch goose is sure to delight every visitor who comes over this holiday season. Deputy shopping editor Katie Bandurski dresses up her Porch Goose all year long, but the holidays are especially fun. “For Christmas, there are a bevy of fun costumes for your gaggle to choose from. Think—Santa and Mrs. Claus, a gingerbread man and even a penguin,” she writes in her holiday goose roundup.

I was gifted this Little Debbie Christmas Tree at our annual Christmas party last year and it was an instant favorite. This blow mold stands 22-inches tall and emits a warm glow when plugged in. Looking for something a bit more classic? Try this nostalgic snowman blow mold instead.

When I was a kid, this lighted ceramic Christmas tree was a staple in every home I visited. Now, I have one of my own. I opted for an 18-inch green tree, but there are three sizes and a variety of colors to choose from.

Trim up the tree with Old World Christmas. The brand, which is known for its hand-painted, blown glass Christmas ornaments, has an impressive selection of retro and vintage-style ornaments that will brighten up your room. Choose from fun designs like this I Love The 90s cassette tape ornament or VHS tape. If you prefer a more classic look, opt for a red peppermint reflection ornament and  retro tree top.

We were thrilled by the return of the nostalgic Lenox Spice Village but we are absolutely in love with the brand’s Mistletoe Park Village collection. This collection features charming figurines so you can create the ultimate Christmas village. Each figurine features the brand’s signature creamy porcelain exterior and 24k gold accents. Most of the larger buildings light up to really bring your village to life.

Put this animated Santa by your tree for a holly jolly Christmas. He climbs up and down his 42-inch ladder with a string of brightly colored Christmas lights. Rather than toys, his sack holds a speaker which plays 15 different Christmas carols.

Rifle Paper Co. makes some of the best throw blankets we’ve tested. We especially love this Beary Christmas blanket, which is made of 100% cotton and features an array of nostalgic teddy bears dressed in their cozy best.

Hang these needlepoint stockings by the chimney with care. Each stocking is made of 100% cotton with polyester batting and measures 9-inches wide and 19.5-inches long. That means there’s plenty of room for stocking stuffers! Better still, these stockings can be personalized for each member of your family.

A proposed shift in recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination in the U.S. could leave millions of young adults unprotected, a new modeling study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A proposed change to decades-old guidance on hepatitis B vaccination would lead to a dramatic increase in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections among young people, a new modeling study predicts.

Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advised ending this recommendation, and the CDC accepted that advice.

The new guidance would recommend birth doses only to babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV or whose HBV status was unknown. The guidance suggests that mothers who test negative should instead ask their doctors about whether their child needs a birth dose — an approach the CDC calls "shared clinical decision-making." The new recommendation states that babies who forgo the birth dose should be at least 2 months old before starting the HBV vaccine series.

Health experts widely criticized the proposed change when it was announced, and for the moment, its implementation has been put on pause by legal action. The modeling study, published Oct. 19 in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, predicts what would happen if it came to pass.

"Overall, this modeling study has many strengths and I think presents an accurate projection of how the vaccine recommendations may impact future chronic HBV in the U.S.," Dr. Norah Terrault, a transplant hepatologist at the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine who wasn't involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

When caught in infancy or early childhood, over 90% of HBV infections become chronic. About 15% to 25% of people with chronic HBV go on to develop liver scarring (cirrhosis), a form of liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma, or another chronic liver disease. So, an uptick in chronic HBV infections would translate to an uptick in these harmful liver conditions.

"Not every pregnant person is tested for hepatitis B," said study co-author Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-diseases physician-investigator at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. For those who are tested, there's a chance their results are inaccurate or that they're not provided the right care after testing positive. "Something can be missed at any step in the care process, so the vaccine dose at birth provides protection," he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Mohareb and his colleagues built a simulation model using published data, including the current prevalence of HBV and the screening rate among pregnant people. The team also factored in the HBV test's sensitivity, the share of children who are fully vaccinated by age 2, and the risk of developing chronic HBV infection in different age groups. They made estimates of how often children are exposed to the virus through contact with infected household or community members.

HBV is "very, very transmissible," Mohareb said. It can spread from mother to child at birth or through exposure to tiny amounts of bodily fluids, like blood from a scratch, after birth. So, even if a baby does not get HBV from their mother, if they are unvaccinated, they can still get from another family member or from other children.

Infants and young children have a greater risk of their HBV infections becoming chronic than people infected in adulthood.

With this data, the researchers tested what would happen if vaccination were postponed to 2 months of age for babies whose mothers tested negative. Among babies born in 2026, 19% more would have chronic HBV infections by age 20, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination, they found.

In this scenario, the babies would still start the HBV vaccine series, albeit two months later than usual. However, the CDC's proposed recommendation offers more wiggle room; it says that parents should consult with their children's doctors to "decide when or if their child will begin the hepatitis B vaccine series" at all.

The researchers ran a stimulation to compare these two scenarios: one where kids get their first shot two months late and one intended to capture this looser "shared clinical decision-making" scenario.

"Other vaccines whose recommendations employ similar language had uptake as low as 25%," Mohareb noted. This aspect of their modeling has some uncertainty, he emphasized, since it's unknown exactly how the public will respond to such loosening of the guidance.

The researchers assumed that about 87% of kids would complete the vaccine series by age 2 under the deferred strategy, while only 50% would under the shared decision-making strategy. That 50% coverage, in turn, would increase chronic HBV infections acquired by age 20 by 83%, and about 50% and 70% of those born under that guidance would be susceptible to HBV infection at age 20.

That's about 1.8 million people in this age group per year, compared with fewer than 250,000 under universal birth-dose vaccination. "This represents a population that is at risk for acquiring HBV via sex, drug use etc — behaviors more prevalent among young adults," Terrault said.

To test the robustness of the findings, Mohareb's team varied the most uncertain inputs across wide ranges and ran the model 1,000 times. In every simulation, the birth-dose strategy led to fewer chronic infections than either alternative.

These conclusions seem "robust" because "they are the same conclusions no matter how we change the numbers of the model," Mohereb noted. Though of course "the specific magnitude of change depends on how many people defer vaccination," he said.

The new study does not specifically show how many additional cases of liver disease or cancer would result from the uptick in HBV infections. But Terrault said that the risks of liver failure, cirrhosis and liver cancer "would be anticipated to increase due to the missed opportunity to protect against infection."

Mohareb stressed that he is in no way opposed to the principle of shared decision-making between doctors and patients. "They should always make the decision together," he said. "But we rely on our public health agencies not to tell us that we should be making decisions with the patient, but rather to tell us what policy would make us healthier as a country."

Childhood HBV infections in the U.S. dropped from more than 25,000 cases a year in 1985 to fewer than 100 reported cases in 2024. This steep decline is credited to HBV screening during pregnancy, antibody treatment for babies born to HBV-positive mothers and universal birth-dose vaccination.

"Certainly without following a universal dose vaccination recommendation there would be a lot more hep B infections early in life," Dr. Brian McMahon, a hepatologist and the director of the Liver Disease and Hepatitis Program at the Alaska Native Medical Center, told Live Science in an email.

Projected effect of 2026 federal changes to the childhood immunization schedule on chronic hepatitis B virus infections in the United States. #6611. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6610. Popeye’s Is Bringing Back This Side Dish for the First Time Since the ’90s

Popeyes is bringing back a nostalgic side dish on Nov. 2, and fans will have plenty to celebrate.

There are two kinds of people in this world: those who go to Popeyes for the chicken and those who will make a special visit just to eat the Cajun fries. Personally, I’m in the second camp. Granted, I have nothing against Popeyes chicken! But the Cajun fries are so deliciously seasoned and perfectly crispy that sometimes I will drive-thru and get them as a snack.

And if you’re also a fan of Popeyes’ side dishes, I have some particularly good news. The Louisiana chicken chain is reaching into its menu archives to bring back a nostalgic favorite that hasn’t been widely available since the ’90s. Let’s just say your next Popeyes order might look a little different!

Popeyes has a long history of serving up more than just fried chicken. When the chain first opened in 1976, its menu featured everything from fried clams to chicken liver. Among those early offerings was a beloved side that eventually disappeared from menus in most markets. But it’s about to make its triumphant return because Popeyes is bringing back Cajun Onion Rings!

The hand-sliced, hand-battered onion rings were slathered with Cajun seasoning. With a distinctive crispy bite, they became a fan favorite almost immediately. In fact, I have family members who constantly compare other fast-food onion ring offerings to the Popeyes version they remember from childhood. In their memories, the Popeyes onion rings were always better!

But the onion rings slowly disappeared from menus. Some locations served them until the 1990s, but by then it was mostly a thing of the past. Now, nearly three decades later, the side dish is finally making its way back.

Onion rings are officially back on the Popeyes lineup now. Availability may vary by location, but this is when you should expect to see them on menus at your local Popeyes.

Priced at $3.99, the Cajun Onion Rings are designed for sharing, although I certainly wouldn’t blame anyone for keeping the whole order to themselves. After all, crispy onion rings are pretty hard to resist. I might even order the onion rings and fries and mix ’em together.

Will you be ordering the new Cajun Onion Rings? Let us know in the comments below!

#6609. 5 Cookbooks That Go Deep on a Single Ingredient

If you’ve ever been starstruck by a perfect Cinderella pumpkin or a stately stalk of Brussels sprouts, you likely understand the appeal of a book focused on a single fruit or vegetable. While books like this aren’t always long, they typically go deep, with the fervor of an author who is fully obsessed.

One charming example, The Core of an Onion: Peeling the Rarest Common Food by Mark Kurlansky, melds authority with a dose of irreverence. First published in 2023, it’s a slim 200 pages, but the writer (who’s also written nonfiction books dedicated to oysters, salt, and cod) packs a lot in. “Onions have a way of taking on unexpected significance,” he posits. The first section covers the allium’s history and cultural impact. (Did you know that ancient Egyptians tied them to mummies’ feet as a preservative?) Kurlansky then offers loosely structured recipes for breads, sauces, and more, all centering the humble bulb.

Elevating a perhaps overlooked ingredient is a core tenet of single-­subject cookbookery. In The Compleat Squash: A Passionate Grower’s Guide to Pumpkins, Squash, and Gourds, a canonical 2004 ode to members of the Cucurbitaceae ­family, master ­gardener Amy Goldman Fowler’s passion is abundantly evident. “Sometimes I don’t know where pumpkins begin and I end,” she writes, before segueing into a series of squash and gourd portraits, each showing an individual specimen more striking than the last. Fowler shares recipes too, in addition to breed spotlights, resources for seed ­buying, and advice on growing your own.

Some such tomes aim to introduce the reader to the joys of less ubiquitous ingredients. Lane Selman and Margarett Waterbury’s Radicchio: A Celebration of the Beloved Italian Vegetable tells the “human and natural history” of the bitter chicory, along with instructions for how to grow it and cook with it. Selman is the founder of the Culinary Breeding Network, an initiative that rallies scientists, farmers, and chefs to geek out over new produce varieties. The book gets weird in the best way possible, with profiles of Italian growers and recipes including gnocchi with radicchio pesto, radicchio with prosciutto ­gratin, and chocolate–radicchio cake (why not?).

Radicchio reads almost like a community cookbook, and that’s intentional. Selman’s inspiration to pursue the topic was the sheer lack of writing on this oddball vegetable: “All of these people that we’ve met on our way down the rabbit hole needed to be included,” she says. “They’re the ones who have given us all this information. Sometimes it takes a village.”

Other single-subject cookbooks showcase pantry ­staples that are rarely in the spotlight. Anna Hezel’s Little Book of Olives: A Guide to Cooking, Eating, and Drinking for the Brine-Inclined presents recipes including cantaloupe and crushed-olive panzanella, Castelvetrano and pistachio pesto, and a whole chapter of olive desserts, plus shopping tips and a breakdown of varieties. The book’s retro aesthetic lends ­gravitas to an ingredient often relegated to garnish status.

Finally, some books exist more to dazzle than to inform, as is the case with pop artist Ed Ruscha and River Café chef Ruthie Rogers’s 2025 release Squeeze Me: Lemon Recipes & Art. In the pair’s high-gloss love letter to the lemon, pop art–coded photos with cheeky captions and a suite of minimalist recipes—such as lemon–­mascarpone tart and limoncello—make this ode to the simple citrus equally at home on a coffee table or the kitchen shelf.

While styles and forms vary, these books serve a ­common goal: to illuminate the sometimes surprising pleasures of a particular fruit or vegetable. That they manage to do so in such delightful fashion is proof that, once in a while, ­working with less really is more.

These laser-focused titles geek out on radicchio, lemons, olives, and more.

If you’ve ever been starstruck by a perfect Cinderella pumpkin or a stately stalk of Brussels sprouts, you likely understand the appeal of a book focused on a single fruit or vegetable. While books like this aren’t always long, they typically go deep, with the fervor of an author who is fully obsessed.

One charming example, The Core of an Onion: Peeling the Rarest Common Food by Mark Kurlansky, melds authority with a dose of irreverence. First published in 2023, it’s a slim 200 pages, but the writer (who’s also written nonfiction books dedicated to oysters, salt, and cod) packs a lot in. “Onions have a way of taking on unexpected significance,” he posits. The first section covers the allium’s history and cultural impact. (Did you know that ancient Egyptians tied them to mummies’ feet as a preservative?) Kurlansky then offers loosely structured recipes for breads, sauces, and more, all centering the humble bulb.

Elevating a perhaps overlooked ingredient is a core tenet of single-­subject cookbookery. In The Compleat Squash: A Passionate Grower’s Guide to Pumpkins, Squash, and Gourds, a canonical 2004 ode to members of the Cucurbitaceae ­family, master ­gardener Amy Goldman Fowler’s passion is abundantly evident. “Sometimes I don’t know where pumpkins begin and I end,” she writes, before segueing into a series of squash and gourd portraits, each showing an individual specimen more striking than the last. #6608. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6607. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6606. Butterball Made a Tiny Turkey That Assigns Thanksgiving Chores—And It’s Free

Turkey, stuffing and a little accountability are on the menu this year.

There’s always that one Thanksgiving guest who says, “Just tell me what to do!” while somehow managing to avoid doing anything. Well, Butterball has a tiny turkey for that.

On Monday, Nov. 2, the turkey brand took to Instagram to introduce the Butterball Buddy, a tiny electronic taskmaster that hands out Thanksgiving chores so the host doesn’t have to. It looks like something straight out of the ’90s, and the best part? It won’t cost you a dime.

As silly as a chore-assigning turkey sounds, the company might be onto something. Its 2026 Togetherness Report found that 85% of Thanksgiving hosts would prefer guests to offer to help, but only 38% ask. Nearly half say the final cleanup is where they could use an extra hand.

Once everyone arrives, guests pass the Buddy around like a hot potato. When it chimes and vibrates, whoever’s holding it gets a task, whether that’s setting the table before dinner or tackling the dishes afterward. Finish the job, pass it along, and it’s the next lucky helper’s turn. Think Tamagotchi, except instead of keeping a digital pet alive, you’re keeping the kitchen from turning into a disaster area.

Set an alarm. The first batch dropped Nov. 2, and two more are coming at 1 p.m. ET on Monday, Nov. 9, and Monday, Nov. 16, at ButterballBuddy.com. Quantities are limited, so the early birds get the turkey. The giveaway is open to legal U.S. residents ages 18 and older, and no purchase is necessary.

The Buddies may be in short supply, but Butterball’s cooking advice isn’t. Its Turkey Talk-Line is celebrating its 45th anniversary this year, with more than 50 experts answering questions about everything from thawing to checking for doneness through Dec. 24. You can call 1-800-BUTTERBALL, text 844-877-3456 or chat live at Butterball.com. The hotline’s contact information is printed on the back of every Buddy, too.

Who would you hand the Butterball Buddy to first? Let us know in the comments below!

#6605. Baltimore Yat Gaw Mein

Yat gaw mein, also known as Baltimore yak or dirty yak, is Baltimore carryout comfort food at its finest. A Chinese American remix of Beijing’s zha jiang mian, the dish dates back to the late 19th century, when Chinese immigrants started settling in the city. Setting up shop in traditionally Black and working-class neighborhoods, Chinese cooks adapted their recipes to locally available ingredients, swapping fermented pastes for a simpler, soy-based gravy. Over time, something new emerged: savory wheat noodles, stir-fried with shrimp, beef, and vegetables and punctuated with a hard-boiled egg. Today you can find the beloved dish at counter spots around town like Jimmy’s Carryout, Danny’s, and Pimlico Chinese Carry Out.

In this at-home version from Steve Chu, the chef behind Baltimore’s Ekiben, smoky wok-charred noodles are tossed with umami-packed soy sauce and oyster sauce, rich fat, and sweet caramelized onions. What makes the dish “dirty” is the flavor that develops when soy sauce, sugar, and aromatics scorch against the hot metal of the wok, creating deep savory notes balanced by subtle sweetness. Be sure to keep the wok on high heat and stir frequently, since this allows the wok hei—which translates to “the breath of a wok” and refers to that elusive smokiness—to work its magic. The finishing squeeze of ketchup might sound unusual, but it delivers the acidic punch that makes the dish complete.

Scientists sequenced the genome of a woman who lived 30,000 years ago and discovered that she had mixed Eastern and Western European ancestry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have sequenced the genomes of three Late Stone Age people who lived in Europe 30,000 years ago and discovered that they had closer biological ties than researchers previously thought. The new finding suggests that places like southwestern France may have been critical cultural hubs during the last ice age.

Shortly after Neanderthals disappeared from Europe, a Stone Age culture known as the Gravettian spread across the continent. Artifacts found during archaeological excavations ‪—‬ including portable art, such as "Venus figurines" ‪—‬ have shown that the Gravettian culture lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. But ancient DNA has been recovered from only two dozen human skeletons from the Gravettian period, so questions about these people's ancestry remain unanswered.

Based on the small number of genomes from Gravettian people that were previously sequenced, experts believed that groups in Western Europe were largely separate from groups in Eastern Europe. But in a study published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Advances, researchers sequenced the genomes of three people who lived in what are now Spain, France and Italy during the Gravettian period. They discovered that one person had mixed genetic ancestry that revealed East-West exchange at least 30,000 years ago.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," study first author Pere Gelabert, an evolutionary anthropologist at the University of Vienna, said in a statement.

The new information about mixed ancestry comes from a woman who died around 30,000 years ago and whose bones were found in Isturitz Cave in southwestern France. Originally used by Neanderthals, Isturitz Cave was occupied off and on from about 80,000 to 10,000 years ago. Cups made out of human skulls dated to roughly 15,000 to 12,000 years ago have also been found in Isturitz Cave.

Researchers found that the DNA from the Gravettian woman in Isturitz Cave was most similar to the previously known Western European genomes, but with an intriguing connection to Eastern and Central European groups.

This discovery of gene flow from the East is uncommon for the Late Stone Age, also known as the Upper Paleolithic, the researchers wrote in the study. It "could be explained by movements of people from Eastern Europe during the Gravettian period, which eventually contributed to this ancestry in Isturitz." Specifically, the researchers dated this "pulse" of gene flow to about 31,500 to 32,500 years ago.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The DNA evidence supports the archaeological theory that Isturitz Cave was an important cultural and biological hub for tens of thousands of years during the Late Stone Age, as the cave was located at a critical passage between continental Europe and the Iberian Peninsula, the researchers wrote.

All three newly sequenced Gravettian genomes revealed close biological connections to Western European groups, as well as genetic traits suggesting they had dark skin, dark hair and dark eyes. What's more, all of them had parents who weren't closely related to each other, suggesting that those populations may have actively avoided inbreeding.

"Overall, our results suggest that population structure and gene flow in western Europe during the Gravettian were more complex and dynamic than previously assumed," the researchers wrote.

Gelabert, P., Sawyer, S., Villalba-Mouco, V., Cheronet, O., Oberreiter, V., Gárate, D., Normand, C., Straus, L. G., González Morales, M. R., Gutiérrez-Zugasti, I., Cuenca-Solana, D., Darricau, J., de Lumley, H., Tejero, J.-M., Stahlschmidt, M., Higham, T., Giannì, M., van der Sluis, L. G., Gómez-Montes, C., … Pinhasi, R. (2026). Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM. Science Advances, 12(43). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6603. Ditch Your Fleet of Coffeemakers—The Chefman Coffee Station Pro Handles Everything

Can't decide between a drip coffee maker, Nespresso, Keurig or an espresso machine? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro does all four—and takes up very little room.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

As Kevin Malone famously said in Season 8, Episode 2 of The Office, “Why waste time say lot word when few word do trick?” In my opinion, the same concept should apply to countertop appliances. After ditching my microwave, countertop oven, air fryer and toaster for the all-encompassing Panasonic HomeChef, I began to wonder what else I could condense into a singular appliance.

After musing over my fleet of five(!!!) coffeemakers consisting of Keurig and Nespresso machines, an automatic espresso maker, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker, I realized that it was time to address the barista elephant in the room. I had to reclaim my coffee bar counter space—but how? The answer, it turns out, is the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Here’s how I tested it over several months and why it’s become my go-to coffee machine.

Can't decide on a brew method? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro tackles them all. Yes, really.

In the age of the all-in-one appliance, maximizing countertop space just makes sense. In small kitchens especially, cramming half a dozen different-yet-similar appliances into limited space feels like such a waste. And sure, you don’t need both a blender and a food processor, but it’s nice to have the choice between the two. That’s why combo machines like the Ninja CrushBoss came out and started changing the game. That’s also the idea behind the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Unlike other x-in-one machines that incorporate a couple of different brewing methods (looking at you, Keurig K-Duo), the Chefman Coffee Station Pro combines 10 different functionalities into one machine. Craving a quick single cup? You can use it with both K-cups and Nespresso pods. Need to fill up a full carafe for a party? It does that, too. But what if you want to leisurely enjoy an iced latte or a shot of espresso on the weekend? Well, that’s also an option with the built-in manual espresso machine and automatic milk frother.

In terms of functionality, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro offers espresso, cappuccino, latte, single-serve coffee, 12-cup carafe, cold brew, cold-pressed espresso, coffee over ice, hot milk and cold foam. To try it out, I packed up all my other coffee makers and made it my primary coffee machine for two months.

You’d probably expect a machine with so many capabilities to be enormous, heavy, complicated, unwieldily. Not so with the Coffee Station Pro. It’s so simple to set up and use, I didn’t even need to read through the provided booklet before I was whipping up drinks. It also takes up barely more space than a dedicated espresso machine.

Right off the bat, I brewed a pot of drip coffee. First, I’m super impressed with the way the machine can read what I’m brewing based on the basket insert I choose. Pop in the drip basket, and it’s prompting me to choose the number of cups. Swap it out with the K-Cup pod holder, and it’s now asking how many ounces I’d like. It’s truly like magic!

Then, there’s the customization. First, pick between a single cup or a whole carafe. Then, choose to enjoy your coffee either hot or over ice. You also get the option of brewing a cup or a whole pot of cold brew for summertime get-togethers. There’s even a delay brew function, which makes it easy to prep your poison of choice the night before.

As I mentioned, the machine changes its touchscreen prompts based on which brew basket you choose. When you pop in a K-cup, you’re given the option of having it hot or over ice. There’s also a choice of 4-, 6-, 8-, 10- and 12-ounce cups. Then, you can adjust the strength and temperature, with three different settings for each. Finally, there’s a small flip-down platform to rest your cup on so that it doesn’t splash everywhere as it brews.

Want to use a Nespresso capsule instead? A pod insert pops into the K-cup adapter. Again, the machine will intuit this automatically and adjust accordingly. Overall, this aspect of the machine is incredibly intuitive. Plus, you can save specific settings as one of three “favorites,” if you want to speed things up with one-touch operation.

As for espressos, this thing does work. It boasts a 20-bar pressure system that brews espressos topped in a beautiful, silky crema. Pick from a single or double shot, or opt for a cappuccino or latte, both with a choice of single or double. If you choose a milk-based drink, ensure the milk reservoir is filled and angle the metal wand into your cup—the machine does the rest.

If you’re familiar with a standard manual espresso machine, you already know how to operate the portafilter. If not, no worries—there are helpful videos from Chefman to guide you through the process. You can also opt for hot milk, or warm or cold foam on its own by choosing the “froth” setting if you want to add any of those to your cup of regular coffee.

On the top of the machine next to the brew basket is an area with accessory storage for the portafilter baskets, Nespresso adapter and combination scoop/tamper. On the side of the coffee station is a place to stow the portafilter. While there’s no built-in storage for the brew basket, K-cup basket and carafe when they’re not in use, I do love that the smaller accessories have a dedicated space so they won’t be misplaced.

In terms of cleaning, this might be one of the easier machines I’ve ever used. All of the inserts simply rinse clean. But the part I really love is the milk frother. Instead of nooks and crannies that collect smells and residue, the entire thing comes apart into several pieces, so you can thoroughly rinse and wash every single part that touches milk. Win!

Chefman isn’t the only brand to claim that they’ve created an “all-in-one” solution for flexible baristas. In our research, we also found three other similar machines: The De’Longhi All-in-One, the Ninja Prestige Dual Brew Coffee Maker and, of course, the classic  Keurig K-Duo.

The only issue? We couldn’t find a single other appliance that offered K-Cup compatibility and Nespresso pod capability and a carafe and a manual espresso machine and automated milk frothing/latte settings. All of the options above offer at least two functions. Maybe four. But not all five. That crown belongs to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro alone.

Hopefully, we see more options pop up in the near future. But for now, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro is in its own category of coffee maker.

In my home, I used to have five different coffeemakers, including a Keurig, a Nespresso, an automatic espresso machine, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker. In fact, there were so many appliances that they began spilling into my dining room after I ran out of space on my dedicated coffee bar. After converting to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro, I’ve pared that number down to just one. One!

The only changes I’d make after using this machine since August 2026 are minor gripes. I do wish that there was a built-in coffee grinder, since having a separate bean grinder means having yet another appliance. And while I appreciate that there is a small storage cavity for tinier accessories, I don’t love having to find a place in my cupboard for the carafe and basket inserts when I’m not using them.

But honestly? Even with these small annoyances, I wouldn’t even knock off a full star on my final rating. The size, ease of use and cleanliness of the machine make it more than worth it—especially for flexible home baristas like me.

Condense five coffeemakers into just one with this ingenious appliance.

Want to clear up your counter space and join me in the future? You can snag this new appliance on the Chefman website or on Amazon. At $400, the Coffee Station Pro is absolutely an investment. And for some folks who won’t use all the different settings, it may not be worth the cost. But for coffee lovers who want to brew based on vibes (or who already have a long lineup of machines like I used to), the price point feels totally fair. After all, you’re getting five different machines in one!

The easier question is what can’t it make? It’s capable of espresso, single-serve coffee, a 12-cup carafe, cold brew and coffee over ice. While it’s not programmable to make specific drinks such as a cafe crema or Americano like some automatic espresso machines, the manual espresso component and automatic milk frother still offers extreme flexibility for budding baristas.

As Taste of Home’s shopping editor, Emily has covered everything from Pioneer Woman kitchen launches to finding the best pizza ovens. She also has four years of experience in shopping editor roles at Reader’s Digest, Taste of Home and Family Handyman. Her specialties lie in food and drink categories, as well as appliance testing and deal sourcing. #6602. These Prosciutto di Parma and Grana Padano Recipes Deserve a Spot on Your Holiday Table

Preparing a memorable holiday meal doesn’t mean that things need to be complicated; simplicity can often be the best route to success. It’s easy to get hung up on overcomplicated techniques, expensive and hard-to-source ingredients, and combinations of flavors that sometimes require a leap of faith.When we cook for our friends and families, the dishes we return to time and again tend to have a few things in common: They make the most of what you have on hand, and they rely on the best ingredients possible. We’d much rather have a small amount of something exceptional than a large quantity of a substitute that just doesn’t measure up. Grana Padano PDO and Prosciutto di Parma PDO are two such ingredients, made according to generations-old traditions and held to strict production standards.Both are protected by the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO), which guarantees that each is produced in its designated region of Italy using time-tested methods. Grana Padano is aged for at least nine months to develop its mellow, nutty flavor and granular texture, while Prosciutto di Parma is cured for a minimum of 400 days and made with just pork and sea salt. Their quality and versatility make them just as useful for everyday cooking as for a more celebratory meal.

For your next big gathering, these six recipes from our archive show just how much you can do with a few good ingredients.

Celery root adds an earthy sweetness to these mashed potatoes, which are whipped with butter, half-and-half, and Grana Padano until smooth and creamy. A generous amount of the aged Italian cheese gives the mash a salted, savory depth that makes it the perfect cozy side dish on an autumn table or as part of a holiday feast. Get the recipe >

Inspired by panisse, the famous Provençal chickpea fritters, these crisp polenta fries are enriched with butter and Grana Padano, then fried until golden and crunchy. The creamy roasted garlic dipping sauce gets a touch of heat from chipotle peppers and hot sauce, providing the perfect pairing for the rich, crispy polenta. Get the recipe >

Thinly sliced raw kale gets a bright, savory treatment in this simple salad. Grana Padano lends creamy depth, while fresh lemon juice and dried currants bring acidity and sweetness to balance the slightly bitter greens. Allowing the salad to rest briefly softens the kale and encourages the flavors to meld. Get the recipe >

Cloaked in a creamy buttermilk sauce brightened with lemon, this pasta gets a salty, savory note from thinly sliced Prosciutto di Parma folded in just before serving. Grana Padano lends a nutty finish, while poppy seeds cooked in butter bring an aromatic, toasty quality. Get the recipe >

Peas are gently simmered in a broth seasoned with olive oil, garlic, parsley, and small pieces of Prosciutto di Parma, allowing the ham to season the liquid as it cooks. A touch of sugar brings out the peas’ natural sweetness, while the prosciutto’s salty character balances the dish, making for a simple, deeply flavorful side. Get the recipe >

Garlicky sautéed escarole is layered with two kinds of Prosciutto di Parma: chopped pieces that cook with the greens, and thin strips that are fried until crisp, adding texture and crunch. Chile flakes and lemon juice round everything out, balancing the ham’s saltiness with heat and acidity. Get the recipe >

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Grana Padano PDO and Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

#6601. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6600. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6599. This Olive Oil Discovery Set is a Surprisingly Thoughtful Gift for Foodies

This highly versatile olive oil gift set includes five distinct flavors meant to spark home cooks' imaginations.

If you’re shopping for a true foodie, nothing can top a gourmet gift basket. But if you go that route, you have to do your research. After all, not all food gifts are the same. The last thing you want to do is send your epicurean friend or family member yet another disappointing fruit basket or a block of shelf-stable, gummy cheese!

Instead, for something ready-to-eat, opt for beloved foods with an established fanbase—perhaps one of the editor-loved finds on Goldbelly. Or, if you want to really impress them, high-quality ingredients are sure to inspire their culinary creativity. That’s why my go-to food gift is an olive oil gift set from Enzo’s Table.

The Signature Selection gift set offers a diverse lineup of flavors to impress your favorite foodies.

Folks at Enzo’s Table have been farming their vineyard in California’s fertile San Joaquin Valley for nearly a century. This gives their gourmand products a farm-to-table feel that’s backed by decades of know-how. In fact, over the years, the brand has proudly received over 200 awards for its signature olive oils, jams and biscotti!

The Signature Selection olive oil gift set is a fleet consisting of four of Enzo’s famous olive oils, plus their signature balsamic vinegar. All five 100ml bottles are organic, having been produced in the San Joaquin Valley vineyard. The gift set contains the following:

The Delicate EVOO offers a buttery flavor and incredibly mild yet peppery finish, making it a perfectly smooth pick for dipping bread or incorporating into salad dressings. I love using it for roasting wintery vegetables and crafting homemade tomato sauce for spaghetti, since it doesn’t overpower acidic or umami flavors found in fresh tomatoes and mushrooms.

Enzo’s Bold EVOO is best for imparting lasting flavor. I love it for roasted meats in particular, like the rotisserie chicken my husband makes on his grill. It leaves quite the impression with its peppery, spicy profile, especially on milder meats like chicken breast.

The Clementine Crush EVOO is probably my favorite of the five. This one goes well in salad dressings, cakes—anything that benefits from a fruity, acidic punch. Because it’s milled with fresh organic California mandarins, it’s a good EVOO to add a little brightness to dishes. Personally, it’s also my favorite option for delicate fish and sautéing shrimp.

Enzo’s Basil Crush EVOO is, as you’d expect, herby and earthy. It’s another option that’s particularly good for roasts, especially red meats. I also love adding a splash on caprese salad.

The Traditional Balsamic Vinegar is incredibly versatile in all the ways you love to see with balsamic. Because it’s crafted from sweet, organic Lambrusco and Trebbiano grapes, it shines brightest on summery dishes like grilled fruits and balsamic Brussels sprouts. I’ve tried a lot of balsamic over the years, and this one might be the thickest, richest blend I’ve enjoyed.

Delight your favorite foodie with a full fleet of flavors when you gift them an Enzo Olive Oil gift set!

Folks seeking the perfect gift for foodies can’t go wrong with the highly versatile Signature Selection gift set. With so many unique flavors inside and generous portions of each offering, it’s a wonderfully simple way to spark inspiration in the kitchen!

If your recipient finds any fast favorites while they work through their discovery set, another great gift idea is one of their olive oil subscriptions. This is also a good way to save on Enzo olive oil if you’re a big fan yourself.
